entries.en: He studied the Stone Drum Inscriptions, Li Si's Mount Yi and Mount Tai inscriptions, the Han Kaimu stone que, the Dunhuang prefect stele, Wu Su Jian's Guoshan stele, Huang Xiang's Tianfa Shenchen stele, and Tang Li Yangbing's City God Temple stele and Record of the Three Tombs—making a hundred copies of each.
entries.literal: He loved the Stone Drum Inscriptions, Li Si's Mount Yi stele and Mount Tai inscription, the Han Kaimu stone que, the Dunhuang prefect stele, Wu Su Jian's Guoshan stele, the Huangxiang Tianfa Shenchen stele, and Tang Li Yangbing's City God Temple stele and Record of the Three Tombs—of each kind he made a hundred copies.

entries.zh: 又苦篆體不備，寫說文解字二十本。
entries.en: Finding seal forms still incomplete, he copied out the Shuowen Jiezi twenty times.
entries.literal: He also grieved that seal forms were incomplete and wrote out twenty copies of the Shuowen Jiezi.

entries.zh: 帝搜三代鐘鼎，秦、漢瓦當、碑額。
entries.en: The Qianlong Emperor was then gathering bells and tripods of the Three Dynasties along with Qin and Han tile-ends and stele crowns.
entries.literal: The emperor searched out bells and tripods of the Three Dynasties and Qin-Han tile-ends and stele crowns.

entries.zh: 五年，篆書成。
entries.en: After five years he had mastered seal script.
entries.literal: After five years his seal script was accomplished.

entries.zh: 乃學漢分，臨史晨前、後碑，華山碑，白石神君，張遷，潘校官，孔羨，受禪，大饗諸碑，各五十本。
entries.en: He then turned to Han clerical script, copying the front and back Shi Chen steles, the Mount Hua stele, the White Stone Spirit Lord, Zhang Qian, Pan the Commandant, Kong Xian, the Accession to the Throne, the Grand Sacrifice, and other classics—fifty copies apiece.
entries.literal: He then studied Han clerical script, copying the front and back Shi Chen steles, the Mount Hua stele, the White Stone Spirit Lord, Zhang Qian, Pan the Commandant, Kong Xian, the Accession to the Throne, the Grand Sacrifice, and other steles—fifty copies of each.

entries.zh: 三年，分書成。
entries.en: Three years later he had mastered clerical script.
entries.literal: After three years his clerical script was accomplished.

entries.zh: 石如篆法以二李為宗，縱橫闢闔，得之史籀，稍參隸意，殺鋒以取勁折，字體微方，與秦、漢當額為近。
entries.en: Shiru's seal script took the two Li masters as its models; in its sweeping expansiveness it drew on Shi Zhou, with a touch of clerical influence; he pared the brush tip to achieve sharp turns, and his forms were slightly square, close to Qin and Han stele crowns.
entries.literal: Shiru's seal method took the two Lis as patriarchs; in breadth and expansion he obtained it from Shi Zhou, with slight clerical influence; he cut the tip to gain forceful turns; the character forms were slightly square, close to Qin and Han stele crowns.

entries.zh: 分書結體嚴重，約嶧山、國山之法而為之。
entries.en: His clerical script was grave in structure, broadly following the manners of the Mount Yi and Mount Guo inscriptions.
entries.literal: His clerical script's structure was grave and solemn, roughly following the methods of Mount Yi and Mount Guo.

entries.zh: 自謂：「吾篆未及陽冰，而分不減梁鵠。」
entries.en: He said of himself, 'My seal script has not yet matched Li Yangbing, but my clerical script is no worse than Liang He's.'
entries.literal: He said of himself: 'My seal script has not reached Yangbing, but my clerical script is not inferior to Liang He.'

entries.zh: 王澍蔣衡徐用錫王文治梁巘梁同書
entries.en: Wang Shu, Jiang Heng, Xu Yongxi, Wang Wenzhi, Liang Yan, and Liang Tongshu
entries.literal: Wang Shu, Jiang Heng, Xu Yongxi, Wang Wenzhi, Liang Yan, Liang Tongshu

entries.zh: 喜任俠，接人和易，見者不知為賁、育。
entries.en: He loved the life of the knight-errant and treated everyone with easy warmth. Those who met him never guessed he was another Ben or Yu.
entries.literal: He delighted in chivalry, received people with easy warmth — those who met him did not know he was a Ben or Yu.

entries.zh: 雍正中，浙江總督李衛捕治江寧顧云如邪術不軌獄，株連百數十人，鳳池亦被逮，讞擬大辟。
entries.en: During the Yongzheng reign, Zhejiang governor-general Li Wei prosecuted Gu Yunru of Jiangning for heterodox arts and seditious plotting; more than a hundred people were implicated. Fengchi was arrested too, and the sentence proposed was death.
entries.literal: In the Yongzheng reign Zhejiang Governor-General Li Wei arrested and tried the case of Gu Yunru of Jiangning for heterodox arts and seditious conduct, implicating over a hundred people; Fengchi was also seized and the verdict proposed capital punishment.

entries.zh: 世宗於此獄從寬，未盡駢誅。
entries.en: The Yongzheng Emperor showed mercy in the affair and did not execute the whole lot.
entries.literal: The Yongzheng Emperor showed leniency in this case and did not carry out wholesale execution.

entries.zh: 或云鳳池年八十餘，終於家。
entries.en: Some say Fengchi lived past eighty and died at home.
entries.literal: Some say Fengchi lived to over eighty and died at home.

entries.zh: 江湖間流傳其佚事多荒誕，著其可信者。
entries.en: The rivers-and-lakes world is full of wild stories about him; only those that seem credible are set down here.
entries.literal: Among the jianghu world many absurd tales of him circulate; here only the believable ones are recorded.

entries.zh: 王來咸褚士寶馮行貞甘鳳池曹竹齋潘佩言
entries.en: Wang Laixian, Chu Shibao, Feng Xingzhen, Gan Fengchi, Cao Zhuzhai, and Pan Peiyan.
entries.literal: Wang Laixian; Chu Shibao; Feng Xingzhen; Gan Fengchi; Cao Zhuzhai; Pan Peiyan.

entries.zh: 雍正初，改土歸流之議起。
entries.en: Early in the Yongzheng reign, the court began debating the policy of replacing native chiefs with appointed officials.
entries.literal: At the beginning of Yongzheng, the proposal to replace native rule with regular administration arose.

entries.zh: 四年夏，先革東川土目，即進圖烏蒙。
entries.en: In the summer of the fourth year of Yongzheng (1726), reform began with the native chiefs of Dongchuan, and attention turned at once to Wumeng.
entries.literal: In the summer of the fourth year, the native chiefs of Dongchuan were first abolished, and plans were immediately advanced for Wumeng.

entries.zh: 時烏蒙土府祿萬鍾、鎮雄土府隴慶侯皆年少，兵權皆握于其叔祿鼎坤、隴聯星。
entries.en: The native prefects of Wumeng and Zhenxiong—Lu Wanzhong and Long Qinghou—were both young men, and real military authority rested with their uncles Lu Dingkun and Long Lianxing.
entries.literal: At that time, the native prefect of Wumeng, Lu Wanzhong, and the native prefect of Zhenxiong, Long Qinghou, were both young; military power was held by their uncles Lu Dingkun and Long Lianxing respectively.

entries.zh: 鄂爾泰令總兵劉起元屯東川，招降祿鼎坤。
entries.en: Ortai stationed Regional Commander Liu Qiyuan at Dongchuan and sought to win Lu Dingkun's surrender.
entries.literal: Ortai ordered Regional Commander Liu Qiyuan to garrison Dongchuan and win Lu Dingkun over by surrender.

entries.zh: 惟祿萬鍾制于漢奸，約鎮雄兵三千攻鼎坤于魯甸，鄂爾泰遣遊擊哈元生敗之；
entries.en: Lu Wanzhong, however, was controlled by a Han collaborator; he arranged for three thousand troops from Zhenxiong to attack Dingkun at Ludian; Ortai dispatched Mobile Corps Commander Ha Yuansheng, who routed them;
entries.literal: Only Lu Wanzhong was controlled by a Han collaborator; he arranged for three thousand troops from Zhenxiong to attack Dingkun at Ludian; Ortai sent Mobile Corps Commander Ha Yuansheng to defeat them;

entries.zh: 又檄其相仇之阿底土兵共搗烏蒙，連破關隘，賊遂敗走鎮雄。
entries.en: He also called on the Adi native troops, who were at odds with them, to join in an assault on Wumeng. Government forces broke through pass after pass, and the rebels retreated in defeat toward Zhenxiong.
entries.literal: He also ordered the mutually hostile native troops of Adi to strike Wumeng together; passes were taken in succession, and the rebels then fled in defeat toward Zhenxiong.

entries.zh: 鄂爾泰復招降隴聯星，而鼎坤亦以兵三千攻鎮雄之脅，兩酋皆遁四川，於是兩土府旬日平。
entries.en: Ortai again induced Long Lianxing to surrender, while Dingkun in turn led three thousand men against Zhenxiong's flank. Both chieftains fled into Sichuan, and within ten days the two native prefectures were subdued.
entries.literal: Ortai again won Long Lianxing over by surrender, while Dingkun also led three thousand troops to strike at Zhenxiong's flank; both chieftains fled into Sichuan, and within ten days the two native prefectures were pacified.

entries.zh: 以烏蒙設府，鎮雄設州，又設鎮于烏蒙，控制三屬，由四川改隸雲南，以一事權。
entries.en: Wumeng was elevated to a prefecture and Zhenxiong to a subprefecture; a military garrison was placed at Wumeng to oversee the three dependencies, and the region was transferred from Sichuan to Yunnan jurisdiction so that authority might rest in one hand.
entries.literal: Wumeng was made a prefecture and Zhenxiong a subprefecture; a garrison was also established at Wumeng to control the three dependencies; jurisdiction was transferred from Sichuan to Yunnan, unifying authority.

entries.zh: 其東川法戛土目祿天祐、烏蒙米貼土目祿永孝，尚各據巢患邊。
entries.en: The Faga native chief of Dongchuan, Lu Tianyou, and the Mitie native chief of Wumeng, Lu Yongxiao, still held out in their strongholds and harassed the frontier.
entries.literal: The native chiefs of Faga in Dongchuan, Lu Tianyou, and of Mitie in Wumeng, Lu Yongxiao, still each held their lairs and troubled the border.

entries.zh: 六年春，遣兵破擒法戛，又遣副將郭壽域以兵三百捕米貼賊，逃渡小金沙江，糾四川沙馬司及建昌、涼山各夷倮數千潛回，襲陷官兵。
entries.en: In the spring of the sixth year (1728), government forces broke Faga and took its chief prisoner. Deputy Commander Guo Shouyu was sent with three hundred men after the Mitie rebels, who escaped across the Lesser Jinsha. They then rallied several thousand Yi and Luo from Shama in Sichuan and from Jianchang and Liangshan, stole back by hidden routes, and overran the government detachment.
entries.literal: In the spring of the sixth year, troops were sent to defeat and capture Faga; Deputy Commander Guo Shouyu was also sent with three hundred men to capture the Mitie rebels; they fled across the Lesser Jinsha River, rallied several thousand Yi and Luo from Shama Subprefecture in Sichuan and from Jianchang and Liangshan, slipped back in secret, and fell upon and overwhelmed government troops.

entries.zh: 鄂爾泰遣總兵張耀祖、參將哈元生三路搜討。
entries.en: Ortai sent Regional Commander Zhang Yaozu and Brigade Commander Ha Yuansheng on three converging columns to hunt the rebels down.
entries.literal: Ortai dispatched Regional Commander Zhang Yaozu and Brigade Commander Ha Yuansheng on three routes to search out and suppress them.

entries.zh: 詔四川建昌、永寧官兵聽鄂爾泰節制。
entries.en: An imperial edict placed the Jianchang and Yongning forces of Sichuan under Ortai's command.
entries.literal: An edict placed the troops of Jianchang and Yongning in Sichuan under Ortai's command.

entries.zh: 於是自小金沙江外，沙馬、雷波、吞都、黃螂諸土司地，直抵建昌，袤千餘里，皆置營汛，形聯勢控，並擒雷波土司楊明義；
entries.en: From beyond the Lesser Jinsha through the domains of Shama, Leibo, Tundu, Huanglang, and other native chiefs, all the way to Jianchang—a belt more than a thousand li long—garrisons and patrol posts were set up in a linked chain, and the Leibo native chief Yang Mingyi was taken prisoner;
entries.literal: Thereupon, from beyond the Lesser Jinsha River, through the territories of the native chiefs of Shama, Leibo, Tundu, and Huanglang, straight to Jianchang—a stretch of more than a thousand li—garrisons and patrol posts were established in linked formation to control the terrain, and the Leibo native chief Yang Mingyi was also captured;

entries.zh: 而哈元生回軍復敗阿盧土司之眾數千，屯田東川，歲收二萬餘石，課礦歲萬金，資兵餉。
entries.en: On his return march Ha Yuansheng again routed several thousand followers of the Alu native chief. He established military colonies in Dongchuan that yielded more than twenty thousand piculs of grain a year and mines that produced ten thousand taels annually to support the troops.
entries.literal: Ha Yuansheng, on his return march, again defeated several thousand men of the Alu native chief; he opened military colonies in Dongchuan, harvesting more than twenty thousand piculs a year and levying ten thousand taels annually from mines to supply the army.

entries.zh: 軍甫定，祿鼎坤以功擢河南參將，怏怏失望。
entries.en: Hardly had the army been settled when Lu Dingkun, rewarded for his service with promotion to Brigade Vice-Commander in Henan, grew resentful and discontented.
entries.literal: The army had just been settled when Lu Dingkun, for his merit, was promoted to Brigade Vice-Commander in Henan; resentful and disappointed,

entries.zh: 其子祿萬福乞回魯甸治產，見總兵劉起元軍律不肅，陰會其舊部謀變。
entries.en: His son Lu Wanfu petitioned to return to Ludian to manage the family estates. Seeing that Regional Commander Liu Qiyuan's troops were slack in discipline, he secretly rallied his former followers to plot a revolt.
entries.literal: his son Lu Wanfu begged to return to Ludian to manage his estates; seeing that Regional Commander Liu Qiyuan's troops were undisciplined, he secretly gathered his old followers to plot rebellion.

entries.zh: 時烏蒙商民萬計，有險可扼，且賊止標弩，無大砲，而劉起元惟媮餒賄和，賊遂陷鎮城，盡戕兵民，遍煽東川、鎮雄及四川涼山蠻數萬叛。
entries.en: Tens of thousands of merchants and townspeople were then in Wumeng, and the terrain offered defiles that could be held. The rebels carried only poisoned bolts and crossbows, no heavy artillery—yet Liu Qiyuan merely pilfered rations and took bribes to negotiate peace. The rebels overran the garrison town, massacred soldiers and civilians, and stirred up tens of thousands of tribesmen in Dongchuan, Zhenxiong, and Liangshan in Sichuan to rise in revolt.
entries.literal: At that time tens of thousands of merchants and commoners were in Wumeng; there were defiles that could be held; moreover the rebels had only poisoned bolts and crossbows, no heavy cannon—yet Liu Qiyuan only stole rations and accepted bribes to make peace; the rebels thereupon took the garrison town, slaughtered soldiers and civilians alike, and incited rebellion among tens of thousands of barbarians in Dongchuan, Zhenxiong, and Liangshan in Sichuan.

entries.zh: 鄂爾泰奏言：「臣用人僨事，請別簡大臣總督兩省，暫假臣提督，將兵討賊雪憤。」
entries.en: Ortai memorialized: "I have failed in my choice of men. I beg Your Majesty to appoint another senior minister to govern both provinces, and to grant me temporary rank as Provincial Military Commissioner so that I may lead troops against the rebels and redeem this disgrace."
entries.literal: Ortai memorialized: "Your servant's choice of personnel has caused failure. I beg that another senior minister be selected to govern both provinces; grant your servant temporary rank as Provincial Military Commissioner, that I may lead troops to suppress the rebels and wash away this shame."

entries.zh: 世宗慰留之。
entries.en: The Yongzheng Emperor comforted him and kept him at his post.
entries.literal: The Yongzheng Emperor comforted him and kept him in post.

entries.zh: 鄂爾泰調官兵萬餘，土兵半之，三路進攻。
entries.en: Ortai assembled more than ten thousand regular troops, with native auxiliaries numbering half as many, and advanced in three columns.
entries.literal: Ortai mobilized more than ten thousand regular troops, with native troops equal to half that number, and advanced on three routes.

entries.zh: 先令總兵魏翥國率兵二千，七日馳抵東川，得不陷；
entries.en: He first sent Regional Commander Wei Zhuguo with two thousand men, who reached Dongchuan in seven days' forced march and kept the city from falling;
entries.literal: He first ordered Regional Commander Wei Zhuguo to lead two thousand men; in seven days they galloped to Dongchuan, which thus did not fall;

entries.zh: 而魏翥國旋為祿鼎明刺傷，乃以官祿代翥國。
entries.en: but Wei Zhuguo was soon stabbed and wounded by Lu Dingming, and Guan Lu was appointed in his place.
entries.literal: but Wei Zhuguo was soon stabbed and wounded by Lu Dingming, whereupon Guan Lu replaced Zhuguo.

entries.zh: 烏蒙委總兵哈元生、副將徐成貴，鎮雄委參將韓勳。
entries.en: Ha Yuansheng and Deputy Commander Xu Chenggui were assigned to Wumeng; Brigade Commander Han Xun to Zhenxiong.
entries.literal: Wumeng was entrusted to Regional Commander Ha Yuansheng and Deputy Commander Xu Chenggui; Zhenxiong to Brigade Commander Han Xun.

entries.zh: 勳以兵四百扼奎鄉，敗賊四千，連破四寨。
entries.en: With four hundred men Han Xun held Kuixiang, routed four thousand rebels, and took four stockades in succession.
entries.literal: Xun with four hundred men held Kuixiang, defeated four thousand rebels, and captured four stockades in succession.

entries.zh: 哈元生以千餘兵討烏蒙，先至得勝坡，遇賊二萬。
entries.en: Ha Yuansheng marched on Wumeng with a little over a thousand men. At Desheng Slope he met twenty thousand rebels.
entries.literal: Ha Yuansheng with somewhat more than a thousand men campaigned against Wumeng, first reaching Desheng Slope, where he encountered twenty thousand rebels.

entries.zh: 其黑寡、暮末二渠皆萬人敵。
entries.en: Their two chieftains, Heigua and Mumo, were each said to be a match for ten thousand men.
entries.literal: Their two chieftains Heigua and Mumo were each a match for ten thousand men.

entries.zh: 黑寡持長槍，直犯元生，元生左格槍，右拔矢，應手殪之；
entries.en: Heigua charged at Yuansheng with a long spear; Yuansheng parried with his left hand, drew an arrow with his right, and killed him on the spot;
entries.literal: Heigua bore a long spear and charged straight at Yuansheng; Yuansheng parried the spear with his left hand, drew an arrow with his right, and killed him on the spot;

entries.zh: 又射殪暮末，即竿揭二首以進，賊奪氣。
entries.en: He then shot Mumo dead, had both heads raised on poles and carried forward, and the rebels' morale collapsed.
entries.literal: He then shot and killed Mumo, immediately raised both heads on poles and advanced, and the rebels lost heart.

entries.zh: 再戰再捷，進至倚那岡。
entries.en: Victory followed victory until they reached Yina Ridge.
entries.literal: Battle after battle brought victory, and they advanced to Yina Ridge.

entries.zh: 賊數萬，連營十餘里。
entries.en: Tens of thousands of rebels had pitched camp along more than ten li of ground.
entries.literal: The rebels numbered tens of thousands, their camps stretching more than ten li.

entries.zh: 我兵三千、土兵千，夜設伏賊營左右，而嚴陣以待。
entries.en: With three thousand regulars and a thousand native auxiliaries, they laid ambushes on both flanks of the rebel camp by night and held the main line in battle order.
entries.literal: Our troops were three thousand, native troops one thousand; by night ambushes were set on both flanks of the rebel camp while the main force waited in battle order.

entries.zh: 黎明，賊數路來犯，不動。
entries.en: At dawn the rebels attacked from several directions; the government line held firm.
entries.literal: At dawn the rebels attacked on several routes; our forces did not stir.

entries.zh: 將偪陣，砲起，大呼奮擊，山后伏兵左右夾攻，賊大潰，盡破其八十餘營，獲甲械輜重山積。
entries.en: As the rebels pressed the line, the guns opened fire and the troops charged with a great shout. Ambush parties on the hills struck from both flanks, and the rebels broke in rout. More than eighty camps were overrun, and captured arms and baggage heaped up like hills.
entries.literal: As they were about to close on the line, cannon fired; with loud shouts our men charged; ambush troops behind the hills attacked from both sides; the rebels broke in great disorder; more than eighty camps were all taken; armor, weapons, and baggage piled like hills.

entries.zh: 即日抵烏蒙，賊見元生旗，即反走，克三關，祿萬福兄弟、祿鼎坤均伏誅。
entries.en: That same day they reached Wumeng. At sight of Yuansheng's banner the rebels turned and fled. Three passes were taken, and Lu Wanfu, his brothers, and Lu Dingkun were all put to death.
entries.literal: That same day they reached Wumeng; at sight of Yuansheng's banner the rebels at once turned and fled; three passes were taken; Lu Wanfu and his brothers and Lu Dingkun were all executed.

entries.zh: 雲南古滇國。
entries.en: Yunnan was once the territory of the ancient Dian kingdom.
entries.literal: Yunnan was the ancient state of Dian.

entries.zh: 自越巂蠻夷任貴自領太守，漢光武即授以印綬，不以內地官守例之。
entries.en: When the Yuexi Yi chieftain Ren Gui had himself proclaimed Grand Administrator, Emperor Guangwu of Han at once invested him with the seal and ribbon of office, without treating him by the same rules as officials in the heartland.
entries.literal: From the time when the Yi of Yuexi, Ren Gui, held the post of Grand Administrator on his own authority, Emperor Guangwu of Han immediately granted him seals and ribbons, not applying to him the standard precedent for officials in the interior.

entries.zh: 若爨、若蒙，皆以本土大姓，就官累世，為一方長。
entries.en: Families such as the Cuan and the Meng drew on powerful local lineages and, holding office for generations, ruled their respective regions.
entries.literal: Such clans as the Cuan and the Meng all relied on local great surnames; generation after generation they took office and became regional leaders.

entries.zh: 元封梁王於滇，與大理之段分治。
entries.en: The Yuan enfeoffed the Prince of Liang in Dian, while the Duan of Dali governed their domain in parallel.
entries.literal: Under the Yuan, a Prince of Liang was enfeoffed in Dian, ruling jointly with the Duan clan of Dali.

entries.zh: 明破梁王，滅大理，就土官而統馭之，分宣慰使、宣撫使、安撫使、正副長官司、土府、土州以治之。
entries.en: When the Ming defeated the Prince of Liang and extinguished Dali, they ruled through native chiefs, organizing the region into Pacification Commissioners, Pacification Supervisors, Reassurance Commissioners, principal and deputy native chiefs, native prefectures, and native subprefectures.
entries.literal: The Ming defeated the Prince of Liang, destroyed Dali, and governed through native officials, dividing administration among Pacification Commissioners, Pacification Supervisors, Reassurance Commissioners, chief officials (principal and deputy), native prefectures, and native subprefectures.

entries.zh: 冬十一月癸卯，令曰：「諸將征伐，士卒死亡者或未收斂，吾甚哀之；
entries.en: On the guimao day in the eleventh month of winter he issued an edict: "When armies march, fallen soldiers are sometimes left unburied—I mourn them bitterly;
entries.literal: Winter, eleventh month, on Guimao, an edict said: "When the various generals campaign and soldiers die, sometimes they are not gathered for burial—I deeply grieve for them;

entries.zh: 其告郡國給槥
entries.en: instruct every commandery and principality to issue coffins
entries.literal: let it be announced to the commanderies and kingdoms to supply hui (coffins)

entries.zh: 〈槥音衞〉
entries.en: 〈Pronunciation gloss: the character (hui) is read the same as the common word wei, "defend."〉
entries.literal: 〈 hui is pronounced wei 〉

entries.zh: 櫝殯斂，送致其家，官爲設祭。」
entries.en: For encoffining and laying out the remains, ship each body home, and let the officials sponsor the sacrificial offerings."
entries.literal: enclosed burial receptacles for laying out and dressing the dead, convey them to their homes, and let officials perform sacrifices for them."

entries.zh: 〈《漢書》高祖八月令曰：「士卒從軍死，爲槥。」
entries.en: 〈The Han shu quotes Emperor Gaozu's eighth-month decree: "Men who die on campaign shall receive a burial coffin (hui)."
entries.literal: 〈The Han Book August edict of Emperor Gaozu said: "Soldiers who die following the army—supply hui."

entries.zh: 應劭曰：「槥，小棺也，今謂之櫝。」
entries.en: Ying Shao glosses: "Hui is a small coffin—today we call it a case (du)."
entries.literal: Ying Shao said: "Hui is a small coffin; nowadays it is called du (case)."

entries.zh: 應璩百一詩曰：「槥車在道路，征夫不得休。」
entries.en: Ying Qu's "Hundred and One" poems say: "Coffin wagons line the roads while conscripts never rest."
entries.literal: Ying Qu's Hundred and One Poem says: "The hui cart is on the road; the campaigner cannot rest."

entries.zh: 陸機大墓賦曰：「觀細木而悶遲，覩洪櫝而念槥。」〉
entries.en: Lu Ji's Rhapsody on a Princely Tomb says: "The sight of plain boards brought gloom; the great outer coffin recalled the simple hui."〉
entries.literal: Lu Ji's Rhapsody on the Great Tomb says: "Gazing on fine wood I am depressed and slow; beholding a great case I think of hui."〉

entries.zh: 丙午，行至曲蠡。
entries.en: On the bingwu day he marched as far as Quli.
entries.literal: On Bingwu, traveling reached Quli.

entries.zh: 六年春二月，遣使者循行許昌以東盡沛郡，問民所疾苦，貧者振貸之。
entries.en: In the second month of spring of the sixth year inspectors toured from Xuchang east through Pei commandery, inquiring after hardships and granting grain loans to the poor.
entries.literal: Sixth year spring second month, dispatched envoys touring east of Xuchang to reach Pei commandery, asking people what bitter ailments; poor ones relieved lent them.

entries.zh: 〈《魏略》載詔曰：「昔軒轅建四面之號，周武稱『予有亂臣十人』，斯蓋先聖所以體國君民，亮成天工，多賢爲貴也。
entries.en: 〈The Wei Summary preserves an edict: "The Yellow Emperor posted advisers on four sides; King Wu spoke of ten ministers who could cure chaos—because sage rulers cherish worthy ministers when ordering state and heaven's task alike.
entries.literal: 〈Wei Summary carries edict saying: "Formerly Xuanyuan established four-side titles; Zhou Wu called 'I have disorder ministers ten persons'—this covers former sages thereby embodying state ruling people, bright completing heavenly work, many worthies as noble.

entries.zh: 今內有公卿以鎮京師，外設牧伯以監四方，至於元戎出征，則軍中宜有柱石之賢帥，輜重所在，又宜有鎮守之重臣，然後車駕可以周行天下，無內外之慮。
entries.en: At court ministers stabilize Luoyang; in the regions governors watch the corners—when the supreme commander campaigns there must be stalwart generals in the field and trustworthy ministers guarding supply lines; only then can the emperor journey safely without dread inside or out.
entries.literal: Now inside have dukes and ministers to guard capital city; outside establish shepherds and elders to supervise four quarters—as for commander-in-chief going campaign, then army center ought have pillar-stone worthy commander; baggage trains located place, again ought have guarding heavy ministers—then afterward imperial carriage can circle journey all-under-heaven, without internal-external worries.

entries.zh: 吾今當征賊，欲守之積年。
entries.en: I am about to strike the rebels and expect the duty to last several years.
entries.literal: I now about to campaign rebels, wish guard them accumulated years.

entries.zh: 其以尚書令潁鄉侯陳羣爲鎮軍大將軍，尚書僕射西鄉侯司馬懿爲撫軍大將軍。
entries.en: Chen Qun, Marquis of Yingxiang, is named General Who Guards the Army, and Sima Yi, Marquis of Xixiang, General Who Pacifies the Army.
entries.literal: Let Supervisor of the Secretariat Yingxiang Marquis Chen Qun be General Who Guards the Army; Deputy Director of the Secretariat Xixiang Marquis Sima Yi be General Who Pacifies the Army.

entries.zh: 若吾臨江授諸將方略，則撫軍當留許昌，督後諸軍，錄後臺文書事；
entries.en: If I take the front line to brief the generals, the Pacification general stays in Xuchang to coordinate rear echelons and handle secretariat paperwork;
entries.literal: If I along river grant generals plans, then Pacify Army should remain Xuchang, supervise rear various armies, record rear platform document affairs;

entries.zh: 鎮軍隨車駕，當董督衆軍，錄行尚書事；
entries.en: the general who guards the army escorts the throne, commands the host, and holds traveling authority as head of the secretariat;
entries.literal: Guard Army follows imperial carriage, should superintend oversee host of armies, record traveling Supervisor of Secretariat affairs;

entries.zh: 皆假節鼓吹，給中軍兵騎六百人。
entries.en: each receives the credential, musicians, and six hundred guards from the central army.
entries.literal: all lent credential drum-blow, supply center army soldiers cavalry six hundred men.

entries.zh: 吾欲去江數里，築宮室，往來其中，見賊可擊之形，便出奇兵擊之；
entries.en: I will build a redoubt a few li from the river, move between it and the camp, and when the enemy offers a target I will sally with picked troops;
entries.literal: I wish go several li from river, build palace rooms, go-come within them, see enemy can strike form, then issue strange troops strike them;

entries.zh: 若或未可，則當舒六軍以遊獵，饗賜軍士。」〉
entries.en: if no opening appears I will exercise the six armies on hunt maneuvers and feast the troops."〉"
entries.literal: if or not yet possible, then should extend six armies to roam hunt, feast bestow soldiers."〉"

entries.zh: 三月，行幸召陵，通討虜渠。
entries.en: In March he visited Shaoling and reopened the Taolu canal.
entries.literal: Third month, progressed favor Shaoling, opened Taolu canal.

entries.zh: 乙巳，還許昌宮。
entries.en: On the yisi day he returned to Xuchang Palace.
entries.literal: Yisi, returned Xuchang Palace.

entries.zh: 并州刺史梁習討鮮卑軻比能，大破之。
entries.en: Liang Xi, inspector of Bing province, attacked the Xianbei chief Kebineng and routed him.
entries.literal: Bing Province Inspector Liang Xi campaigned against Xianbei Ke Bineng, greatly defeated him.

entries.zh: 辛未，帝爲舟師東征。
entries.en: On the xinwei day the emperor led the river fleet east.
entries.literal: Xinwei, Emperor made naval army east campaign.

entries.zh: 五月戊申，幸譙。
entries.en: On the wushen day in the fifth month he visited Qiao.
entries.literal: Fifth month Wushen, favored Qiao.

entries.zh: 壬戌，熒惑入太微。
entries.en: On the renxu day Mars entered the Supreme Palace enclosure.
entries.literal: Renxu, Sparkling Deluder entered Supreme Subtlety.

entries.zh: 七年春正月，將幸許昌，許昌城南門無故自崩，帝心惡之，遂不入。
entries.en: In the first month of spring of the seventh year he meant to visit Xuchang, but the south gate collapsed without cause; taking it as an ill omen he turned back.
entries.literal: Seventh year spring first month, about to favor Xuchang—Xuchang city south gate without cause self collapsed—Emperor heart loathed it—thereupon did not enter.

entries.zh: 壬子，行還洛陽宮。
entries.en: On the renzi day he returned to Luoyang Palace.
entries.literal: Renzi, progressed returned Luoyang Palace.

entries.zh: 三月，築九華臺。
entries.en: In March he built the Nine Splendors Terrace.
entries.literal: Third month, built Nine Splendor Terrace.

entries.zh: 夏五月丙辰，帝疾篤，召中軍大將軍曹真、鎮軍大將軍陳羣、征東大將軍曹休、撫軍大將軍司馬宣王，並受遺詔輔嗣主。
entries.en: On bingchen in the fifth month of summer, when the emperor’s illness was grave, he summoned Grand General of the Central Army Cao Zhen, Grand General Who Guards the Army Chen Qun, Grand General Who Campaigns East Cao Xiu, and Grand General Who Pacifies the Army Sima Yi; all received the testamentary edict to assist the succeeding ruler.
entries.literal: Summer fifth month Bingchen, Emperor illness severe—summoned Central Army Grand General Cao Zhen, Guard Army Grand General Chen Qun, East Campaign Grand General Cao Xiu, Pacify Army Grand General Sima Xuanwang—all received testament edict assisting heir lord.

entries.zh: 遣後宮淑媛、昭儀已下歸其家。
entries.en: Concubines ranked gentle ladies and below were sent home to their families.
entries.literal: Dispatched rear palace Shuyuan, Zhaoyi and below return their homes.

entries.zh: 丁巳，帝崩于嘉福殿，時年四十。
entries.en: On the dingsi day he died in Jiafu Hall at the age of forty.
entries.literal: Dingsi, Emperor collapsed at Jiafu Hall, age then forty.

entries.zh: 〈《魏書》曰：殯於崇華前殿。〉
entries.en: 〈The Wei Book states that his bier rested in the front hall of Chonghua.
entries.literal: 〈Wei Book says: Laying out at Chonghua Front Hall.

entries.zh: 六月戊寅，葬首陽陵。
entries.en: On the wuyin day in the sixth month he was buried at Shouyang Mausoleum.
entries.literal: Sixth month Wuyin, buried Shouyang Mausoleum.

entries.zh: 自殯及葬，皆以終制從事。
entries.en: From lying in state to interment every rite followed his own austere "final instructions."
entries.literal: From laying out to burial, all by final regulations conducted affairs.

entries.zh: 〈《魏氏春秋》曰：明帝將送葬，曹真、陳羣、王朗等以暑熱固諫，乃止。
entries.en: 〈The Wei shi chunqiu notes that Emperor Ming meant to join the funeral train but Cao Zhen, Chen Qun, Wang Lang, and others dissuaded him in the sweltering heat—so he desisted.
entries.literal: 〈Wei Family Spring and Autumn says: Ming Di was about to escort burial—Cao Zhen, Chen Qun, Wang Lang etc. by summer heat firmly remonstrated—then stopped.

entries.zh: 孫盛曰：夫窀穸之事，孝子之極痛也，人倫之道，於斯莫重。
entries.en: Sun Sheng remarks that laying a parent to rest is the filial son's sharpest grief—nothing weightier in human duty.
entries.literal: Sun Sheng says: As for burial vault affairs—filial son's utmost pain; human relations way—here nothing heavier.

entries.zh: 故天子七月而葬，同軌畢至。
entries.en: Hence the emperor waits seven months for burial so every carriage track may converge.
entries.literal: Therefore Son of Heaven seventh month then bury—same track all arrive.

entries.zh: 夫以義感之情，猶盡臨隧之哀，況乎天性發中，敦禮者重之哉！
entries.en: Even ritual bonds demand the full grief at the grave—how much more the bond of nature for those who prize propriety!
entries.literal: By righteousness-moved feelings—still exhaust overseeing tunnel grief—how much more heavenly nature issuing center—those who esteem ritual value it!

entries.zh: 魏氏之德，仍世不基矣。
entries.en: Such thin virtue ill suits lasting foundations for the house of Wei.
entries.literal: Wei clan's virtue—still generations not foundation.

entries.zh: 昔華元厚葬，君子以爲棄君於惡，羣等之諫，棄孰甚焉！
entries.en: Long ago Hua Yuan gave a lavish funeral; the nobles read it as abandoning his lord to wrong—what greater betrayal than Chen Qun's counsel to stay away?
entries.literal: Formerly Hua Yuan thick burial—gentleman thought abandoned lord in evil—Qun etc.'s remonstrance—abandonance which more extreme!

entries.zh: 鄄城侯植爲誄曰：「惟黃初七年五月七日，大行皇帝崩，嗚呼哀哉！
entries.en: The Marquis of Juancheng, Cao Zhi, composed a dirge: "On the seventh day of the fifth month of Huangchu seven (226 CE) the late emperor passed away—alas, the sorrow!
entries.literal: Marquis of Juancheng Zhi composed a dirge saying: "Only Huangchu seventh year fifth month seventh day, the Grand Procession Emperor collapsed—alas, how bitter is our grief!

entries.zh: 于時天震地駭，崩山隕霜，陽精薄景，五緯錯行，百姓呼嗟，萬國悲悼，若喪考妣，恩過墓唐，擗踊郊野，仰想穹蒼，僉曰何辜，早世殞喪，嗚呼哀哉！
entries.en: Heaven trembled and earth reeled; peaks shattered and frost fell; the sun's fire dimmed; the five planets left their tracks; people wailed and every polity grieved as for lost parents; kindness deeper than at Tang's tomb; mourners beat their breasts in the outer suburbs and scanned the sky—why must guilt strike him who died before his time? Alas, the sorrow!
entries.literal: Then Heaven quaked and Earth was shaken; mountains split and frost fell; the sun's essence thinned its glory; the five planetary traces ran awry; the hundred surnames cried aloud; the myriad regions mourned—as mourning father and mother; kindness surpassed tomb-site Tang; beating breasts and stamping in the suburban wilds; looking up pondering deep azure—all said what guilt—early age perished loss—alas, how bitter is our grief!

entries.zh: 悲夫大行，忽焉光滅，永棄萬國，雲往雨絕。
entries.en: Alas for the departed sovereign—his light snuffed in an instant, forever lost to the realm; clouds have fled and the rains ceased.
entries.literal: Alas for Grand Procession—suddenly radiance extinguished; forever cast off from myriad regions; clouds gone rain cut off.

entries.zh: 承問荒忽，惛懵哽咽，袖鋒抽刃，歎自僵斃，追慕三良，甘心同穴。
entries.en: When the news reached me I reeled in confusion, voice choked—I would have drawn steel and struck myself down; I envied the three Good Men who followed Duke Mu into death and wished to share one tomb.
entries.literal: Receiving tidings wild confused, dark dull choking—sleeve blade draw dagger—sigh self rigid death—long for Three Good Men—glad heart same cave.

entries.zh: 感惟南風，惟以鬱滯，終於偕沒，指景自誓。
entries.en: The south wind stirs grief still pent within us—we shall perish together; I swear by the moving sun.
entries.literal: Moved only south wind—only thereby pent stagnant—in end together perish—point shadow self swear.

entries.zh: 考諸先記，尋之哲言，生若浮寄，惟德可論，朝聞夕逝，孔志所存。
entries.en: Ancient texts and wise men taught that life is fleeting lodging and only virtue endures; "hear the Way at dawn, die content at dusk"—such was Confucius's pledge.
entries.literal: Examine various former records—trace them sage words—life like floating lodging—only virtue can be discussed—dawn hear dusk depart—Kong resolve stored.

entries.zh: 皇雖一沒，天祿永延，何以述德？
entries.en: Though he has passed in one stroke, Heaven's blessing flows onward—how shall we proclaim his merit?
entries.literal: Sovereign though once gone—Heaven salary forever extended—how thereby narrate virtue?

entries.zh: 表之素旃。
entries.en: We inscribe it on the white funeral banner.
entries.literal: Display them plain white banners.

entries.zh: 何以詠功？
entries.en: How shall we sing his achievements?
entries.literal: How thereby chant merit?

entries.zh: 宣之管絃。
entries.en: Let pipes and strings carry them abroad.
entries.literal: Proclaim them pipes strings.

entries.zh: 乃作誄曰：皓皓太素，兩儀始分，中和產物，肈有人倫，爰曁三皇，寔秉道真，降逮五帝，繼以懿純，三代製作，踵武立勳。
entries.en: The dirge continues: "Bright primal purity split into yin and yang and yielded the human order; the Three Sovereigns grasped the true Dao, the Five Thearchs followed in unstained line, and the Three Dynasties built institutions and trod the path of merit.
entries.literal: Thus composing dirge says: Bright bright Great Simplicity—two powers first divided—center harmony produced creatures—thereupon human relations—then reaching Three August Ones—truly grasped Way true—descending reaching Five Thearchs—in succession with pure grace—Three Ages fashioned institutions—heel-print martial raised merit.

entries.zh: 季嗣不維，網漏于秦，崩樂滅學，儒坑禮焚，二世而殲，漢氏乃因，弗求古訓，嬴政是遵，王綱帝典，闃爾無聞。
entries.en: Successors failed their bond; Qin's net tore—music fell and learning died, Confucians were buried and ritual texts burned; Er Shi fell within two reigns. Han arose yet spurned antique teaching and copied the First Emperor until royal norms seemed lost in silence.
entries.literal: Later heirs not bind—net leaked under Qin—collapse music destroy learning—Ru buried ritual burned—Second Generation then destroyed—Han clan thereupon continued—not seeking ancient instructions—Ying Zheng this followed—kingly cord imperial canon—silent indeed unheard.

entries.zh: 末光幽昧，道究運遷，乾坤迴歷，簡聖授賢，乃眷大行，屬以黎元。
entries.en: Twilight deepened until fortune shifted; heaven and earth rolled through cycles until the canon chose sages—and then He turned to the late emperor and entrusted him with the black-haired masses.
entries.literal: Last gleam dark dim—Way exhausted fortune shift—Qian Kun circuit rounds—select sage grant worthy—then favor Grand Procession—entrust with black-haired masses.

entries.zh: 龍飛啟祚，合契上玄，五行定紀，改號革年，明明赫赫，受命于天。
entries.en: The dragon throne rose, cosmic tallies aligned with High Heaven, the Five Agents received their stations, reign titles and years were renewed—radiant and august, he bore Heaven's mandate.
entries.literal: Dragon fly open fortune—combine tally Upper Dark—Five Phases fix records—change designation reform year—bright bright blazing blazing—receive mandate from Heaven.

entries.zh: 仁風偃物，德以禮宣；
entries.en: His humane breezes bowed all creation; his power moved through ritual;
entries.literal: Humane wind lay things low—virtue by ritual proclaimed;

entries.zh: 祥惟聖質，嶷在幼妍。
entries.en: augury marked his sacred nature, steadfast even in childhood grace.
entries.literal: Auspicious only sage substance—towering in youth grace.

entries.zh: 庻幾六典，學不過庭，潛心無罔，亢志青冥。
entries.en: He aspired to the Six Canons, studied within his courtyard, pondered without guile, and raised his purpose toward the empyrean.
entries.literal: Almost Six Canons—learning not passing courtyard—sink heart without deceit—raise resolve blue-dark.

entries.zh: 才秀藻朗，如玉之瑩，聽察無嚮，瞻覩未形。
entries.en: Talent shone clear as polished jade; his hearing needed no prompting, his sight pierced what had not yet taken shape.
entries.literal: Talent splendid polish bright—like jade's luster—hearing examining without direction—gazing seeing unformed.

entries.zh: 其剛如金，其貞如瓊，如氷之絜，如砥之平。
entries.en: He was hard as metal, constant as jade, pure as ice, level as a whetstone.
entries.literal: His hardness like gold—his constancy like fine jade—like ice's purity—like whetstone's level.

entries.zh: 爵公無私，戮違無輕，心鏡萬機，攬照下情。
entries.en: He enfeoffed without favoritism and punished rebels without laxity; his mind mirrored every policy and illumined the people's plight.
entries.literal: Ennobling dukes without selfishness—punishing rebels without lightness—heart mirrors myriad mechanisms—gather shine lower feelings.

entries.zh: 思良股肱，嘉昔伊呂，搜揚側陋，舉湯代禹；
entries.en: He sought worthy limbs of state, praised Yi Yin and Lü Wang, searched humble lanes and raised men like Tang's ministers;
entries.literal: Thought good thighs arms—praised former Yi Lü—search raise humble obscure—raise Tang replace Yu;

entries.zh: 拔才巖穴，取士蓬戶，唯德是縈，弗拘禰祖。
entries.en: he drew talent from mountain caves and brushwood gates, binding office to virtue alone without respect to pedigree.
entries.literal: Pull talent cave grottoes—take scholars brushwood doors—only virtue is bound—not constrain Mi Zu.

entries.zh: 宅土之表，道義是圖，弗營厥險，六合是虞。
entries.en: Beyond the nine provinces he sought righteousness, scorned mere terrain, and watched over the six directions.
entries.literal: Dwelling earth's surface—Way righteousness this plan—not fortify those perils—six unions this guard.

entries.zh: 齊契共遵，下以純民，恢折規矩，克紹前人。
entries.en: All signed the covenant to guide the folk in simplicity, broadened the norms, and carried on the work of past kings.
entries.literal: Level tally together obey—below thereby pure people—expand break compass-square—able continue former men.

entries.zh: 科條品制，襃貶以因。
entries.en: Statutes and ranks framed praise and blame by precedent.
entries.literal: Statutes articles grades systems—praise blame thereby follow.

entries.zh: 乘殷之輅，行夏之辰。
entries.en: He rode Yin-style chariots and kept Xia's calendar.
entries.literal: Ride Yin's chariot—practice Xia's calendar.

entries.zh: 金根黃屋，翠葆龍鱗，紼冕崇麗，衡紞惟新，尊肅禮容，矚之若神。
entries.en: Gold-decked chariot and yellow canopy, kingfisher pennons and dragon scales on regalia; cords and crowns rose in splendor, hatstrings gleamed anew—his solemn ritual awe struck every eye like a god.
entries.literal: Gold Root Yellow Canopy—emerald feather dragon scales—cord cap lofty splendid—cross-cord only new—revere solemn ritual bearing—gaze it like spirit.

entries.zh: 方牧妙舉，欽於恤民，虎將荷節，鎮彼四鄰；
entries.en: Regional governors were wisely chosen and cherished the people; tiger generals bore credentials and pacified the marches;
entries.literal: Regional shepherds wonderful selections—revere at relieving people—tiger generals bearing credential—guard those four neighbors;

entries.zh: 朱旗所勦，九壤被震，疇克不若？
entries.en: Wherever crimson banners swept the nine regions trembled—who could refuse submission?
entries.literal: Red flags wherever strike—nine soils struck quake—who can not submit?

entries.zh: 孰敢不臣？
entries.en: Who dared withhold allegiance?
entries.literal: Who dares not minister?

entries.zh: 縣旌海表，萬里無塵。
entries.en: Banners flew beyond the eastern sea and ten thousand li knew no raider's dust.
entries.literal: Suspend banners sea beyond—ten thousand li without dust.

entries.zh: 虜備凶徹，鳥殪江岷，權若涸魚，乾腊矯鱗，肅慎納貢，越裳效珍，條支絕域，侍子內賔。
entries.en: Liu Bei's host was broken along the rivers; Sun Quan gasped like a fish on dry land; Sushen sent tribute, Yuechang offered jades, even far Tiaozhi sent hostages to court.
entries.literal: Captive Bei fierce exhausted—birds destroyed Jiang Min—Quan like dried fish—dried flesh stiff scales—Sushen bring tribute—Yuechang present treasures—Tiaozhi cut-off region—hostage sons inner guests.

entries.zh: 德儕先皇，功侔太古。
entries.en: His virtue matched the ancient sovereigns; his deeds rivaled high antiquity.
entries.literal: Virtue equal Former Emperor—merit match Grand Antiquity.

entries.zh: 上靈降瑞，黃初叔祜：河龍洛龜，淩波游下；
entries.en: High Heaven sent omens and Huangchu knew felicity: dragons rose from the Yellow River and tortoises from the Luo, breasting the waves;
entries.literal: Upper spirits descend auspicious—Huangchu secondary blessing: River Dragon Luo Tortoise—stride waves swim down;

entries.zh: 平鈞應繩，神鸞翔舞；
entries.en: the measuring cord hung true and divine phoenixes wheeled in dance;
entries.literal: Level jun responds cord—divine luan soar dance;

entries.zh: 數莢階除，系風扇暑；
entries.en: auspicious grain sprouted on the stairs; gentle winds turned aside the summer heat;
entries.literal: Repeated pods stair steps—tie wind fan summer;

entries.zh: 皓獸素禽，飛走郊野；
entries.en: white beasts and bright-plumed birds crossed the suburban preserves;
entries.literal: White beasts plain birds—fly run suburban wilds;

entries.zh: 神鍾寶鼎，形自舊土；
entries.en: spirit bells and bronze tripods took shape from native earth;
entries.literal: Divine bell precious tripod—forms from old soil;

entries.zh: 雲英甘露，瀸塗被宇；
entries.en: sweet nectar washed the dust and bathed the palace roof;
entries.literal: Cloud essence sweet dew—moisten mud cover roof;

entries.zh: 靈芝冒沼，朱華陰渚。
entries.en: magic fungus crowned the ponds and crimson flowers shaded the islets.
entries.literal: Numinous fungus cover marsh—red flowers shade islet.

entries.zh: 回回凱風，祁祁甘雨，稼穡豐登，我稷我黍。
entries.en: Soft southern breezes brought abundant rains; grain stood thick—our wheat and millet flourished.
entries.literal: Whirling triumphant wind—vast vast sweet rain—grain crops abundant rising—our millet our glutinous millet.

entries.zh: 家佩惠君，戶蒙慈父。
entries.en: Every home cherished him as a gracious lord; every door knew him as a kindly father.
entries.literal: Households wear gracious lord—doors receive kindly father.

entries.zh: 圖致太和，洽德全義。
entries.en: He aimed at supreme harmony and mingled virtue with perfect righteousness.
entries.literal: Plan reach Grand Harmony—moisten virtue complete righteousness.

entries.zh: 將登介山，先皇作儷。
entries.en: He prepared to climb Mount Jie as Shun once did, pairing ritual with the founder.
entries.literal: About to ascend Jie Mountain—Former Emperor made mate.

entries.zh: 鐫石紀勳，兼錄衆瑞，方隆封禪，歸功天地，賔禮百靈，勳命視規，望祭四嶽，燎封奉柴，肅于南郊，宗祀上帝。
entries.en: He carved stone to record deeds and gathered every omen; about to mount Feng and Shan he returned merit to Heaven and earth, feasted the hundred spirits, inspected ordinances, sacrificed to the Four Peaks, burned grain offerings at the suburban altar, and honored High God in the ancestral shrine.
entries.literal: Carve stone record merit—also record crowd auspicious—about to elevate Feng Shan—return merit Heaven Earth—guest-ritual hundred spirits—merit mandate inspect regulation—gaze sacrifice Four Marchmounts—blaze seal offer firewood—solemn at southern suburb—ancestral sacrifice Supreme Lord.

entries.zh: 三牲旣供，夏禘秋甞，元侯佐祭，獻璧奉璋。
entries.en: Tripods steamed with three beasts; summer di and autumn chang rites brought chief marquises to assist, presenting disks and libation tablets.
entries.literal: Three victims already supplied—summer di autumn taste—chief marquises assist sacrifice—present jade disk offer jade tablet.

entries.zh: 鸞輿幽藹，龍旂太常，爰迄太廟，鍾鼓鍠鍠，頌德詠功，八佾鏘鏘。
entries.en: Phoenix carriages drifted in gloom; dragon banners flew from the Grand Constant guard; entering the Grand Temple bells and drums thundered while eight rows of dancers praised virtue and rehearsed his deeds.
entries.literal: Luan carriage dim mist—dragon pennant Grand Constant—thereupon reach Grand Temple—bells drums clang clang—praise virtue chant merit—eight rows clang clang.

entries.zh: 皇祖旣饗，烈考來享，神具醉止，降茲福祥。
entries.en: Imperial ancestors received the feast; his father joined in joy—the spirits drank their fill and poured forth fortune.
entries.literal: Imperial Grandfather already feast—Fiery Deceased comes enjoy—spirits all drunk stop—descend this blessing auspicious.

entries.zh: 天地震蕩，大行康之；
entries.en: When heaven and earth convulsed, the late emperor brought peace;
entries.literal: Heaven Earth shake surge—Grand Procession rested them;

entries.zh: 三辰暗昧，大行光之；
entries.en: when sun, moon, and stars grew dim, he lit them anew;
entries.literal: Three luminaries dark dim—Grand Procession brightened them;

entries.zh: 皇紘絕維，大行綱之；
entries.en: when the royal net snapped, he restrung it;
entries.literal: Imperial cord cut rope—Grand Procession corded them;

entries.zh: 神器莫統，大行當之；
entries.en: when the sacred regalia lacked a master, he took it up;
entries.literal: Divine vessel none unify—Grand Procession bore it;

entries.zh: 禮樂廢弛，大行張之；
entries.en: when ritual and music collapsed, he stretched them taut;
entries.literal: Rite music abandoned slack—Grand Procession stretched them;

entries.zh: 仁義陸沈，大行揚之；
entries.en: when humanity and justice sank from sight, he raised them high;
entries.literal: Benevolence righteousness sunk land—Grand Procession raised them;

entries.zh: 潛龍隱鳳，大行翔之；
entries.en: when dragons hid and phoenixes vanished, he gave them flight;
entries.literal: Hidden dragon concealed phoenix—Grand Procession soared them;

entries.zh: 疏狄遐康，大行匡之。
entries.en: when distant Di tribes lacked peace, he set them right.
entries.literal: Distant Di far Kang—Grand Procession corrected them.

entries.zh: 在位七載，元功仍舉，將永太和，絕迹三五，宜作物師，長爲神主，壽終金石，等筭東父，如何奄忽，摧身后土，俾我棾棾，靡瞻靡顧。
entries.en: Seven years on the throne—great deeds piled toward lasting harmony, rivaling the Three Dynasties—fit to be maker of laws and everlasting lord, to live long as bronze stone like Dongfang Shuo—yet suddenly earth swallowed him, leaving us orphaned with nowhere to turn our eyes.
entries.literal: On throne seven years—prime merit still raised—about to eternal Grand Harmony—cut traces Three Five—should serve creation teacher—long as spirit lord—life end metal stone—equal reckon Eastern Father—how sudden abruptly—break body rear earth—cause me solitary solitary—none gaze none look.

entries.zh: 嗟嗟皇穹，胡寧忍務？
entries.en: O mighty Heaven—how could you bear this deed?
entries.literal: Alas alas august vault—how indeed endure task?

entries.zh: 嗚呼哀哉！
entries.en: Alas, the sorrow!
entries.literal: Alas how bitter grief!

entries.zh: 明監吉凶，體遠存亡，深垂典制，申之嗣皇。
entries.en: Clear-eyed toward fortune and fate, he gauged life and death from afar—his ordinances reach deep and instruct the heir.
entries.literal: Bright mirror auspicious inauspicious—embody far survival loss—deep suspend canon regulations—extend them heir emperor.

entries.zh: 聖上虔奉，是順是將，乃剏玄宇，基爲首陽，擬迹穀林，追堯慕唐，合山同陵，不樹不疆，塗車芻靈，珠玉靡藏。
entries.en: The sacred heir reverently follows—raising dark halls on Shouyang as Yao at Grain Grove—honoring Tang without mound rings or jeweled grave goods, only clay hearses and straw figures—no pearls hidden below.
entries.literal: Holy superior reverently uphold—this obey this lead—thereupon carve Dark Hall—foundation be Shouyang—trace footprints Grain Grove—pursue Yao admire Tang—join mountains same mound—not trees not borders—clay cart straw spirits—pearls jades none bury.

entries.zh: 百神警侍，來賔幽堂，耕禽田獸，望魂之翔。
entries.en: Spirits stand vigil as guests enter the shadowed hall; sacrificial oxen and penned beasts await the soaring soul.
entries.literal: Hundred spirits alert attend—come guest dark hall—plough birds field beasts—gaze soul's soar.

entries.zh: 於是，俟大隧之致功兮，練元辰之淑禎，潛華體於梓宮兮，馮正殿以居靈。
entries.en: Now we await the tunnel's completion and choose an auspicious hour—the splendid form rests in the catalpa coffin while his spirit holds court in the main hall.
entries.literal: Thereupon—wait great tunnel's achieve merit—practice primal day's fine auspicious—sink splendid body in catalpa palace—by main hall to dwell spirit.

entries.zh: 顧望嗣之號咷兮，存臨者之悲聲，悼晏駕之旣修兮，感容車之速征。
entries.en: The heir's keening rings out; mourners sob beside him—the curtained hearse departs all too soon.
entries.literal: Look hope heir's wail—exist attendant's grief sound—mourn dawn-chariot's already prepared—feel funeral-carriage's swift campaign.

entries.zh: 浮飛魂於輕霄兮，就黃墟以滅形，背三光之昭晰兮，歸玄宅之冥冥。
entries.en: His soaring soul mounts thin air and sinks into yellow earth—turning from sun, moon, and stars it enters the shadow underworld.
entries.literal: Float flying soul in light sky—approach yellow mound to extinguish form—turn back three luminaries' brightness—return dark dwelling's dark-dark.

entries.zh: 嗟一往之不反兮，痛閟闥之長扃。
entries.en: Alas—there is no returning from that journey; grief bolts the inner gate forever.
entries.literal: Alas one-go's not return—pain bolt-door's long bar.

entries.zh: 咨遠臣之眇眇兮，成凶諱以怛驚，心孤絕而靡告兮，紛流涕而交頸。
entries.en: We distant ministers stand helpless—news of death strikes like thunder; hearts break with none to tell; tears stream until cheeks meet.
entries.literal: Sigh distant ministers' tiny tiny—complete ominous taboo thereby sore shock—heart lone cut none tell—many shed tears cross necks.

entries.zh: 思恩榮以橫奔兮，閡闕塞之嶢崢，顧衰絰以輕舉兮，迫關防之我嬰。
entries.en: Imperial grace bids me gallop thither—yet palace gates rise sheer; I finger mourning hemp yet frontier posts bind me still.
entries.literal: Think grace glory to dash cross—block palace pass steep towering—look mourning sash light rise—press barrier ward's me bind.

entries.zh: 欲高飛而遙憩兮，憚天網之遠經，遙投骨於山足兮，報恩養於下庭。
entries.en: I would soar far to rest yet dread Heaven's wide net—I would cast my bones at the foothill and repay kindness in the lower court.
entries.literal: Wish high fly remote rest—fear Heaven-net's far warp—far cast bones at mountain foot—repay grace nurture at lower court.

entries.zh: 慨拊心而自悼兮，懼施重而命輕，嗟微驅之是效兮，甘九死而忘生，幾司命之役籍兮，先黃髮而隕零，天蓋高而察卑兮，冀神明之我聽。
entries.en: Beating my breast I mourn—duty weighs heavy yet life seems slight; this mean frame would gladly die nine deaths for him—yet fate's ledger strikes gray heads first; Heaven is high yet sees the low—may spirits hear my plea.
entries.literal: Sigh strike heart self mourn—fear burden heavy life light—alas slight body's this effect—sweet nine deaths forget life—almost Director of Fate's service register—before yellow hair fall scatter—Heaven cover high examine low—hope spirit-brilliant's me hear.

entries.zh: 獨鬱伊而莫愬兮，追顧景而憐形，奏斯文以寫思兮，結翰墨以敷誠。
entries.en: Brooding alone with none to speak—I pity this fading shadow and set forth these lines to lay bare devotion.
entries.literal: Alone depressed yi none complain—trace look shadow pity form—present this text write thought—tie brush ink spread sincerity.

entries.zh: 嗚呼哀哉！」〉
entries.en: Alas, the sorrow!"〉"
entries.literal: Alas how bitter grief!"〉"

entries.zh: 文皇帝諱丕，字子桓，武帝太子也。
entries.en: Emperor Wen—whose personal name was Pi and courtesy name Zihuan—was the heir apparent of Emperor Wu (Cao Cao).
entries.literal: Emperor Wen, taboo name Pi, courtesy name Zihuan, was the heir son of Emperor Wu.

entries.zh: 中平四年冬，生于譙。
entries.en: He was born at Qiao in the winter of the fourth year of the Zhongping era (187 CE).
entries.literal: In the winter of the fourth year of Zhongping, he was born in Qiao.

entries.zh: 〈《魏書》曰：帝生時，有雲氣青色而圜如車盖當其上，終日，望氣者以爲至貴之證，非人臣之氣。
entries.en: 〈The Wei Book records that at his birth a greenish aura hung above him in a disk like a carriage canopy for the whole day; diviners of qi pronounced it the sign of supreme eminence—not the kind of portent that attends an ordinary minister.
entries.literal: 〈The Wei Book says: When the Emperor was born, there was green cloud vapor, round like a carriage canopy, suspended above him all day; those who read auspicious vapors took it as proof of the utmost nobility, not the aura of a mere subject.

entries.zh: 年八歲，能屬文。
entries.en: At eight he could already write polished compositions.
entries.literal: At age eight, he could compose connected literary pieces.

entries.zh: 有逸才，遂博貫古今經傳諸子百家之書。
entries.en: Gifted with extraordinary ability, he went on to command the classics and their commentaries and the writings of the hundred schools past and present.
entries.literal: He had outstanding talent, and thereupon broadly mastered the classics and commentaries and the writings of the hundred schools from ancient to modern times.

entries.zh: 善騎射，好擊劔。
entries.en: He excelled at horsemanship and archery and delighted in swordplay.
entries.literal: He was skilled at riding and archery, and fond of fencing.

entries.zh: 舉茂才，不行。
entries.en: Nominated as a "flourishing talent," he declined to serve.
entries.literal: He was recommended as a maocai (flourishing talent), but did not take office.

entries.zh: 《獻帝起居注》曰：建安十五年，爲司徒趙溫所辟。
entries.en: According to the Daily Records of Emperor Xian, in Jian'an 15 (210 CE) he was recruited by Minister of Education Zhao Wen.
entries.literal: The Daily Records of Emperor Xian says: In the fifteenth year of Jian'an, he was summoned by Minister of Education Zhao Wen.

entries.zh: 太祖表「溫辟臣子弟，選舉故不以實」。
entries.en: The Grand Progenitor memorialized: "Zhao Wen has summoned my sons and younger relatives; therefore the selection is not according to reality."
entries.literal: The Grand Progenitor memorialized: "Zhao Wen has summoned my sons and younger relatives; therefore the selection is not according to reality."

entries.zh: 使侍中守光祿勳郗慮持節奉策免溫官。〉
entries.en: He had Palace Attendant and acting Supervisor of the Household Xi Lu carry the credential and deliver the edict stripping Zhao Wen of his post.〉
entries.literal: He ordered Palace Attendant acting Supervisor of the Household Xi Lu, bearing the insignia, to present the edict and dismiss Zhao Wen from office.〉

entries.zh: 建安十六年，爲五官中郎將、副丞相。
entries.en: In Jian'an 16 (211 CE) he was appointed General of the Household for All Purposes and deputy to the Chancellor.
entries.literal: In the sixteenth year of Jian'an, he became General of the Household for All Purposes and deputy to the Chancellor.

entries.zh: 二十二年，立爲魏太子。
entries.en: In the twenty-second year of Jian'an (217 CE) he was named heir apparent of Wei.
entries.literal: In the twenty-second year, he was established as heir apparent of Wei.

entries.zh: 〈《魏略》曰：太祖不時立太子，太子自疑。
entries.en: 〈The Wei Summary notes that Cao Cao had long delayed naming an heir, and the crown prince began to doubt his position.
entries.literal: 〈The Wei Summary says: The Grand Progenitor did not promptly establish an heir apparent; the heir apparent himself grew doubtful.

entries.zh: 是時有高元呂者，善相人，乃呼問之，對曰：「其貴乃不可言。」
entries.en: There was a physiognomist named Gao Yuanlü whom Pi summoned and questioned; Gao answered, "The degree of eminence is beyond words."
entries.literal: At this time there was a man named Gao Yuanlü who was skilled at physiognomy; he was summoned and asked, and replied: "His nobility cannot be described in words."

entries.zh: 問：「壽幾何？」
entries.en: Pi asked, "How long will he live?"
entries.literal: He was asked: "How long will his lifespan be?"

entries.zh: 元呂曰：「其壽，至四十當有小苦，過是無憂也。」
entries.en: Gao Yuanlü replied, "He will meet a brief ordeal at forty; after that, nothing to fear."
entries.literal: Yuanlü said: "As for his lifespan, when he reaches forty there will be a small hardship; beyond that there will be no worries."

entries.zh: 後無幾而立爲王太子，至年四十而薨。〉
entries.en: Soon afterward Pi was installed as heir apparent of the King of Wei; he died in his fortieth year.
entries.literal: Not long afterward he was established as heir apparent of the king; he reached age forty and died.

entries.zh: 太祖崩，嗣位爲丞相、魏王。
entries.en: When Cao Cao died, Pi succeeded him as Chancellor and King of Wei.
entries.literal: The Grand Progenitor died; he succeeded to the posts of Chancellor and King of Wei.

entries.zh: 〈袁宏《漢紀》載漢帝詔曰：「魏太子丕：昔皇天授乃顯考以翼我皇家，遂攘除羣凶，拓定九州，弘功茂績，光于宇宙，朕用垂拱負扆二十有餘載。
entries.en: 〈Yuan Hong's Han Annals preserves an imperial edict: "Heir apparent Pi of Wei: High Heaven once entrusted your late father to uphold Our house; he crushed the rebels, pacified the Nine Regions, and left achievements that fill heaven and earth—while I, leaning on the cushions at court, reigned at ease for more than twenty years.
entries.literal: 〈Yuan Hong's Han Annals carries an edict of the Han Emperor: "Wei heir apparent Pi: Formerly August Heaven entrusted your illustrious father to aid Our royal house; thereupon he swept away the multitude of villains and expanded and settled the Nine Provinces; his grand merit and abundant deeds shine through the universe; I therefore leaned on the rail with folded arms for more than twenty years.

entries.zh: 天不憖遺一老，永保余一人，早世潛神，哀悼傷切。
entries.en: Heaven would not spare one wise elder to shelter Me alone; he left the world too soon, and My sorrow cuts deep.
entries.literal: Heaven is not willing to leave Us one elder to forever protect Us alone; he departed the world early and concealed his spirit; Our grief and mourning are cutting.

entries.zh: 丕奕世宣明，宜秉文武，紹熙前緒。
entries.en: Pi carries forward a luminous succession; he should wield both civil and military authority and carry on the work begun before him.
entries.literal: Pi in successive generations shines brightly; he should grasp civil and military affairs and continue and brighten the former threads.

entries.zh: 今使使持節御史大夫華歆奉策詔授丕丞相印綬、魏王璽紱，領冀州牧。
entries.en: I therefore dispatch Bearer of the Imperial Insignia and Imperial Counselor Hua Xin to deliver the edict investing Pi with the Chancellor's seal and ribbon, the regalia of the King of Wei, and the governorship of Ji Province.
entries.literal: Now sending Bearer of the Imperial Insignia Imperial Counselor Hua Xin to present by edict and confer on Pi the Chancellor's seal-cord, the King of Wei's seal and ribbon, and headship as Governor of Ji Province.

entries.zh: 方今外有遺虜，遐夷未賔，旗鼓猶在邊境，干戈不得韜刃，斯乃播揚洪烈，立功垂名之秋也。
entries.en: Barbarians still linger beyond the frontiers, distant peoples have not yet come to court, signal drums stand posted along the borders, and arms cannot yet be laid aside—this is the very hour to broadcast great deeds and win lasting fame.
entries.literal: At present beyond Us there remain remnant barbarians; distant tribes have not yet submitted; banners and drums are still at the borders; weapons cannot sheath their blades—this is indeed the autumn season for spreading abroad mighty deeds and establishing merit to leave a name.

entries.zh: 豈得脩諒闇之禮，究曾、閔之志哉？
entries.en: How could you confine yourself to solitary mourning like a common heir or imitate only the filial retreats of Zengzi and Min Ziqian?
entries.literal: How can one observe the rites of silent mourning in the dark chamber and exhaust the intentions of Zeng and Min?

entries.zh: 其敬服朕命，抑弭憂懷，旁祗厥緒，時亮庶功，以稱朕意。
entries.en: Therefore obey this charge with reverence: set anxiety aside, uphold the legacy on every side, and in due course bring every task to fruition, that My wishes may be fulfilled.
entries.literal: Respectfully obey Our command; suppress and extinguish anxious thoughts; broadly reverence its continuation; seasonally brighten the various achievements, thereby matching Our intention.

entries.zh: 於戲，可不勉與！」〉
entries.en: Ah—how could you do otherwise than strive with all your might!"〉"
entries.literal: Alas, can you not exert yourself!"〉"

entries.zh: 尊王后曰王太后。
entries.en: The queen consort was elevated to Queen Dowager of Wei.
entries.literal: The queen consort was honored as Queen Dowager of the King.

entries.zh: 改建安二十五年爲延康元年。
entries.en: The twenty-fifth year of Jian'an was redesignated the first year of the Yan Kang era (220 CE).
entries.literal: He changed the twenty-fifth year of Jian'an to be the first year of Yan Kang.

entries.zh: 十七年，董昭等謂太祖宜進爵國公，九錫備物，以彰殊勳，密以諮彧。
entries.en: In the seventeenth year, Dong Zhao and others urged that the Grand Progenitor be raised to Duke of a State with the full nine bestowals to honor his exceptional achievements, and they quietly sought Yu's counsel.
entries.literal: In the seventeenth year, Dong Zhao and others said the Grand Progenitor should be advanced to the rank of Duke of a State, with the nine bestowals and all their appurtenances, to manifest extraordinary merit, and secretly consulted Yu about it.

entries.zh: 彧以爲太祖本興義兵以匡朝寧國，秉忠貞之誠，守退讓之實；
entries.en: Yu held that the Grand Progenitor had originally raised righteous armies to restore the dynasty and pacify the realm, maintaining loyal integrity and the virtue of modest restraint;
entries.literal: Yu believed that the Grand Progenitor had originally raised righteous troops to rectify the court and pacify the state, holding to the sincerity of loyalty and steadfastness, and keeping to the reality of yielding and modesty;

entries.zh: 君子愛人以德，不宜如此。
entries.en: A gentleman shows care for others through virtue — such a course was inappropriate.
entries.literal: A gentleman loves others through virtue; it is not fitting to act thus.

entries.zh: 太祖由是心不能平。
entries.en: The Grand Progenitor consequently took this badly at heart.
entries.literal: Because of this, the Grand Progenitor's heart could not be at ease.

entries.zh: 會征孫權，表請彧勞軍于譙，因輒留彧，以侍中光祿大夫持節，參丞相軍事。
entries.en: When Cao Cao marched against Sun Quan, he petitioned to have Yu encourage the troops at Qiao, then kept him there — appointing him Palace Attendant and Household Counsellor with credentials of authority to assist the Chancellor in military affairs.
entries.literal: It happened that when campaigning against Sun Quan, he memorialized requesting that Yu encourage the troops at Qiao, and on this pretext detained Yu, appointing him Palace Attendant and Household Counsellor bearing credentials of authority, to participate in military affairs of the Chancellor.

entries.zh: 太祖軍至濡須，彧疾留壽春，以憂薨，時年五十。
entries.en: When the Grand Progenitor's army reached Ruxu, Yu fell ill and remained at Shouchun, where he died of grief at the age of fifty.
entries.literal: When the Grand Progenitor's army reached Ruxu, Yu fell ill and remained at Shouchun; he died of grief, aged fifty at the time.

entries.zh: 諡曰敬侯。
entries.en: He was posthumously titled Marquis Jing.
entries.literal: His posthumous title was Marquis Jing.

entries.zh: 明年，太祖遂爲魏公矣。
entries.en: The following year, the Grand Progenitor became Duke of Wei.
entries.literal: The next year, the Grand Progenitor then became Duke of Wei.

entries.zh: 《魏氏春秋》曰：太祖饋彧食，發之乃空器也，於是飲藥而卒。
entries.en: The Wei Clan Annals says that the Grand Progenitor sent Yu food, but when he opened it, the container was empty — whereupon Yu drank poison and died.
entries.literal: The Wei Clan Annals states: The Grand Progenitor sent Yu food; when he opened it, it was an empty vessel; whereupon he drank medicine and died.

entries.zh: 咸熙二年，贈彧太尉。
entries.en: In the second year of Xianxi, Yu was posthumously awarded the rank of Grand Commandant.
entries.literal: In the second year of Xianxi, Yu was posthumously granted the office of Grand Commandant.

entries.zh: 《彧別傳》曰：彧自爲尚書令，常以書陳事，臨薨，皆焚毀之，故奇策密謀不得盡聞也。
entries.en: The Separate Biography of Yu records that from his time as Director of the Masters of Writing, he habitually submitted affairs in writing; on his deathbed he burned them all, so his most ingenious strategies were never fully known.
entries.literal: The Separate Biography of Yu states: From the time Yu served as Director of the Masters of Writing, he often submitted affairs in written memorials; on the verge of death, he burned and destroyed them all; therefore extraordinary plans and secret stratagems could not be fully heard of.

entries.zh: 是時征役草創，制度多所興復，彧嘗言於太祖曰：「昔舜分命禹、稷、契、皐陶以揆庶績，教化征伐，並時而用。
entries.en: At that time campaigns and corvée were still being organized and many institutions were being revived. Yu once told the Grand Progenitor: "Long ago, Shun separately charged Yu, Ji, Qi, and Gao Yao with governing the people's affairs — civilizing instruction and military campaigns were pursued at the same time.
entries.literal: At that time military campaigns and corvée labor were in their initial stages, and institutions were being widely revived; Yu once said to the Grand Progenitor: "In ancient times Shun separately appointed Yu, Ji, Qi, and Gao Yao to oversee the multitude of achievements; civilizing instruction and military expeditions were employed simultaneously.

entries.zh: 及髙祖之初，金革方殷，猶舉民能善教訓者，叔孫通習禮儀於戎旅之閒，世祖有投戈講藝、息馬論道之事，君子無終食之閒違仁。
entries.en: Even at the beginning of the Han, when warfare was still fierce, the court still sought out men capable of teaching and instruction — Shusun Tong mastered ritual amid military encampments, and Emperor Guangwu set aside arms to lecture on the classics and rested horses to discuss the Way. A gentleman does not neglect benevolence even for the span of a single meal.
entries.literal: At the beginning of the High Ancestor's reign, the clash of arms and armor was still intense, yet he still elevated those among the people able to teach and instruct well; Shusun Tong became versed in ritual propriety amid military camps; the World Ancestor had occasions for casting aside weapons to lecture on the arts and resting horses to discuss the Way; a gentleman has not even the interval of a single meal in which to depart from benevolence.

entries.zh: 今公外定武功，内興文學，使干戈戢睦，大道流行，國難方弭，六禮倶治，此姬旦宰周之所以速平也。
entries.en: Now you have subdued the realm by force abroad and are fostering scholarship at home — weapons are being laid aside, the Great Way spreads, national crisis is being resolved, and the six rites are being restored. This is how the Duke of Zhou governed Zhou and brought peace so swiftly.
entries.literal: Now my lord outwardly settles martial achievements and inwardly raises literary studies, causing weapons and armor to be laid aside in peace, the Great Way to spread, national troubles just to be quelled, and the six rites all to be governed — this is why the Duke of Zhou governed Zhou and brought rapid peace.

entries.zh: 旣立德立功，而又兼立言，成仲尼述作之意；
entries.en: You have established virtue and merit, and by adding literary achievement you fulfill Confucius's purpose in his writings;
entries.literal: Having already established virtue and established merit, and furthermore also establishing words, fulfilling the intent of Zhongni's compositions;

entries.zh: 顯制度於當時，揚名於後世，豈不盛哉！
entries.en: making your institutions manifest in your own age and your fame endure for posterity — what could be more splendid!
entries.literal: displaying institutions in the present age, spreading one's fame in later generations — how could it not be magnificent!

entries.zh: 若須武事畢而後制作，以稽治化，於事未敏。
entries.en: If you wait until all military matters are finished before turning to cultural institutions in order to examine governance and transformation, you will have been too slow.
entries.literal: If one must wait until military affairs are concluded before then undertaking cultural creation, in order to examine governance and transformation, in affairs this lacks keenness.

entries.zh: 宜集天下大才通儒，考論六經，刊定傳記，存古今之學，除其煩重，以一聖眞，並隆禮學，漸敦教化，則王道兩濟。」
entries.en: You should assemble the empire's greatest scholars and Confucian experts to examine and discuss the Six Classics, standardize the commentarial traditions, preserve learning ancient and modern while eliminating what is redundant, unify them around the sage's true teaching, and together elevate ritual learning to gradually deepen civilizing instruction — then the royal Way will be fully realized on both fronts."
entries.literal: It would be fitting to gather the great talents and thoroughly learned Confucians of the empire, examine and discuss the Six Classics, edit and fix the commentarial traditions, preserve the learning of past and present, remove what is cumbersome and redundant, unite them in the one true teaching of the sage, and together elevate the study of ritual, gradually thickening civilizing instruction — then the royal Way would be served on both sides."

entries.zh: 彧從容與太祖論治道，如此之類甚衆，太祖常嘉納之。
entries.en: Yu often discussed principles of governance with the Grand Progenitor in an unhurried manner; the Grand Progenitor frequently approved and adopted his counsel.
entries.literal: Yu calmly discussed principles of governance with the Grand Progenitor; matters of this sort were very numerous; the Grand Progenitor often commended and accepted them.

entries.zh: 彧德行周備，非正道不用心，名重天下，莫不以爲儀表，海内英儁咸宗焉。
entries.en: Yu's virtue and conduct were complete in every respect; he devoted himself only to the right path. His fame resounded throughout the realm, and all regarded him as a model — the most distinguished men in the land looked up to him.
entries.literal: Yu's virtue and conduct were comprehensive and complete; he would not apply his mind except to the correct Way; his renown weighed heavily throughout the realm; none did not regard him as a model; eminent talents within the seas all looked up to him.

entries.zh: 司馬宣王常稱書傳遠事，吾自耳目所從聞見，逮百數十年間，賢才未有及荀令君者也。
entries.en: The Lord of Xuan (Sima Yi) often said: "In historical records and in what I myself have witnessed over more than a hundred years, I have seen no talent to equal Director Xun."
entries.literal: The Lord of Xuan, Sima Yi, often said: "In what is recorded in books and transmitted from distant events, and in what I myself have heard and seen from my own eyes and ears, spanning a hundred and some decades, there has been no talented man who could match Director Xun."

entries.zh: 前後所舉者，命世大才，邦邑則荀攸、鍾繇、陳羣，海内則司馬宣王，及引致當世知名郗慮、華歆、王朗、荀恱、杜襲、辛毗、趙儼之儔，終爲卿相，以十數人。
entries.en: Those he recommended over the years were truly exceptional talents: Xun You, Zhong Yao, and Chen Qun from his home region; the Lord of Xuan from across the realm; and he also recruited such celebrated figures as Xi Lu, Hua Xin, Wang Lang, Xun Yue, Du Xi, Xin Pi, and Zhao Yan — more than a dozen in all who rose to ministerial rank.
entries.literal: Those he recommended before and after were world-shaking great talents: within his native region, Xun You, Zhong Yao, and Chen Qun; within the seas, the Lord of Xuan; and he also brought in the well-known men of the age, Xi Lu, Hua Xin, Wang Lang, Xun Yue, Du Xi, Xin Pi, Zhao Yan, and the like — who in the end became ministers and chancellors, numbering more than a dozen.

entries.zh: 取士不以一揆，戲志才、郭嘉等有負俗之譏，杜畿簡傲少文，皆以智策舉之，終各顯名。
entries.en: He did not select men by a single standard: Xi Zhicai and Guo Jia had reputations for violating convention, and Du Ji was austere, proud, and unpolished — yet he recommended all of them for their strategic brilliance, and each rose to prominence.
entries.literal: In selecting scholars he did not use a single standard; Xi Zhicai and Guo Jia and others bore criticisms for violating custom; Du Ji was frugal, proud, and lacking in refinement — all were recommended through their strategic intelligence, and in the end each achieved distinguished fame.

entries.zh: 荀攸後爲魏尚書令，亦推賢進士。
entries.en: Xun You later served as Wei Director of the Masters of Writing and likewise promoted worthy talents.
entries.literal: Xun You later served as Director of the Masters of Writing for Wei and also promoted worthy men and advanced scholars.

entries.zh: 太祖曰：「二荀令之論人，久而益信，吾沒世不忘。」
entries.en: The Grand Progenitor said: "The two Directors Xun judged men so well that time only confirms their judgment — I shall never forget it."
entries.literal: The Grand Progenitor said: "The two Directors Xun's judgments of men, the longer they stand the more trustworthy they prove — I shall not forget them while I live."

entries.zh: 鍾繇以爲顏子旣沒，能備九德，不貳其過，唯荀彧然。
entries.en: Zhong Yao believed that since Yan Hui's death, only Xun Yu had possessed all nine virtues without wavering from his principles.
entries.literal: Zhong Yao held that since Yanzi died, only Xun Yu could possess all nine virtues and not stray from his errors.

entries.zh: 或問繇曰：「君雅重荀君，比之顏子，自以不及，可得聞乎？」
entries.en: Someone asked Zhong Yao: "You greatly esteem Lord Xun and compare him to Yan Hui, yet say you cannot match him — may we hear why?"
entries.literal: Someone asked Yao: "You greatly esteem Lord Xun, comparing him to Yanzi, yet consider yourself unequal — may we hear your reasons?"

entries.zh: 曰：「夫明君師臣，其次友之。
entries.en: He replied: "An enlightened lord treats his minister as a teacher, or at least as a friend.
entries.literal: He said: "An enlightened lord treats his minister as a teacher, or at least as a friend.

entries.zh: 以太祖之聦明，毎有大事，常先諮之荀君，是則古師友之義也。
entries.en: Given the Grand Progenitor's brilliance, whenever a major matter arose he always consulted Lord Xun first — that is the ancient ideal of a teacher-friend relationship.
entries.literal: With the Grand Progenitor's brilliance, whenever there was a major affair, he would always first consult Lord Xun — this is the ancient meaning of teacher and friend.

entries.zh: 吾等受命而行，猶或不盡，相去顧不遠邪！」
entries.en: We merely receive orders and carry them out, and even then we sometimes fall short — are we not rather close to each other in standing!"
entries.literal: We receive orders and carry them out, yet still sometimes fall short — the distance between us, does it not seem not far!"

entries.zh: 《獻帝春秋》曰：董承之誅，伏后與父完書，言司空殺董承，帝方爲報怨。
entries.en: The Spring and Autumn Annals of Emperor Xian records that after Dong Cheng's execution, Empress Fu wrote to her father Fu Wan, saying the Minister of Works had killed Dong Cheng and the Emperor was now bent on revenge.
entries.literal: The Spring and Autumn Annals of Emperor Xian states: After Dong Cheng's execution, Empress Fu wrote to her father Wan, saying the Minister of Works had killed Dong Cheng and the Emperor was now seeking revenge.

entries.zh: 完得書以示彧，彧惡之，久隱而不言。
entries.en: Fu Wan received the letter and showed it to Yu; Yu was appalled but kept silent about it for a long time.
entries.literal: Wan received the letter and showed it to Yu; Yu hated it and for a long time concealed it without speaking.

entries.zh: 完以示妻弟樊普，普封以呈太祖，太祖陰爲之備。
entries.en: Fu Wan showed it to his wife's younger brother Fan Pu, who sealed it and presented it to the Grand Progenitor; Cao Cao secretly began to prepare against the threat.
entries.literal: Wan showed it to his wife's younger brother Fan Pu; Pu sealed it and presented it to the Grand Progenitor; the Grand Progenitor secretly made preparations on account of it.

entries.zh: 彧後恐事覺，欲自發之，因求使至鄴，勸太祖以女配帝。
entries.en: Yu later feared discovery and wished to expose the matter himself; he requested permission to go to Ye as envoy and urged the Grand Progenitor to marry his daughter to the Emperor.
entries.literal: Yu later feared the matter would be discovered and wished to expose it himself; he therefore requested to be sent as envoy to Ye, and urged the Grand Progenitor to marry his daughter to the Emperor.

entries.zh: 太祖曰：「今朝廷有伏后，吾女何得以配上，吾以微功見録，位爲宰相，豈復賴女寵乎！」
entries.en: The Grand Progenitor said: "The court already has Empress Fu — how can my daughter be made empress? I rose to the chancellorship on modest merit alone — must I rely on my daughter's favor now?"
entries.literal: The Grand Progenitor said: "Now the court has Empress Fu — how could my daughter be matched to ascend the throne? I was recorded for minor achievements and occupy the post of chancellor — would I still depend on my daughter's favor!"

entries.zh: 彧曰：「伏后無子，性又凶邪，往常與父書，言辭醜惡，可因此廢也。」
entries.en: Yu said: "Empress Fu has no children, and her nature is vicious and depraved. Her letters to her father were full of ugly and vile language — she can be deposed on that basis."
entries.literal: Yu said: "Empress Fu has no son, and her nature is also fierce and wicked; she often wrote to her father with ugly and vile language — she can be deposed on this account."

entries.zh: 太祖曰：「卿昔何不道之？」
entries.en: The Grand Progenitor said: "Why didn't you tell me this before?"
entries.literal: The Grand Progenitor said: "Why did you not speak of this before?"

entries.zh: 彧陽驚曰：「昔已嘗爲公言也。」
entries.en: Yu feigned surprise and said: "I already told you about it long ago."
entries.literal: Yu feigned surprise and said: "In the past I had already spoken to you about it."

entries.zh: 太祖曰：「此豈小事而吾忘之！」
entries.en: The Grand Progenitor said: "This is hardly a trifling matter — how could I have forgotten it!"
entries.literal: The Grand Progenitor said: "How could this be a minor matter and I have forgotten it!"

entries.zh: 彧又驚曰：「誠未語公邪！
entries.en: Yu feigned surprise again: "Truly I never told you, my lord!
entries.literal: Yu was surprised again and said: "Truly I did not tell you, my lord!

entries.zh: 昔公在官渡與袁紹相持，恐增内顧之念，故不言爾。」
entries.en: When you were at Guandu in stalemate with Yuan Shao, I feared it would distract you with domestic worries, so I said nothing."
entries.literal: In the past when you were at Guandu locked in stalemate with Yuan Shao, I feared increasing thoughts of looking back within — therefore I did not speak of it."

entries.zh: 太祖曰：「官渡事後何以不言？」
entries.en: The Grand Progenitor said: "Why didn't you speak after Guandu?"
entries.literal: The Grand Progenitor said: "After the affair at Guandu, why did you not speak?"

entries.zh: 彧無對，謝闕而已。
entries.en: Yu had no answer and could only apologize for his failure.
entries.literal: Yu had no reply; he merely apologized for his lapse.

entries.zh: 太祖以此恨彧，而外含容之，故世莫得知。
entries.en: The Grand Progenitor harbored resentment over this but concealed it outwardly, so the world never knew.
