entries.literal: The Grand Progenitor on this account bore resentment toward Yu, yet outwardly tolerated him; therefore the world did not know of it.

entries.zh: 至董昭建立魏公之議，彧意不同，欲言之於太祖。
entries.en: When Dong Zhao proposed establishing the Duke of Wei, Yu disagreed and wished to speak to the Grand Progenitor about it.
entries.literal: When it came to Dong Zhao's proposal to establish the Grand Progenitor as Duke of Wei, Yu's view differed; he wished to speak of it to the Grand Progenitor.

entries.zh: 及齎璽書犒軍，飲饗禮畢，彧留請閒。
entries.en: When Yu arrived bearing the imperial edict to reward the troops and the banquet concluded, he stayed behind to request a private audience.
entries.literal: When he brought the imperial edict written on jade to reward the troops and the banquet rites were concluded, Yu remained to request a private audience.

entries.zh: 太祖知彧欲言封事，揖而遣之，彧遂不得言。
entries.en: The Grand Progenitor knew Yu wanted to discuss the enfeoffment; he bowed and dismissed him, and Yu never got to speak.
entries.literal: The Grand Progenitor knew Yu wished to speak about the enfeoffment matter; he bowed and dismissed him; Yu thus could not speak.

entries.zh: 彧卒於壽春，壽春亡者告孫權，言太祖使彧殺伏后，彧不從，故自殺。
entries.en: When Yu died at Shouchun, a refugee from that city told Sun Quan that the Grand Progenitor had ordered Yu to kill Empress Fu, that Yu refused, and therefore killed himself.
entries.literal: Yu died at Shouchun; a refugee from Shouchun informed Sun Quan, saying the Grand Progenitor had ordered Yu to kill Empress Fu and Yu refused, therefore killing himself.

entries.zh: 權以露布於蜀，劉備聞之，曰：「老賊不死，禍亂未已。」
entries.en: Sun Quan publicized this account to Shu; when Liu Bei heard it, he said: "That old villain is not dead — the turmoil is far from over."
entries.literal: Sun Quan broadcast this by open proclamation to Shu; when Liu Bei heard it, he said: "The old villain does not die — calamity and disorder are not yet ended."

entries.zh: 臣松之案《獻帝春秋》云彧欲發伏后事而求使至鄴，而方誣太祖云「昔已嘗言」。
entries.en: Pei Songzhi notes: The Spring and Autumn Annals of Emperor Xian says Yu wished to expose the Empress Fu affair and sought an envoy mission to Ye, yet then falsely told the Grand Progenitor "I had already told you."
entries.literal: Your servant Songzhi investigates: The Spring and Autumn Annals of Emperor Xian says that Yu wished to expose the Empress Fu matter and therefore requested to be sent to Ye, yet then falsely accused the Grand Progenitor, saying "I had already spoken before."

entries.zh: 言旣無徴，迴託以官渡之虞，俛仰之間，辭情頓屈，雖在庸人，猶不至此，何以玷累賢哲哉！
entries.en: His claim had no basis; he then pivoted to the excuse of Guandu — and in that exchange his argument collapsed utterly. Even an ordinary man would not behave so — how could such conduct be imputed to a worthy sage!
entries.literal: The words had no evidence; he then turned and excused himself with the worry at Guandu; in the lowering and raising of his head, his words and feelings suddenly collapsed — even among ordinary men, it would not reach this point; how could it stain and burden a worthy sage!

entries.zh: 凡諸云云，皆出自鄙俚，可謂以吾儕之言而厚誣君子者矣。
entries.en: All such accounts come from vulgar sources — they use the words of common folk to slander a gentleman most unjustly.
entries.literal: All such talk in every case originates from vulgar folk; it may be said to use words of people like us to falsely and heavily accuse a gentleman.

entries.zh: 袁暐虚罔之類，此最爲甚也。
entries.en: Among fabricators like Yuan Hui, this case is the worst.
entries.literal: Among the false and groundless sorts like Yuan Hui, this is the most extreme.

entries.zh: 子惲，嗣侯，官至虎賁中郎將。
entries.en: His son Yun succeeded to the marquisate and rose to Tiger Guard Commander of the Central.
entries.literal: His son Yun succeeded to the marquisate and reached the office of Tiger Guard Commander of the Central.

entries.zh: 初，文帝與平原侯植並有擬論，文帝曲禮事彧。
entries.en: Early on, both Emperor Wen and the Marquis of Pingyuan (Cao Zhi) were contenders for succession; Emperor Wen treated Yu with especial courtesy.
entries.literal: Initially, Emperor Wen and the Marquis of Pingyuan Zhi both had aspirations to succession; Emperor Wen bent to courtesy in serving Yu.

entries.zh: 及彧卒，惲又與植善，而與夏侯尚不穆，文帝深恨惲。
entries.en: After Yu's death, Yun remained friendly with Cao Zhi but was on bad terms with Xiahou Shang; Emperor Wen deeply resented him.
entries.literal: When Yu died, Yun was again on good terms with Zhi, yet was not harmonious with Xiahou Shang; Emperor Wen deeply resented Yun.

entries.zh: 惲早卒，子甝、霬，音翼。
entries.en: Yun died young, leaving sons Kan and Hui (the latter pronounced Yi).
entries.literal: Yun died young; his sons Kan and Hui — Hui is pronounced Yi.

entries.zh: 以外甥故猶寵待。
entries.en: Because of the family connection by marriage, they were still treated with favor.
entries.literal: Because of the connection as nephew by marriage, he was still treated with favor.

entries.zh: 惲弟俁，御史中丞，俁弟詵，大將軍從事中郎，皆知名，早卒。
entries.en: Yun's younger brother Hou served as Censor-in-Chief; Hou's younger brother Shen served as Staff Officer to the General-in-Chief — all were well known and died young.
entries.literal: Yun's younger brother Hou was Censor-in-Chief; Hou's younger brother Shen was Staff Officer to the General-in-Chief — all were well known and died young.

entries.zh: 《荀氏家傳》曰：惲字長倩，俁字叔倩，詵字曼倩，俁子寓，字景伯。
entries.en: The Genealogical Biography of the Xun Clan records: Yun styled Changqian, Hou styled Shuqian, Shen styled Manqian, and Hou's son Yu styled Jingbo.
entries.literal: The Genealogical Biography of the Xun Clan states: Yun's style name was Changqian, Hou's was Shuqian, Shen's was Manqian, and Hou's son Yu's style name was Jingbo.

entries.zh: 《世語》曰：寓少與裴楷、王戎、杜默倶有名京邑，仕晉，位至尚書，名見顯著。
entries.en: The Tales of the Age records that in youth Yu was as famous in the capital as Pei Kai, Wang Rong, and Du Mo; serving Jin, he rose to Master of Writing with great renown.
entries.literal: The Tales of the Age states: Yu in his youth was together with Pei Kai, Wang Rong, and Du Mo equally famous in the capital; he served Jin and reached the office of Master of Writing; his fame was conspicuous.

entries.zh: 子羽嗣，位至尚書。
entries.en: His son Yu succeeded him and rose to Master of Writing.
entries.literal: His son Yu succeeded and reached the office of Master of Writing.

entries.zh: 詵弟顗，咸熙中爲司空。
entries.en: Shen's younger brother Yi served as Minister of Works during the Xianxi period.
entries.literal: Shen's younger brother Yi, in the Xianxi period served as Minister of Works.

entries.zh: 《晉陽秋》曰：顗字景倩，幼爲姊夫陳羣所異。
entries.en: The Spring and Autumn Annals of Jin records that Yi styled Jingqian and was recognized as extraordinary in youth by his brother-in-law Chen Qun.
entries.literal: The Spring and Autumn Annals of Jin states: Yi's style name was Jingqian; in youth he was regarded as extraordinary by his sister's husband Chen Qun.

entries.zh: 博學洽聞，意思愼密。
entries.en: He was erudite and well informed, with careful and penetrating judgment.
entries.literal: He was broadly learned and well informed; his thoughts were careful and close.

entries.zh: 司馬宣王見顗，奇之，曰：「荀令君之子也。
entries.en: When the Lord of Xuan (Sima Yi) met Yi, he was struck by him and said: "He is Director Xun's son.
entries.literal: The Lord of Xuan saw Yi and marveled at him, saying: "This is the son of Director Xun.

entries.zh: 近見袁偘，亦曜卿之子也。」
entries.en: I recently met Yuan Kan — he too is Lord Yao's son."
entries.literal: Recently I saw Yuan Kan — he too is the son of Lord Yao."

entries.zh: 擢拜散騎侍郎。
entries.en: He was promoted to Gentleman of the Central Secretariat.
entries.literal: He was promoted and appointed Gentleman of the Central Secretariat.

entries.zh: 顗佐命晉室，位至太尉，封臨淮康公。
entries.en: Yi assisted in establishing the Jin dynasty, rose to Grand Commandant, and was enfeoffed as Duke Kang of Linhuai.
entries.literal: Yi assisted in founding the Jin house, reached the office of Grand Commandant, and was enfeoffed as Duke Kang of Linhuai.

entries.zh: 嘗難鍾會「易無互體」，見稱於世。
entries.en: He once disputed Zhong Hui's claim that "the Book of Changes has no mutual imagery," earning renown throughout the realm.
entries.literal: He once challenged Zhong Hui's proposition that "there is no mutual imagery in the Changes," and was praised by the world.

entries.zh: 顗弟粲，字奉倩。
entries.en: Yi's younger brother Can styled Fengqian.
entries.literal: Yi's younger brother Can's style name was Fengqian.

entries.zh: 何劭爲粲傳曰：粲字奉倩，粲諸兄並以儒術論議，而粲獨好言道，常以爲子貢稱夫子之言性與天道，不可得聞，然則六籍雖存，固聖人之糠粃。
entries.en: He Shao wrote a biography of Can: Can styled Fengqian. His elder brothers all debated in the Confucian tradition, but Can alone loved to discuss the Way. He often argued that since Zigong said the Master's words on human nature and the Way of Heaven could not be fully conveyed, the Six Classics, though preserved, are but the sage's chaff.
entries.literal: He Shao wrote a biography of Can stating: Can's style name was Fengqian; Can's elder brothers all engaged in Confucian learning and debate, but Can alone delighted in discussing the Way; he often held that when Zigong said the Master's words on human nature and the Way of Heaven could not be heard, then although the Six Classics remained, they were truly the chaff of the sage.

entries.zh: 粲兄俁難曰：「易亦云聖人立象以盡意，繫辭焉以盡言，則微言胡爲不可得而聞見哉？」
entries.en: Can's elder brother Hou objected: "The Book of Changes says the sage established images to fully express meaning and appended words to fully express speech — then why could subtle teachings not be heard?"
entries.literal: Can's elder brother Hou challenged him, saying: "The Changes also says the sage established images to fully express meaning and attached words to fully express speech — then why could subtle words not be obtained and heard and seen?"

entries.zh: 粲荅曰：「蓋理之微者，非物象之所舉也。
entries.en: Can replied: "Subtle principles cannot be fully conveyed through material images.
entries.literal: Can replied: "Principles that are subtle are not what material images can fully express.

entries.zh: 今稱立象以盡意，此非通于意外者也。
entries.en: To say that establishing images fully expresses meaning is not to penetrate beyond the image itself.
entries.literal: Now to say that establishing images fully expresses meaning — this does not penetrate beyond the image.

entries.zh: 繫辭焉以盡言，此非言乎繫表者也；
entries.en: Attaching words to fully express speech is not to speak of what is merely attached to the surface;
entries.literal: Attaching words to fully express speech — this is not speaking of what is attached to the surface;

entries.zh: 斯則象外之意，繫表之言，固蘊而不出矣。」
entries.en: the meaning beyond the images and the words beyond the surface are inherently contained and do not emerge."
entries.literal: then the meaning beyond the image and the words attached to the surface are originally hidden and do not emerge."

entries.zh: 及當時能言者不能屈也。
entries.en: At the time, none of the leading debaters could defeat him.
entries.literal: At the time, those skilled in discourse could not refute him.

entries.zh: 又論父彧不如從兄攸。
entries.en: He also argued that his father Yu was inferior to his cousin Xun You.
entries.literal: He also argued that his father Yu was not equal to his cousin You.

entries.zh: 彧立德髙整，軌儀以訓物，而攸不治外形，愼密自居而已。
entries.en: Yu's virtue was lofty and orderly, teaching others through standard and ceremony; Xun You did not cultivate appearances outwardly, contenting himself with careful inward reserve.
entries.literal: Yu established virtue that was lofty and ordered, using standards and ceremony to instruct things; You did not cultivate external appearance, merely keeping careful secrecy to himself.

entries.zh: 粲以此言善攸，諸兄怒而不能迴也。
entries.en: Can used this argument to praise Xun You; his elder brothers were furious but could not change his mind.
entries.literal: Can with these words praised You; his elder brothers were angry but could not turn him back.

entries.zh: 太和初，到京邑與傅嘏談。
entries.en: Early in the Taihe reign, he came to the capital and discussed philosophy with Fu Gu.
entries.literal: At the beginning of the Taihe reign, he arrived at the capital and conversed with Fu Gu.

entries.zh: 嘏善名理而粲尚玄遠，宗致雖同，倉卒時或有格而不相得意。
entries.en: Fu Gu excelled at logical disputation while Can favored the abstruse and metaphysical; though they shared fundamental aims, in quick exchanges they sometimes clashed and failed to understand each other.
entries.literal: Gu was skilled in the principles of naming while Can esteemed the abstruse and far-reaching; although their fundamental aims were the same, in hasty moments there were sometimes clashes and mutual incomprehension.

entries.zh: 裴徽通彼我之懷，爲二家騎驛，頃之，粲與嘏善。
entries.en: Pei Hui understood both men's perspectives and mediated between them; before long, Can and Fu Gu became friends.
entries.literal: Pei Hui understood the feelings of both sides and served as a relay rider between the two schools; shortly thereafter, Can and Gu became friends.

entries.zh: 夏侯玄亦親。
entries.en: He was also close to Xiahou Xuan.
entries.literal: Xiahou Xuan was also close to him.

entries.zh: 常謂嘏、玄曰：「子等在世塗間，功名必勝我，但識劣我耳！」
entries.en: He often told Fu Gu and Xiahou Xuan: "You will surpass me in worldly fame and achievement, but your understanding falls short of mine!"
entries.literal: He often said to Gu and Xuan: "You gentlemen on the path of worldly life — your fame and achievement will surely surpass mine, but your insight is inferior to mine!"

entries.zh: 嘏難曰：「能盛功名者，識也。
entries.en: Fu Gu objected: "It is insight that produces great fame and achievement.
entries.literal: Gu challenged him, saying: "Those who can flourish in fame and achievement — that is insight.

entries.zh: 天下孰有本不足而末有餘者邪？」
entries.en: Who in the world has a weak foundation but abundant fruit?"
entries.literal: In all the world, is there anyone whose root is insufficient yet whose branches are abundant?"

entries.zh: 粲曰：「功名者，志局之所獎也。
entries.en: Can replied: "Fame and achievement are the rewards of ambition and vision.
entries.literal: Can said: "Fame and achievement are what ambition and design reward.

entries.zh: 然則志局自一物耳，固非識之所獨濟也。
entries.en: Ambition and vision are one thing — they are not achieved by insight alone.
entries.literal: Thus ambition and design are themselves one thing; they are certainly not what insight alone can accomplish.

entries.zh: 我以能使子等爲貴，然未必齊子等所爲也。」
entries.en: I take pride in being able to make men like you succeed, yet I may not equal what men like you achieve."
entries.literal: I take as my honor that I can make gentlemen like you succeed, yet I am not necessarily equal to what gentlemen like you accomplish."

entries.zh: 粲常以婦人者，才智不足論，自宜以色爲主。
entries.en: Can often said that a woman's intellect was not worth discussing — beauty was what mattered.
entries.literal: Can often held that as for women, intellectual talent was not worth discussing; they should naturally take beauty as their main quality.

entries.zh: 驃騎將軍曹洪女有美色，粲於是娉焉，容服帷帳甚麗，專房歡宴。
entries.en: The daughter of General of Agile Cavalry Cao Hong was renowned for her beauty; Can married her, furnishing their private chamber lavishly and devoting himself to her exclusively.
entries.literal: The daughter of General of Agile Cavalry Cao Hong had beautiful looks; Can therefore married her; her dress, furnishings, and curtains were very sumptuous; he kept her in a private chamber for joyous feasting.

entries.zh: 歴年後，婦病亡，未殯，傅嘏往喭粲；
entries.en: After several years his wife died of illness; before the funeral, Fu Gu came to console Can;
entries.literal: After some years, his wife died of illness; before the burial, Fu Gu went to console Can;

entries.zh: 粲不哭而神傷。
entries.en: Can did not weep outwardly, but his spirit was crushed.
entries.literal: Can did not weep but his spirit was wounded.

entries.zh: 嘏問曰：「婦人才色並茂爲難。
entries.en: Fu Gu asked: "It is rare for a woman to possess both talent and beauty.
entries.literal: Gu asked, saying: "For a woman to possess both talent and beauty in abundance is difficult.

entries.zh: 子之娶也，遺才而好色。
entries.en: In marrying, you set aside talent and chose beauty alone.
entries.literal: In your marriage, you left aside talent and favored beauty.

entries.zh: 此自易遇，今何哀之甚？」
entries.en: That should be easy to replace — why grieve so deeply?"
entries.literal: This is itself easy to encounter — why grieve so deeply now?"

entries.zh: 粲曰：「佳人難再得！
entries.en: Can said: "A woman of such beauty cannot be found again!
entries.literal: Can said: "A beautiful woman is hard to obtain again!

entries.zh: 顧逝者不能有傾國之色，然未可謂之易遇。」
entries.en: She may not have had nation-toppling beauty, but one still cannot call her easy to replace."
entries.literal: Looking at the departed, she could not possess nation-toppling beauty, yet one still cannot say she was easy to encounter."

entries.zh: 痛悼不能已，歳餘亦亡，時年二十九。
entries.en: He could not recover from his grief; a little over a year later he too died, at the age of twenty-nine.
entries.literal: His grief could not cease; after a little more than a year he also died, aged twenty-nine at the time.

entries.zh: 粲簡貴，不能與常人交接，所交皆一時俊傑。
entries.en: Can was refined and aloof; he could not mix with ordinary people and associated only with the age's finest minds.
entries.literal: Can was refined and noble; he could not associate with ordinary people; those he associated with were all outstanding talents of the age.

entries.zh: 至葬夕，赴者裁十餘人，皆同時知名士也，哭之，感慟路人。
entries.en: On the night of his burial, only a dozen or so mourners came — all distinguished men of the day — and their weeping moved passersby to tears.
entries.literal: On the evening of the burial, those who came numbered only a little more than ten — all were well-known scholars of the time; when they wept for him, passersby were moved to grief.

entries.zh: 惲子甝，嗣爲散騎常侍，進爵廣陽鄕侯，年三十薨。
entries.en: Yun's son Kan succeeded him as Regular Attendant of the Central Secretariat, was advanced to Marquis of Guangyang Township, and died at thirty.
entries.literal: Yun's son Kan succeeded and served as Regular Attendant of the Central Secretariat; he was advanced to Marquis of Guangyang Township and died at age thirty.

entries.zh: 子頵嗣。
entries.en: His son Yin succeeded him.
entries.literal: His son Yin succeeded.

entries.zh: 《荀氏家傳》曰：頵字温伯，爲羽林右監，早卒。
entries.en: The Genealogical Biography of the Xun Clan records that Yin styled Wenbo, served as Right Director of the Forest of Feathers, and died young.
entries.literal: The Genealogical Biography of the Xun Clan states: Yin's style name was Wenbo; he served as Right Director of the Forest of Feathers and died young.

entries.zh: 頵子崧，字景猷。
entries.en: Yin's son Song styled Jingyou.
entries.literal: Yin's son Song's style name was Jingyou.

entries.zh: 《晉陽秋》稱崧少有志操，雅好文學，孝義和愛，在朝恪勤，位至左右光祿大夫、開府儀同三司。
entries.en: The Spring and Autumn Annals of Jin praises Song as a youth of noble aspiration, devoted to literature, filial and compassionate; diligent in office, he rose to Household Grandee of the Left and Right and Grand Master with Imperial Carriage Honors.
entries.literal: The Spring and Autumn Annals of Jin praises Song as having lofty aspirations and conduct from youth, elegantly loving literature, filial, righteous, harmonious, and loving; in court he was diligent and careful, reaching the offices of Left and Right Household Grandee and Grand Master with the Honours of an Imperial Carriage and the Three Dignities.

entries.zh: 崧子羨，字令則，淸和有才。
entries.en: Song's son Xian styled Lingze — refined, harmonious, and talented.
entries.literal: Song's son Xian's style name was Lingze; he was pure and harmonious and possessed talent.

entries.zh: 尚公主，少歴顯位，年二十八爲北中郎將，徐、兖二州刺史，假節都督徐、兖、靑三州諸軍事。
entries.en: He married an imperial princess, held distinguished office from youth, and at twenty-eight became General of the North and Central, Governor of Xu and Yan Provinces, with credentials of authority as Commander of military affairs in Xu, Yan, and Qing.
entries.literal: He married an imperial princess; from youth he passed through distinguished offices; at age twenty-eight he was General of the North and Central, Governor of Xu and Yan Provinces, and Provisionally bearing credentials of authority as Commander-in-Chief of all military affairs in Xu, Yan, and Qing Provinces.

entries.zh: 在任十年，遇疾解職，卒於家，追贈驃騎將軍。
entries.en: After ten years in office he fell ill and resigned; he died at home and was posthumously awarded the rank of General of Agile Cavalry.
entries.literal: During ten years in office, he encountered illness and resigned his post; he died at home and was posthumously granted the office of General of Agile Cavalry.

entries.zh: 羨孫伯子，今御史中丞也。
entries.en: Xian's grandson Bozi is the present Censor-in-Chief.
entries.literal: Xian's grandson Bozi — the present Censor-in-Chief.

entries.zh: 霬官至中領軍，薨，諡曰貞侯，追贈驃騎將軍。
entries.en: Hui rose to Central Army Inspector; he died and was posthumously titled Marquis Zhen and awarded the rank of General of Agile Cavalry.
entries.literal: Hui reached the office of Central Army Inspector; he died; his posthumous title was Marquis Zhen; he was posthumously granted the office of General of Agile Cavalry.

entries.zh: 子愷嗣。
entries.en: His son Kai succeeded him.
entries.literal: His son Kai succeeded.

entries.zh: 霬妻，司馬景王、文王之妹也，二王皆與親善。
entries.en: Hui's wife was the younger sister of the Kings of Jing and Wen (Sima Shi and Sima Zhao); both Sima brothers were on close terms with the family.
entries.literal: Hui's wife was the younger sister of Sima the King of Jing and Sima the King of Wen; both kings were on close and friendly terms with him.

entries.zh: 咸熙中，開建五等，霬以著勳前朝，改封愷南頓子。
entries.en: During Xianxi, when the five noble ranks were established, Kai was enfeoffed as Viscount of Nandun in recognition of Hui's merit under the previous dynasty.
entries.literal: In the Xianxi period, when the five ranks of nobility were established, because Hui had displayed merit in the previous dynasty, Kai was changed in enfeoffment to Viscount of Nandun.

entries.zh: 《荀氏家傳》曰：愷，晉武帝時爲侍中。
entries.en: The Genealogical Biography of the Xun Clan records that Kai served as Palace Attendant under Emperor Wu of Jin.
entries.literal: The Genealogical Biography of the Xun Clan states: Kai served as Palace Attendant under Emperor Wu of Jin.

entries.zh: 干寶《晉紀》曰：武帝使侍中荀顗、和嶠倶至東宮，觀察太子。
entries.en: Gan Bao's Annals of Jin records that Emperor Wu sent Palace Attendants Xun Yi and He Qiao together to the Eastern Palace to observe the Crown Prince.
entries.literal: Gan Bao's Annals of Jin states: Emperor Wu sent Palace Attendants Xun Yi and He Qiao together to the Eastern Palace to observe the Crown Prince.

entries.zh: 顗還稱太子德識進茂，而嶠云聖質如初。
entries.en: On returning, Yi reported that the Crown Prince's virtue and insight were flourishing; He Qiao said his sage-like qualities were unchanged.
entries.literal: When Yi returned, he praised the Crown Prince's virtue and insight as advancing and flourishing; He Qiao said his sage-like quality was as at first.

entries.zh: 孫盛曰「遣荀勗」，其餘語則同。
entries.en: Sun Sheng writes "sent Xun Xu"; the rest is the same.
entries.literal: Sun Sheng says "sent Xun Xu"; the rest of the wording is the same.

entries.zh: 臣松之案和嶠爲侍中，荀顗亡沒久矣。
entries.en: Pei Songzhi notes: He Qiao was Palace Attendant, but Xun Yi had long been dead.
entries.literal: Your servant Songzhi investigates: He Qiao served as Palace Attendant; Xun Yi had long since died.

entries.zh: 荀勗位亞台司，不與嶠同班，無縁方稱侍中。
entries.en: Xun Xu ranked just below the chief ministers and was not in He Qiao's cohort — he could not have been called simply "Palace Attendant."
entries.literal: Xun Xu's position was second to the ministers of the Terrace; he was not in the same rank as Qiao; there was no reason he would be called Palace Attendant.

entries.zh: 二書所云，皆爲非也。
entries.en: Both accounts are wrong.
entries.literal: What both books say is all incorrect.

entries.zh: 考其時位，愷寔當之。
entries.en: Considering the dates and offices involved, Kai must have been the man.
entries.literal: Examining the times and positions, Kai truly should have been the one.

entries.zh: 愷位至征西大將軍。
entries.en: Kai rose to General Who Conquers the West.
entries.literal: Kai reached the office of General Who Conquers the West.

entries.zh: 愷兄憺，少府。
entries.en: Kai's elder brother Dan served as Minister Steward.
entries.literal: Kai's elder brother Dan — Minister Steward.

entries.zh: 弟悝，護軍將軍，追贈車騎大將軍。
entries.en: His younger brother Kui served as General Who Guards the Army and was posthumously awarded the rank of General of Chariots and Cavalry.
entries.literal: His younger brother Kui — General Who Guards the Army; posthumously granted General of Chariots and Cavalry.

entries.zh: 荀彧字文若，潁川潁陰人也。
entries.en: Xun Yu, courtesy name Wenruo, came from Yingyin in Yingchuan.
entries.literal: Xun Yu, styled Wenruo, was a man of Yingyin in Yingchuan commandery.

entries.zh: 祖父淑，字季和，朗陵令。
entries.en: His grandfather Shu, courtesy name Jihe, had served as magistrate of Langling.
entries.literal: His grandfather Shu, styled Jihe, was magistrate of Langling.

entries.zh: 當漢順、桓之間，知名當世。
entries.en: Under Emperors Shun and Huan of Han he was already famous in his own day.
entries.literal: During the reigns of Shun and Huan of Han, he was known by name in the age.

entries.zh: 有子八人，號曰八龍。
entries.en: He fathered eight sons, who were known collectively as the Eight Dragons.
entries.literal: He had eight sons, called the Eight Dragons.

entries.zh: 彧父緄，濟南相。
entries.en: Xun Yu’s father, Gun, had been chancellor of the kingdom of Jinan.
entries.literal: Yu’s father Gun was chancellor of Jinan kingdom.

entries.zh: 叔父爽，司空。
entries.en: His uncle Shuang rose to be Minister of Works.
entries.literal: His uncle Shuang was Minister of Works.

entries.zh: 诸葛亮复出祁山，诏郃督诸将西至略阳，亮还保祁山，郃追至木门，与亮军交战，飞矢中郃右膝，薨，
entries.en: When Zhuge Liang again drove toward Qishan, an edict sent Zhang He west to Lueyang; as Zhuge Liang fell back on Qishan, Zhang He pursued to Mumen, where in the fighting an arrow struck his right knee and he died,
entries.literal: When Zhuge Liang again came out to Qishan, an edict ordered He to supervise the various generals west to Lueyang; Liang returned to protect Qishan; He pursued to Mumen, joined battle with Liang's army, a flying arrow struck He's right knee, and he died,

entries.zh: 〈《魏略》曰：亮军退，司马宣王使郃追之，郃曰：“军法，围城必开出路，归军勿追。”
entries.en: 〈The Wei lüe records that when Zhuge Liang withdrew, Sima Yi ordered Zhang He to pursue; Zhang He said, "The art of war says to leave a way out of a siege and never to chase a retreating host."
entries.literal: 〈The Wei lüe says: When Liang's army withdrew, Sima Xuanwang ordered He to pursue them; He said: By military law, "when besieging a city one must open an escape route; do not pursue a withdrawing army."

entries.zh: 宣王不听。
entries.en: Sima Yi would not hear of it.
entries.literal: Xuanwang did not listen.

entries.zh: 郃不得已，遂进。
entries.en: Zhang He had no choice but to advance.
entries.literal: He had no choice and thereupon advanced.

entries.zh: 蜀军乘高布伏，弓弩乱发，矢中郃髀。〉
entries.en: The Shu troops held the heights in ambush and raked him with bolts; an arrow struck him in the thigh.〉
entries.literal: The Shu army rode the heights and laid ambush; crossbows shot wildly; an arrow struck He's thigh.〉

entries.zh: 谥曰壮侯。
entries.en: He was posthumously titled Marquis Zhuang, "the Stalwart."
entries.literal: His posthumous title was Marquis Zhuang.

entries.zh: 子雄嗣。
entries.en: His son Zhang Xiong inherited the title.
entries.literal: The son Xiong inherited.

entries.zh: 郃前后征伐有功，明帝分郃户，封郃四子列侯。
entries.en: For his long record of service Emperor Ming divided his fief and enfeoffed four of Zhang He's sons as full marquises.
entries.literal: He before and after campaigning had merit; Emperor Ming divided He's households and enfeoffed He's four sons as full marquises.

entries.zh: 赐小子爵关内侯。
entries.en: His youngest son received a secondary marquisate at court.
entries.literal: His youngest son was granted the noble rank of secondary marquis within the passes.

entries.zh: 张辽字文远，雁门马邑人也。
entries.en: Zhang Liao, whose courtesy name was Wenyuan, came from Mayi in Yanmen commandery.
entries.literal: Zhang Liao, courtesy name Wenyuan, was a man of Mayi in Yanmen.

entries.zh: 本聂壹之后，以避怨变姓。
entries.en: He was descended from Nie Yi but had changed his family name to escape a blood feud.
entries.literal: Originally he was a descendant of Nie Yi; to avoid resentment he changed his surname.

entries.zh: 少为郡吏。
entries.en: As a young man he served as a commandery clerk.
entries.literal: In youth he was a clerk of the commandery.

entries.zh: 汉末，并州刺史丁原以辽武力过人，召为从事，使将兵诣京都。
entries.en: Late in the Han, Ding Yuan, inspector of Bingzhou, impressed by Zhang Liao's exceptional fighting ability, appointed him as an aide-de-camp and sent him at the head of troops to the capital.
entries.literal: At the end of Han, the Inspector of Bingzhou, Ding Yuan, because Liao's martial strength surpassed others, summoned him as an aide and ordered him to lead troops to the capital.

entries.zh: 何进遣诣河北募兵，得千餘人。
entries.en: He Jin sent him north of the river to raise troops, and he returned with over a thousand recruits.
entries.literal: He Jin dispatched him to north of the Yellow River to recruit soldiers; he obtained more than a thousand men.

entries.zh: 还，进败，以兵属董卓。
entries.en: By the time he came back, He Jin had already fallen, and Zhang Liao placed his command under Dong Zhuo.
entries.literal: Returning, He Jin had been defeated, and he attached his troops to Dong Zhuo.

entries.zh: 卓败，以兵属吕布，迁骑都尉。
entries.en: After Dong Zhuo's downfall he joined Lü Bu's forces and was promoted to colonel of cavalry.
entries.literal: When Zhuo was defeated, he attached his troops to Lü Bu and was promoted to Colonel of Cavalry.

entries.zh: 布为李傕所败，从布东奔徐州，领鲁相，时年二十八。
entries.en: When Lü Bu was routed by Li Jue, Zhang Liao followed him east into Xu Province, became administrator of Lu, and was twenty-eight at the time.
entries.literal: When Bu was defeated by Li Jue, he followed Bu fleeing east to Xu Province, served as chancellor of Lu, and at that time was twenty-eight years old.

entries.zh: 太祖破吕布於下邳，辽将其众降，拜中郎将，赐爵关内侯。
entries.en: After Cao Cao took Xiapi and broke Lü Bu, Zhang Liao brought his men over in submission and was named a general of the household and enfeoffed as a secondary marquis at court.
entries.literal: The Grand Progenitor defeated Lü Bu at Xiapi; Liao led his multitude in surrender, was appointed General of the Gentlemen of the Household, and was granted the noble rank of secondary marquis within the passes.

entries.zh: 数有战功，迁裨将军。
entries.en: He won distinction again and again in the field and rose to the rank of major general.
entries.literal: Repeatedly he had merit in battle and was promoted to major general.

entries.zh: 袁绍破，别遣辽定鲁国诸县。
entries.en: Once Yuan Shao had been crushed, Cao Cao detached Zhang Liao to secure every county in the state of Lu.
entries.literal: When Yuan Shao was broken, separately he dispatched Liao to pacify the counties of the Lu princedom.

entries.zh: 与夏侯渊围昌豨於东海，数月粮尽，议引军还，辽谓渊曰：“数日已来，每行诸围，豨辄属目视辽。
entries.en: He joined Xiahou Yuan in besieging Chang Xi in Donghai; when months of campaigning had emptied the granaries and the generals talked of pulling back, Zhang Liao told Xiahou Yuan, Lately, whenever I tour the perimeter, "Chang Xi keeps his gaze fixed on me.
entries.literal: Together with Xiahou Yuan he besieged Chang Xi in Donghai; after several months the provisions were exhausted, and they deliberated on withdrawing the army. Liao said to Yuan: For several days now, whenever I have walked the various siege lines, "Xi has always fixed his eyes on Liao.

entries.zh: 又其射矢更稀，此必豨计犹豫，故不力战。
entries.en: His archery has slackened as well; he must be torn about what to do next, which is why he will not commit to a full fight.
entries.literal: Moreover his shooting of arrows has become rarer; this must be because Xi's plans are hesitant, therefore he does not fight hard.

entries.zh: 辽欲挑与语，傥可诱也？”
entries.en: I would like to draw him into conversation—there may be a way to coax him out."
entries.literal: Liao wishes to challenge him to speak; perhaps he can be enticed?"

entries.zh: 乃使谓豨曰：“公有命，使辽传之。”
entries.en: He then sent a messenger to Chang Xi: Our lord has issued orders, "and he has asked me to relay them to you."
entries.literal: Then he sent someone to say to Xi: "The lord has a command; he has ordered Liao to transmit it."

entries.zh: 豨果下与辽语，辽为说“太祖神武，方以德怀四方，先附者受大赏”。
entries.en: Chang Xi did come down to parley, "and Zhang Liao told him that Cao Cao was a formidable leader who was winning the realm by moral authority and that those who submitted early would be richly rewarded."
entries.literal: Xi indeed came down and spoke with Liao, and Liao for him explained that "the Grand Progenitor is divinely martial and is just now by virtue cherishing the four quarters; those who attach first receive great rewards"."

entries.zh: 豨乃许降。
entries.en: Chang Xi agreed to yield.
entries.literal: Xi then promised to surrender.

entries.zh: 辽遂单身上三公山，入豨家，拜妻子。
entries.en: Zhang Liao then went alone up Mount Sangong, walked into Chang Xi's home, and paid his respects to the man's wife and children.
entries.literal: Liao thereupon alone ascended Mount Sangong, entered Xi's house, and bowed to wife and children.

entries.zh: 豨欢喜，随诣太祖。
entries.en: Delighted, Chang Xi accompanied him to Cao Cao's headquarters.
entries.literal: Xi was pleased and followed to go to the Grand Progenitor.

entries.zh: 太祖遣豨还，责辽曰：“此非大将法也。”
entries.en: Cao Cao sent Chang Xi back to his post and rebuked Zhang Liao: "That is not how a senior commander should behave."
entries.literal: The Grand Progenitor sent Xi back and reproached Liao, saying: "This is not the method of a great general."

entries.zh: 辽谢曰：“以明公威信著於四海，辽奉圣旨，豨必不敢害故也。”
entries.en: Zhang Liao bowed and replied, I knew your authority reaches every corner of the land and that I bore your written order, "so Chang Xi would never have dared harm me."
entries.literal: Liao apologized, saying: Because the enlightened lord's prestige and trust are manifest throughout the four seas, and Liao carried out the sage command, "Xi certainly did not dare to harm; that is the reason."

entries.zh: 从讨袁谭、袁尚於黎阳，有功，行中坚将军。
entries.en: He took part in the campaign against Yuan Tan and Yuan Shang at Liyang, distinguished himself, and was given acting rank as general of the central corps.
entries.literal: He followed in attacking Yuan Tan and Yuan Shang at Liyang, had merit, and acted as general of the central solid.

entries.zh: 从攻尚於鄴，尚坚守不下。
entries.en: He joined the assault on Ye, where Yuan Shang held the walls and could not be dislodged.
entries.literal: He followed in attacking Shang at Ye; Shang firmly defended and was not taken.

entries.zh: 太祖还许，使辽与乐进拔阴安，徙其民河南。
entries.en: When Cao Cao withdrew to Xu, he sent Zhang Liao and Yue Jin to take Yin'an and resettle its population south of the river.
entries.literal: The Grand Progenitor returned to Xu and ordered Liao together with Yue Jin to seize Yin'an and move its people south of the Yellow River.

entries.zh: 复从攻鄴，鄴破，辽别徇赵国、常山，招降缘山诸贼及黑山孙轻等。
entries.en: He returned for the siege of Ye, and after the city fell he swept Zhao and Changshan on a separate line, bringing the mountain outlaws and Black Mountain leaders such as Sun Qing to terms.
entries.literal: Again he followed in attacking Ye; when Ye was broken, Liao separately campaigned through Zhao and Changshan, summoning to surrender the various bandits along the mountains and Sun Qing of the Black Mountain band, and others.

entries.zh: 从攻袁谭，谭破，别将徇海滨，破辽东贼柳毅等。
entries.en: He fought in the final campaign against Yuan Tan, then led a detached column along the coast and smashed coastal raiders from Liaodong led by Liu Yi.
entries.literal: He followed in attacking Yuan Tan; when Tan was broken, as a separate general he campaigned along the seacoast and defeated the Liaodong bandits Liu Yi and others.

entries.zh: 还鄴，太祖自出迎辽，引共载，以辽为荡寇将军。
entries.en: Back in Ye, Cao Cao rode out in person to greet him, had him share his carriage, and named him general who sweeps away bandits.
entries.literal: Returning to Ye, the Grand Progenitor himself came out to welcome Liao, led him to ride together in the same carriage, and appointed Liao general who sweeps away bandits.

entries.zh: 复别击荆州，定江夏诸县，还屯临颍，封都亭侯。
entries.en: He campaigned again into Jingzhou, secured the Jiangxia counties, took station at Linying on his return, and received a village marquisate at the capital.
entries.literal: Again separately he struck Jing Province, pacified the counties of Jiangxia, returned and garrisoned Linying, and was enfeoffed as marquis of the metropolitan village.

entries.zh: 从征袁尚於柳城，卒与虏遇，辽劝太祖战，气甚奋，太祖壮之，自以所持麾授辽。
entries.en: During the expedition against Yuan Shang at Liucheng they ran straight into the nomad host; Zhang Liao pressed Cao Cao to give battle, and his fervor so impressed Cao Cao that he passed him his own command banner.
entries.literal: He followed in campaigning against Yuan Shang at Liucheng; suddenly they encountered the barbarians. Liao urged the Grand Progenitor to fight; his spirit was very aroused; the Grand Progenitor thought him brave and personally handed the banner he held to Liao.

entries.zh: 遂击，大破之，斩单于蹋顿。
entries.en: They attacked at once, shattered the enemy, and killed the chanyu Tadun.
entries.literal: Thereupon they attacked, greatly defeated them, and beheaded the Shanyu Tadun.

entries.zh: 〈《傅子》曰：太祖将征柳城，辽谏曰：“夫许，天子之会也。
entries.en: 〈The Fu zi records that when Cao Cao was preparing the Liucheng expedition, Zhang Liao urged him to reconsider: "Xu is where the emperor resides.
entries.literal: 〈The Fu zi says: When the Grand Progenitor was about to campaign to Liucheng, Liao remonstrated, saying: "Now Xu is the assembly place of the Son of Heaven.

entries.zh: 今天子在许，公远北征，若刘表遣刘备袭许，据之以号令四方，公之势去矣。”
entries.en: The sovereign is at Xu while you march deep into the north; if Liu Biao sent Liu Bei to strike the capital, seize it, and issue orders from there, your position would collapse."
entries.literal: Now the Son of Heaven is at Xu; the lord campaigns far to the north; if Liu Biao dispatches Liu Bei to raid Xu, occupies it, and by it issues commands to the four quarters, the lord's situation will be gone."

entries.zh: 太祖策表必不能任备，遂行也。〉
entries.en: Cao Cao judged that Liu Biao would never give Liu Bei real authority, and went ahead with the campaign anyway.
entries.literal: The Grand Progenitor calculated that Biao certainly could not employ Bei, and thereupon proceeded.

entries.zh: 劉焉字君郎，江夏竟陵人也，漢魯恭王之後裔，章帝元和中徙封竟陵，支庶家焉。
entries.en: Liu Yan, courtesy name Junlang, came from Jingling in Jiangxia. His line descended from Han Prince Gong of Lu; during Emperor Zhang’s Yuanhe reign the fief was reassigned to Jingling, where a younger branch of the house made its home.
entries.literal: Liu Yan, courtesy name Junlang, was a man of Jingling in Jiangxia; he was a descendant of Prince Gong of Lu of the Han; in the Yuanhe era of Emperor Zhang his enfeoffment was transferred to Jingling, and a cadet branch of the family settled there.

entries.zh: 焉少仕州郡，以宗室拜中郎，後以師祝公喪去官。
entries.en: As a young man Liu Yan held posts in local government; his status as imperial clansman won him appointment as a gentleman of the palace. He later resigned to observe mourning for his teacher, Duke Zhu.
entries.literal: In youth Yan served in prefecture and commandery offices; because of his imperial-clan status he was appointed Gentleman of the Palace, and later, on account of mourning for his teacher Duke Zhu, left office.

entries.zh: 〈臣松之案：祝公，司徒祝恬也。〉
entries.en: 〈Pei Songzhi remarks: “Duke Zhu was Zhu Tian, who served as minister of education.”〉
entries.literal: 〈Pei Songzhi’s note: Duke Zhu was Zhu Tian, Minister of Education.〉

entries.zh: 居陽城山，積學教授，舉賢良方正，闢司徒府，歷雒陽令、冀州刺史、南陽太守、宗正、太常。
entries.en: He withdrew to Mount Yangcheng, where he studied deeply and taught. Recommended as a worthy and upright candidate, he entered the minister of education’s bureau and rose through Luoyang magistrate, inspector of Ji, grand administrator of Nanyang, director of the imperial clan, and grand master of ceremonies.
entries.literal: He dwelt on Mount Yangcheng, amassed learning and taught students; he was recommended as worthy and good, upright and true; he was summoned to the Minister of Education’s office, and in succession served as magistrate of Luoyang, inspector of Ji Province, grand administrator of Nanyang, director of the imperial clan, and grand master of ceremonies.

entries.zh: 焉睹靈帝政治衰缺，王室多故，乃建議言：「刺史、太守，貨賂為官，割剝百姓，以致離叛。
entries.en: Seeing Emperor Ling’s government falter and the house of Han beset by crisis, Liu Yan proposed: “Prefectural inspectors and grand administrators are buying their posts; they bleed the people until the realm splinters into revolt.
entries.literal: Yan saw that Emperor Ling’s governance was decaying and deficient and the royal house had many troubles; then he proposed, saying: “Inspectors and grand administrators have purchased office with bribes; they flay and strip the common people, thereby bringing about separation and rebellion.

entries.zh: 可選清名重臣以為牧伯，鎮安方夏。」
entries.en: Choose men of unimpeachable name and real weight as regional governors, and charge them with restoring calm across the land.”
entries.literal: It is possible to select men of pure reputation and weighty rank to serve as regional shepherds and command them to pacify and quiet the four directions and the summer realm.”

entries.zh: 焉內求交阯牧，欲避世難。
entries.en: Behind the scenes he angled for the governorship of Jiaozhi, hoping to sit out the gathering storm.
entries.literal: Yan inwardly sought appointment as governor of Jiaozhi, wishing to escape the troubles of the age.

entries.zh: 議未即行，侍中廣漢董扶私謂焉曰：「京師將亂，益州分野有天子氣。」
entries.en: Before the plan could take effect, Palace Attendant Dong Fu of Guanghan took him aside: “Luoyang is heading for turmoil, and the stars over Yizhou show the aura of an emperor.”
entries.literal: The proposal had not yet been put into effect when Palace Attendant Dong Fu of Guanghan privately said to Yan: “The capital is about to be in chaos; in the astrological field of Yizhou there is the qi of the Son of Heaven.”

entries.zh: 焉聞扶言，意更在益州。
entries.en: Those words fixed his mind on Yizhou more firmly than ever.
entries.literal: When Yan heard Fu’s words, his intentions turned still more toward Yizhou.

entries.zh: 會益州刺史郤儉賦斂煩擾，謠言遠聞，儉，郤正祖也。
entries.en: About then Yizhou Inspector Xi Jian was grinding the people with heavy levies until rumor of it spread far; Xi Jian was an ancestor of Xi Zheng.
entries.literal: It happened that Inspector of Yizhou Xi Jian levied taxes in vexing and harassing fashion, and rumors were heard from afar; Jian was the ancestor of Xi Zheng.

entries.zh: 而并州殺刺史張壹，涼州殺刺史耿鄙，焉謀得施。
entries.en: When Bing Province slew Inspector Zhang Yi and Liang slew Inspector Geng Bi, Liu Yan’s scheme could finally move forward.
entries.literal: Meanwhile Bing Province killed Inspector Zhang Yi, and Liang Province killed Inspector Geng Bi; Yan’s plan could be carried out.

entries.zh: 出為監軍使者，領益州牧，封陽城侯，當收儉治罪；
entries.en: He was sent out as supervisory army envoy with the governorship of Yizhou, enfeoffed as Marquis of Yangcheng, and charged to seize Xi Jian and bring him to justice;
entries.literal: He went out as supervisory army envoy, took charge as governor of Yizhou, was enfeoffed as Marquis of Yangcheng, and was to arrest Jian and punish him according to law;

entries.zh: 《續漢書》曰：是時用劉虞為幽州，劉焉為益州，劉表為荊州，賈琮為冀州。
entries.en: The Continuation of the Book of Han records that Liu Yu was made governor of You, Liu Yan of Yizhou, Liu Biao of Jing, and Jia Cong of Ji.
entries.literal: The Continuation of the Book of Han says: At this time Liu Yu was appointed to You Province, Liu Yan to Yizhou, Liu Biao to Jing Province, and Jia Cong to Ji Province.

entries.zh: 虞等皆海內清名之士，或從列卿尚書以選為牧伯，各以本秩居任。
entries.en: All were men of spotless reputation; some were promoted from the ranks of ministers and palace secretaries to provincial governorships while retaining their former titles.
entries.literal: Yu and the others were all men of pure reputation within the realm; some were chosen as regional shepherds from among ranked ministers and masters of writing, each holding office at his original rank.

entries.zh: 舊典：傳車參駕，施赤為帷裳。
entries.en: By ancient custom they traveled in relay carriages with three teams and red drapery as their canopy.
entries.literal: According to old precedent: relay carriages with three teams, red drapery used as curtains and canopies.

entries.zh: 臣松之按：靈帝崩後，義軍起，孫堅殺荊州刺史王叡，然後劉表為荊州，不與焉同時也。
entries.en: Pei Songzhi remarks: After Emperor Ling died and the loyalist armies rose, Sun Jian killed Jing inspector Wang Rui; Liu Biao’s appointment to Jing came only afterward and was not contemporaneous with Liu Yan’s.
entries.literal: Your servant Songzhi notes: After Emperor Ling’s death righteous armies rose; Sun Jian killed Inspector of Jing Province Wang Rui, and only then was Liu Biao made governor of Jing—he was not appointed at the same time as Yan.

entries.zh: 《漢靈帝紀》曰：帝引見焉，宣示方略，加以賞賜，敕焉為益州刺史。
entries.en: The Annals of Emperor Ling record that the emperor received Liu Yan in audience, laid out his plans, rewarded him, and appointed him inspector of Yizhou.
entries.literal: The Annals of Emperor Ling of Han say: The emperor summoned Yan for audience, displayed strategy and plans, bestowed rewards, and ordered Yan to be inspector of Yizhou.

entries.zh: 前刺史劉雋、郤儉皆貪殘放濫，取受狼籍，元元無聊，呼嗟充野，焉到便收攝行法，以示萬姓，勿令漏露，使癰疽決潰，為國生梗。
entries.en: His predecessors Liu Juan and Xi Jian had been rapacious and lawless, their extortion so rampant that the people were destitute and the countryside rang with lament. Yan was to arrest them at once, enforce the law before the people, and drain the abscess before it festered into a national crisis.
entries.literal: The former inspectors Liu Juan and Xi Jian were both greedy, cruel, and unrestrained; their taking and receiving were in disorder; the common people were destitute; cries of lament filled the wilds. When Yan arrived he was to gather them in and enforce the law, to show the myriad people, not letting leaks appear, so that the abscess might burst and drain and not become a running sore for the state.

entries.zh: 焉受命而行，以道路不通，住荊州東界。
entries.en: Liu Yan set out on his commission but, with the roads blocked, halted on Jing Province’s eastern frontier.
entries.literal: Yan received the command and set out; because the roads were impassable, he halted on the eastern border of Jing Province.

entries.zh: 扶亦求為蜀郡西部屬國都尉，及太倉令
entries.en: Dong Fu likewise sought appointment as commandant of the dependent state in western Shu Commandery.
entries.literal: Dong Fu also requested appointment as commandant of the dependent state in the western part of Shu Commandery.

entries.en: Some manuscripts insert “meeting” here.
entries.literal: (hui “meeting” [variant])

entries.zh: 巴西趙韙去官，俱隨焉。
entries.en: Zhao Wei of Baxi, director of the Imperial Granary, resigned his post, and both men went with Liu Yan.
entries.literal: Zhao Wei of Baxi, director of the Imperial Granary, left office, and both followed Yan.

entries.zh: 陳壽《益部耆舊傳》曰：董扶字茂安。
entries.en: Chen Shou’s Records of Elders of Yibu records: Dong Fu, courtesy name Mao’an.
entries.literal: Chen Shou’s Records of Elders of Yibu says: Dong Fu, courtesy name Mao’an.

entries.zh: 少從師學，兼通數經，善歐陽尚書，又事聘士楊厚，究極圖讖。
entries.en: As a youth he studied under several masters, mastered multiple classics and Ouyang Gao’s version of the Book of Documents, and served the reclusive scholar Yang Hou in the study of prognostic charts.
entries.literal: In youth he followed teachers in study, mastered several classics, excelled in Ouyang’s Book of Documents, and also served the reclusive scholar Yang Hou, thoroughly investigating charts and prognostications.

entries.zh: 遂至京師，遊覽太學，還家講授，弟子自遠而至。
entries.en: He went to the capital, studied at the Imperial Academy, then returned home to teach; students came from far and wide.
entries.literal: Then he reached the capital, toured the Imperial Academy, returned home to lecture and teach, and disciples came from afar.

entries.zh: 永康元年167年，日有蝕之，詔舉賢良方正之士，策問得失。
entries.en: In 167, the first year of Yongkang, a solar eclipse prompted an edict summoning worthy and upright candidates for written policy examinations.
entries.literal: In the first year of Yongkang, 167, there was a solar eclipse; an edict summoned worthy and upright candidates, and policy questions were put on gains and losses.

entries.zh: 左馮翊趙謙等舉扶，扶以病不詣，遙於長安上封事，遂稱疾篤歸家。
entries.en: Zhao Qian of Zuofengyi and others recommended him, but Fu pleaded illness and stayed away, submitting a sealed memorial from Chang’an before declaring himself gravely ill and going home.
entries.literal: Zuo Fengyi Zhao Qian and others recommended Fu; Fu, citing illness, did not go; from afar at Chang’an he submitted a sealed memorial, then claimed grave illness and returned home.

entries.zh: 前後宰府十闢，公車三徵，再舉賢良方正、博士、有道皆不就，名稱尤重。
entries.en: Provincial and central offices summoned him ten times, the imperial carriage three times, and he was twice recommended as worthy, erudite, and virtuous—yet he refused every call, and his fame only grew.
entries.literal: Before and after, ten summonses came from chief ministers’ offices, three imperial carriage summonses, and twice he was recommended as worthy and upright, as erudite, and as possessing the Way—he accepted none; his reputation was especially weighty.

entries.zh: 大將軍何進表薦扶曰：「資遊、夏之德，述孔氏之風，內懷焦、董消復之術。
entries.en: Grand General He Jin memorialized in his favor: “He has the virtue of the ancient sages You and Xia, carries forward Confucius’s teaching, and holds within him the restorative arts of Jiao and Dong.
entries.literal: Grand General He Jin memorialized recommending Fu, saying: “He possesses the virtue of You and Xia, expounds the style of the Kong clan, and inwardly holds the restorative arts of Jiao and Dong.

entries.zh: 方今並、涼騷擾，西戎蠢叛，宜敕公車特召，待以異禮，諮謀奇策。」
entries.en: With Bing and Liang in turmoil and the western tribes in revolt, the throne should summon him by imperial carriage with exceptional honors and seek his counsel on extraordinary measures.”
entries.literal: Now Bing and Liang are in turmoil, the western Rong foolishly rebel; it is fitting to order the imperial carriage to summon him specially, treat him with exceptional ceremony, and consult him on extraordinary plans.”

entries.zh: 於是靈帝徵扶，即拜侍中。
entries.en: Emperor Ling then summoned Dong Fu and appointed him palace attendant on the spot.
entries.literal: Thereupon Emperor Ling summoned Fu and immediately appointed him Palace Attendant.

entries.zh: 在朝稱為儒宗，甚見器重。
entries.en: At court he was hailed as the leading Confucian scholar and won deep respect.
entries.literal: At court he was called the patriarch of scholars and was greatly valued and trusted.

entries.zh: 求為蜀郡屬國都尉。
entries.en: He asked for the post of commandant of Shu’s dependent state.
entries.literal: He requested appointment as commandant of the dependent state in Shu Commandery.

entries.zh: 扶出一歲而靈帝崩，天下大亂。
entries.en: A year after he left the capital Emperor Ling died and the empire plunged into chaos.
entries.literal: Fu had been out one year when Emperor Ling died and the realm fell into great chaos.

entries.zh: 後去官，年八十二卒於家。
entries.en: He later resigned and died at home at eighty-two.
entries.literal: Later he left office; at age eighty-two he died at home.

entries.zh: 始扶發辭抗論，益部少雙，故號曰
entries.en: From the start his debating was unmatched in Yizhou, so he was nicknamed
entries.literal: At first, when Fu began to speak in refutation and debate, few in Yibu could match him; therefore he was styled

entries.zh: （致止）
entries.en: Some manuscripts read “Zhizhi” (“he who stops”).
entries.literal: (zhizhi “to stop” [variant])

entries.zh: 至止，言人莫能當，所至而談止也。
entries.en: “Zhizhi”—“the one who stops all talk”—for wherever he went debate fell silent.
entries.literal: [Zhizhi “to the stop”], meaning no one could withstand him—wherever he went discussion ceased.

entries.zh: 後丞相諸葛亮問秦宓以扶所長，宓曰：「董扶褒秋毫之善，貶纖芥之惡。」
entries.en: Later Chancellor Zhuge Liang asked Qin Mi what Dong Fu excelled at. Mi replied: “Dong Fu praises goodness down to the finest hair and condemns wrongdoing down to the smallest flaw.”
entries.literal: Later Chancellor Zhuge Liang asked Qin Mi about Fu’s strengths; Mi said: “Dong Fu praises the good even in an autumn down, and condemns evil even in a fiber of grass.”

entries.zh: 是時益州逆賊馬相、趙祗等於綿竹縣自號黃巾，合聚疲役之民，一二日中得數千人，先殺綿竹令李升，吏民翕集，合萬餘人，便前破雒縣，攻益州殺儉，又到蜀郡、犍為，旬月之間，破壞三郡。
entries.en: About then rebels Ma Xiang and Zhao Qi in Yizhou raised the Yellow Turban banner at Mianzhu, sweeping up worn-out conscripts. Within a day or two they had thousands of followers; they slew Magistrate Li Sheng, and officials and townsfolk rallied until their host passed ten thousand. They took Luoxian, struck down Inspector Xi Jian of Yizhou, then swept through Shu and Qianwei—three commanderies ruined inside a month.
entries.literal: At this time [Yi] Province’s rebel bandits Ma Xiang, Zhao Qi, and others at Mianzhu County styled themselves Yellow Turbans; they gathered exhausted conscripted people; in one or two days they obtained several thousand men; first they killed Mianzhu magistrate Li Sheng; officials and common people flocked together, totaling more than ten thousand; then they advanced and broke Luoxian, attacked Yizhou and killed Jian, then went to Shu Commandery and Qianwei; within a month or so they destroyed three commanderies.

entries.zh: 相自稱天子，眾以萬數。
entries.en: Ma Xiang proclaimed himself emperor, and his following ran to tens of thousands.
entries.literal: Xiang declared himself Son of Heaven; the multitude was counted in the tens of thousands.

entries.zh: 州從事賈龍
entries.en: The provincial clerk Jia Long
entries.literal: Provincial clerk Jia Long

entries.en: Alternate wording marks Jia Long as having long enjoyed local trust.
entries.literal: (su ‘for a long time’ [variant])

entries.zh: 領兵數百人在犍為東界，攝斂吏民，得千馀人，攻相等，數日破走，州界清靜。
entries.en: He led a few hundred soldiers on Qianwei’s eastern march, rallied officials and townsfolk to more than a thousand, struck Ma Xiang’s host, and within days routed them; peace returned to the province.
entries.literal: leading several hundred troops on the eastern border of Qianwei, gathered and collected officials and common people, obtained more than a thousand men, attacked Xiang and the others; in several days he broke them and drove them off; the borders of the province were quiet and pure.

entries.zh: 龍乃選吏卒迎焉。
entries.en: Jia Long then picked officers and troops to escort Liu Yan in.
entries.literal: Long then selected clerks and soldiers to welcome Yan.

entries.zh: 焉徙治綿竹，撫納離叛，務行寬惠，陰圖異計。
entries.en: Liu Yan shifted his seat to Mianzhu, offering refuge to deserters and rebels while preaching mercy—yet all the while he nursed designs of his own.
entries.literal: Yan moved his administration to Mianzhu, comforted and received those who had left or rebelled, strove to practice leniency and kindness, and secretly plotted unusual designs.

entries.zh: 張魯母始以鬼道，又有少容，常往來焉家，故焉遣魯為督義司馬，住漢中，斷絕谷閣，殺害漢使。
entries.en: Zhang Lu’s mother practiced spirit mediumship and still looked young; she was a frequent guest in Liu Yan’s house, so Yan appointed Zhang Lu marshal of righteous command and posted him in Hanzhong. Zhang Lu sealed the mountain defiles and murdered imperial messengers.
entries.literal: Zhang Lu’s mother at first practiced the way of ghosts, and moreover had a youthful appearance; she constantly went back and forth to Yan’s household; therefore Yan dispatched Lu as marshal for supervising righteousness, stationed in Hanzhong, cut off the passes of the ravines, and killed Han envoys.

entries.zh: 焉上書言米賊斷道，不得複通，又託他事殺州中豪強王咸、李權等十馀人，以立威刑。
entries.en: Liu Yan memorialized that “rice-bandit” cultists had severed the roads and cut him off from court, then used other excuses to execute a dozen leading local families—Wang Xian and Li Quan among them—to cow the gentry.
entries.literal: Yan submitted a memorial saying the rice bandits had cut the roads and he could not again communicate; moreover, under other pretexts he killed more than ten powerful magnates of the province such as Wang Xian and Li Quan, in order to establish awe-inspiring punishments.

entries.zh: 〈《益部耆舊雜記》曰：李權字伯豫，為臨邛長。
entries.en: 〈The Miscellaneous Records of the Elders of Yibu records: Li Quan, courtesy Boyu, served as magistrate of Linqiong.
entries.literal: 〈The Miscellaneous Records of the Elders of Yibu says: Li Quan, courtesy name Boyu, was magistrate of Linqiong.

entries.zh: 子福。
entries.en: His son was named Fu.
entries.literal: Son Fu.

entries.zh: 見犍為楊戲《輔臣贊》。〉
entries.en: See Yang Xi of Qianwei’s Encomia on Ministers.
entries.literal: See Yang Xi of Qianwei’s Encomia on Ministers.

entries.zh: 犍為太守任岐及賈龍由此反攻焉，焉擊殺岐、龍。
entries.en: Ren Qi, grand administrator of Qianwei, and Jia Long then turned their arms on Liu Yan; Yan defeated them and put both men to death.
entries.literal: Grand Administrator of Qianwei Ren Qi and Jia Long for this reason turned back and attacked Yan; Yan struck and killed Qi and Long.

entries.zh: 〈《英雄記》曰：劉焉起兵，不與天下討董卓，保州自守。
entries.en: 〈The Record of Heroes states: Liu Yan mobilized his forces but refused to march with the coalition against Dong Zhuo, holding Yizhou for himself.
entries.literal: 〈The Record of Heroes says: Liu Yan raised troops, did not join the realm in attacking Dong Zhuo, and protected the province to guard himself.

entries.zh: 犍為太守任岐自稱將軍，與從事陳超舉兵擊焉，焉擊破之。
entries.en: Ren Qi of Qianwei declared himself a general and, with Clerk Chen Chao, marched against Liu Yan; Yan shattered their army.
entries.literal: Grand Administrator of Qianwei Ren Qi styled himself general; together with clerk Chen Chao he raised troops and struck Yan; Yan struck and broke them.

entries.zh: 董卓使司徒趙謙將兵向州，說校尉賈龍，使引兵還擊焉，焉出青羌與戰，故能破殺。
entries.en: Dong Zhuo dispatched Minister Zhao Qian against the province and won over Colonel Jia Long, turning him against Liu Yan. Yan answered with Qingqiang auxiliaries and so crushed the attack.
entries.literal: Dong Zhuo sent Minister of Education Zhao Qian to lead troops toward the province, persuaded Colonel Jia Long, and made him lead troops back to attack Yan; Yan brought out Qingqiang and fought them, therefore was able to break and kill them.

entries.zh: 岐、龍等皆蜀郡人。〉
entries.en: Ren Qi, Jia Long, and their confederates were natives of Shu Commandery.
entries.literal: Qi, Long, and the others were all men of Shu Commandery.

entries.zh: 焉意漸盛，造作乘輿車具千馀乘。
entries.en: Liu Yan’s ambitions swelled until he was building over a thousand sets of imperial carriage fittings.
entries.literal: Yan’s intentions gradually grew great; he manufactured imperial carriage gear to the number of more than a thousand sets.

entries.zh: 荊州牧劉表表上焉有似子夏在西河疑聖人之論。
entries.en: Governor Liu Biao of Jing memorialized the throne, likening Liu Yan to Zixia west of the River—whose teaching had led men to doubt Confucius himself.
entries.literal: Jing Province Governor Liu Biao memorialized upward that Yan had discourse resembling Zixia west of the He doubting the sage.

entries.zh: 時焉子範為左中郎將，誕治書御史，璋為奉車都尉，皆從獻帝在長安，
entries.en: His sons held court rank in Chang’an with Emperor Xian: Fan as left general of the gentlemen of the palace, Dan as imperial clerk censor, Zhang as commandant for the imperial chariot,
entries.literal: At that time Yan’s son Fan was Left General of the Gentlemen of the Palace, Dan was imperial clerk censor, and Zhang was Commandant of the Chariots; all followed Emperor Xian at Chang’an,

entries.zh: 〈《英雄記》曰：範
entries.en: 〈The Record of Heroes adds: Fan
entries.literal: 〈The Record of Heroes says: Fan

entries.en: One manuscript reads ‘heard’ here.
entries.literal: (heard [variant])

entries.zh: 父焉為益州牧，董卓所徵發，皆不至。
entries.en: He learned that his father was governor of Yizhou and that none of Dong Zhuo’s summons had been obeyed.
entries.literal: father Yan was governor of Yizhou; those whom Dong Zhuo summoned and drafted all did not arrive.

entries.zh: 收范兄弟三人，鎖械於郿塢，為陰獄以系之。〉
entries.en: Dong Zhuo clapped all three brothers in irons at the Mei bastion and locked them in a secret cell.
entries.literal: He seized the three Fan brothers, shackled them at Mei’s bastion, and made a hidden prison to bind them.

entries.zh: 惟
entries.en: Only
entries.literal: Only

entries.en: Some texts read “younger” (son).
entries.literal: (younger [variant])

entries.zh: 子別部司馬瑁素隨焉。
entries.en: The youngest, Mao, a major of a separate division, had stayed with his father in the west.
entries.literal: son Separate-division Major Mao always followed Yan.

entries.zh: 獻帝使璋曉諭焉，焉留璋不遣。
entries.en: The emperor sent Liu Zhang west to reason with his father; Liu Yan kept him and never let him return.
entries.literal: Emperor Xian sent Zhang to enlighten and instruct Yan; Yan detained Zhang and did not send him back.

entries.zh: 〈《典略》曰：時璋為奉車都尉，在京師。
entries.en: 〈The Compendium notes: Liu Zhang was then commandant for the chariot in Luoyang.
entries.literal: 〈The Compendium says: at that time Zhang was Commandant of the Chariots, in the capital.

entries.zh: 焉託疾召璋，璋自表省焉，焉遂留璋不還。〉
entries.en: Liu Yan feigned illness to summon him; Zhang asked leave to visit his father—and never came back to court.
entries.literal: Yan feigned illness and summoned Zhang; Zhang personally memorialized to visit Yan; Yan then detained Zhang and did not return him.

entries.zh: 時征西將軍馬騰屯郿而反，焉及範與騰通謀，引兵襲長安。
entries.en: When Ma Teng, general who conquers the west, rose in rebellion from his camp at Mei, Liu Yan and Liu Fan conspired with him to strike Chang’an.
entries.literal: At that time General Who Conquers the West Ma Teng was stationed at Mei and rebelled; Yan and Fan communicated plots with Teng and led troops to raid Chang’an.

entries.zh: 範謀洩，奔槐里，騰敗，退還涼州，範應時見殺，於是收誕行刑。
entries.en: The plot unraveled: Fan fled to Huaili; Ma Teng was beaten back into Liangzhou; Fan was caught and killed, and Dan went to the executioner’s block.
entries.literal: Fan’s plot leaked; he fled to Huaili; Teng was defeated, withdrew and returned to Liang Province; Fan in due course was seen and killed; thereupon Dan was seized and executed.

entries.zh: 〈《英雄記》曰：範從長安亡之馬騰營，從焉求兵。
entries.en: 〈The Record of Heroes says: Fan slipped out of Chang’an to Ma Teng’s camp and begged his father for reinforcements.
entries.literal: 〈The Record of Heroes says: Fan fled from Chang’an to Ma Teng’s camp and from Yan sought troops.

entries.zh: 焉使校尉孫肇將兵往助之，敗於長安。〉
entries.en: Liu Yan sent Colonel Sun Zhao with troops; they were routed before Chang’an.
entries.literal: Yan ordered Colonel Sun Zhao to lead troops to go aid them; they were defeated at Chang’an.

entries.zh: 議郎河南龐羲與焉通家，乃募將焉諸孫入蜀。
entries.en: Pang Xi of Henan, a gentleman-adviser who was tied to the Liu family by marriage, raised men and shepherded Liu Yan’s grandsons to safety in Shu.
entries.literal: Gentleman-adviser Pang Xi of Henan was connected by family with Yan; then he recruited and led Yan’s various grandsons into Shu.

entries.zh: 時焉被天火燒城，車具蕩盡，延及民家。
entries.en: Heaven-sent fire then consumed his city, devouring the carriage stockpiles and spreading into the commoners’ quarters.
entries.literal: At that time Yan suffered heaven’s fire burning the city; carriage gear was completely swept away; it extended to common people’s homes.

entries.zh: 焉徙治成都，既痛其子，又感祅災，興平元年，癰疽發背而卒。
entries.en: He moved his government to Chengdu. Grief for his executed sons and shock at these portents broke him; in the first year of Xingping a carbuncle on his back killed him.
entries.literal: Yan moved his administration to Chengdu; having already grieved for his sons, and moreover being moved by uncanny disasters, in the first year of Xingping, an abscess-boil erupted on his back and he died.

entries.zh: 州大吏趙韙等貪璋溫仁，共上璋為益州刺史，詔書因以為監軍使者，領益州牧，以韙為征東中郎將，率眾擊劉表。
entries.en: Senior officers led by Zhao Wei, liking Liu Zhang’s mild temper, jointly nominated him inspector of Yizhou. The court named him military overseer and governor of the province, appointed Zhao Wei general of the east who expands might, and ordered him to campaign against Liu Biao.
entries.literal: Great clerks of the province such as Zhao Wei, coveting Zhang’s mild benevolence, jointly memorialized Zhang upward as inspector of Yizhou; an edict thereupon made him overseer of military affairs envoy, concurrently governor of Yizhou; Wei was made General of the East Who Expands Might, leading the host to attack Liu Biao.

entries.zh: 〈《英雄記》曰：焉死，子璋代為刺史。
entries.en: 〈The Record of Heroes adds: When Liu Yan died, his son Liu Zhang succeeded as inspector.
entries.literal: 〈The Record of Heroes says: when Yan died, his son Zhang replaced him as inspector.

entries.zh: 會長安拜潁川扈瑁為刺史，入漢中。
entries.en: Just then Chang’an named Hu Mao of Yingchuan inspector and sent him toward Hanzhong.
entries.literal: It happened that Chang’an appointed Hu Mao of Yingchuan as inspector; he entered Hanzhong.

entries.zh: 荊州別駕劉闔，璋將沈彌、婁發、甘寧反，擊璋不勝，走入荊州。
entries.en: Liu He, chief clerk on Liu Biao’s staff, with Liu Zhang’s officers Shen Mi, Lou Fa, and Gan Ning rose against their master, failed, and bolted into Jingzhou.
entries.literal: Jing Province chief clerk Liu He, Zhang’s generals Shen Mi, Lou Fa, and Gan Ning rebelled; they struck Zhang but did not win, and fled into Jing Province.

entries.zh: 璋使趙韙進攻荊州，屯朐䏰。
entries.en: Liu Zhang dispatched Zhao Wei against Jingzhou; he encamped at Quyi.
entries.literal: Zhang sent Zhao Wei to advance and attack Jing Province, encamping at Quyi.

entries.zh: 上蠢，下如振反。〉
entries.en: Phonetic gloss for the toponym Quyi (first syllable as noted in the commentary; second like zhèn).
entries.literal: Phonetic gloss for the toponym Quyi (first syllable as noted in the commentary; second like zhèn).

entries.zh: 璋字季玉，既襲焉位，而張魯稍驕恣，不承順璋，璋殺魯母及弟，遂為讎敵。
entries.en: Liu Zhang, courtesy Jiyu, inherited his father’s post. Zhang Lu grew insolent and defied him, so Liu Zhang executed Lu’s mother and brother, and the two became bitter enemies.
entries.literal: Zhang, courtesy name Jiyu, having inherited Yan’s position, then Zhang Lu gradually became arrogant and self-indulgent, did not obey and comply with Zhang; Zhang killed Lu’s mother and younger brother; then they became enemy foes.

entries.zh: 璋累遣龐羲等攻魯，數為所破。
entries.en: Liu Zhang sent Pang Xi and others against Zhang Lu time and again, only to be routed repeatedly.
entries.literal: Zhang repeatedly sent Pang Xi and others to attack Lu; several times were broken by him.

entries.zh: 魯部曲多在巴西，故以羲為巴西太守，領兵禦魯。
entries.en: Most of Zhang Lu’s followers were in Ba Commandery, so Liu Zhang named Pang Xi grand administrator there and put him on the northern front against Lu.
entries.literal: Lu’s retainers were mostly in Ba Commandery; therefore Xi was made grand administrator of Ba Commandery, leading troops to resist Lu.

entries.zh: 〈《英雄記》曰：龐羲與璋有舊，又免璋諸子於難，故璋厚德羲，以羲為巴西太守，遂專權勢。〉
entries.en: 〈The Record of Heroes notes: “Pang Xi was an old friend who had rescued Liu Zhang’s sons from peril, so Liu Zhang heaped favor on him, named him grand administrator of Ba, and let him dominate local power.”〉
entries.literal: 〈The Record of Heroes says: Pang Xi had old ties with Zhang, moreover had saved Zhang’s various sons from disaster; therefore Zhang heavily favored Xi, made Xi grand administrator of Ba Commandery, and then he monopolized power and influence.〉

entries.zh: 後羲與璋情好攜隙，趙韙稱兵內向，眾散見殺，皆由璋明斷少而外言入故也。
entries.en: Later Pang Xi and Liu Zhang fell out; Zhao Wei turned his army on Chengdu, his troops melted away, and he was killed—all because Liu Zhang seldom judged matters for himself and let rumor rule his court.
entries.literal: Later Xi and Zhang’s feelings and friendship carried a rift; Zhao Wei raised troops inward toward the capital; the host scattered and he was seen and killed; all was because Zhang had little clear decisive judgment and outside words entered.

entries.zh: 〈《英雄記》曰：先是，南陽、三輔人流入益州數万家，收以為兵，名曰東州兵。
entries.en: 〈The Record of Heroes explains: Refugees from Nanyang and the Three Adjuncts had poured into Yizhou by the tens of thousands; Liu Zhang drafted them as the so-called Eastern Province host.
entries.literal: 〈The Record of Heroes says: before this, people of Nanyang and the Three Adjuncts flowed into Yizhou in several tens of thousands of households; they were collected and made soldiers, named Eastern Province troops.

entries.zh: 璋性寬柔，無威略，東州人侵暴舊民，璋不能禁，政令多闕，益州頗怨。
entries.en: Liu Zhang was easygoing and lacked firm authority, so the easterners bullied the old families unchecked. Edicts went unenforced, and resentment spread through Yizhou.
entries.literal: Zhang’s nature was lenient and soft; he had no awe-inspiring strategy; Eastern Province people violated and abused the old common people; Zhang could not prohibit it; government orders had many gaps; Yizhou was quite resentful.

entries.zh: 趙韙素得人心，璋委任之。
entries.en: Zhao Wei enjoyed wide popularity, and Liu Zhang leaned on him heavily.
entries.literal: Zhao Wei always won people’s hearts; Zhang entrusted him.

entries.zh: 韙因民怨謀叛，乃厚賂荊州請和，陰結州中大姓，與俱起兵，還擊璋。
entries.en: Playing on popular anger, Zhao Wei plotted revolt: he bought a truce with Jingzhou in secret, won the great clans of the province, and marched on Chengdu against Liu Zhang.
entries.literal: Wei because of the people’s resentment plotted rebellion; then he thickly bribed Jing Province to request peace, secretly bound the great surnames of the province, and together with them raised troops, turned back and attacked Zhang.

entries.zh: 蜀郡、廣漢、犍為皆應韙。
entries.en: Shu, Guanghan, and Qianwei all rose in his name.
entries.literal: Shu, Guanghan, and Qianwei all responded to Wei.

entries.zh: 璋馳入成都城守，東州人畏
entries.en: Liu Zhang raced within Chengdu’s walls. The Eastern Province troops, fearing
entries.literal: Zhang galloped into Chengdu city to defend it; men of the Eastern Province feared

entries.en: disaster if the city fell (some editions insert the graph wei here),
entries.literal: (wei ‘might’ [variant graph supplied in some editions]),

entries.zh: 咸同心並力助璋，皆殊死戰，遂破反者，進攻韙於江州。
entries.en: closed ranks behind Liu Zhang and fought to the last man. They shattered the rebels and drove the siege against Zhao Wei at Jiangzhou.
entries.literal: all with one heart and combined strength aided Zhang; all fought to the death; then they broke the rebels and advanced to attack Wei at Jiangzhou.

entries.zh: 韙將龐樂、李異反殺韙軍，斬韙。
entries.en: Zhao Wei’s own generals Pang Le and Li Yi mutinied, cut down his troops, and took his head.
entries.literal: Wei’s generals Pang Le and Li Yi turned mutinous, killed Wei’s army, and beheaded Wei.

entries.zh: 《漢獻帝春秋》曰：漢朝聞益州亂，遣五官中郎將牛亶為益州刺史；
entries.en: The Annals of Emperor Xian records: Learning of the turmoil, the court dispatched Niu Dan, general of the household for all purposes, as inspector of Yizhou;
entries.literal: The Annals of Emperor Xian of Han says: the Han court heard that Yizhou was in chaos and sent General of the Household for All Purposes Niu Dan as inspector of Yizhou;

entries.zh: 徵璋為卿，不至。〉
entries.en: it also summoned Liu Zhang to a ministerial post—which he ignored.
entries.literal: summoned Zhang to be a minister; he did not arrive.

entries.zh: 璋卒，南中豪率雍闓據益郡反，附於吳。
entries.en: When Liu Zhang died, the southern magnate Yong Kai seized Yi commandery in revolt and pledged himself to Wu.
entries.literal: Zhang died; in the south magnate leader Yong Kai occupied Yi commandery and rebelled, attached to Wu.

entries.zh: 權復以璋子闡為益州刺史，處交、益界首。
entries.en: Sun Quan then appointed Liu Zhang’s son Liu Chan inspector of Yizhou and posted him on the Jiao–Yi frontier.
entries.literal: Quan again used Zhang’s son Chan as inspector of Yizhou, placing him at the border head of Jiao and Yi.

entries.zh: 丞相諸葛亮平南土，闡還吳，為御史中丞。
entries.en: After Chancellor Zhuge Liang pacified the south, Liu Chan returned to Wu and was promoted to palace assistant censor-in-chief.
entries.literal: Chancellor Zhuge Liang pacified the southern lands; Chan returned to Wu, became palace assistant censor-in-chief.

entries.zh: 〈《吳書》曰：闡一名緯，為人恭恪，輕財愛義，有仁讓之風，後疾終於家。〉
entries.en: 〈The Book of Wu adds that Liu Chan was also called Liu Wei: a courteous man who prized honor over money and died of illness at home.〉
entries.literal: 〈The Book of Wu says: Chan had another name Wei; as a person he was respectful and careful, lightened wealth and loved righteousness, had the air of benevolence and yielding; later he died of illness at home.〉

entries.zh: 初，璋長子循妻，龐羲女也。
entries.en: Earlier, Liu Zhang’s eldest son Liu Xun had married a daughter of Pang Xi.
entries.literal: At the beginning, Zhang’s eldest son Xun’s wife was Pang Xi’s daughter.

entries.zh: 先主定蜀，羲為左將軍司馬，璋時從羲啟留循，先主以為奉車中郎將。
entries.en: After Liu Bei conquered Shu, Pang Xi served as major to the general of the left. Liu Zhang at that time followed Pang Xi's petition to keep Liu Xun, and Liu Bei then commissioned Liu Xun as gentleman of the household for the chariot.
entries.literal: The Former Lord pacified Shu; Xi was major to the General of the Left; Zhang at that time followed Xi’s memorial to detain Xun; the Former Lord made him gentleman of the household for the chariot.

entries.zh: 是以璋二子之後，分在吳、蜀。
entries.en: Thus the two sons of Liu Zhang afterward lived out their lives apart, one in Wu and one in Shu.
entries.literal: Therefore as for the two sons of Zhang afterward, they were divided between Wu and Shu.

entries.zh: 評曰：昔魏豹聞許負之言則納薄姬於室，
entries.en: The historian’s judgment runs: Long ago Wei Bao listened to the soothsayer Xu Fu and welcomed Lady Bo into his harem,
entries.literal: The appraisal says: Formerly Wei Bao heard Xu Fu’s words then took concubine Bo Ji into the chamber,

entries.zh: 〈孔衍《漢魏春秋》曰：許負，河內溫縣之婦人，漢高祖封為明雌亭侯。
entries.en: 〈Kong Yan’s Springs and Autumns of Han and Wei identifies Xu Fu as a woman of Wen county in Henei whom Han Gaozu supposedly ennobled as mistress of Mingci village.
entries.literal: 〈Kong Yan’s Springs and Autumns of Han and Wei says: Xu Fu was a woman of Wen County in Henei; Han Gaozu enfeoffed her as village mistress of Mingci.

entries.zh: 臣松之以為今東人呼母為負，衍以許負為婦人，如為有似，然漢高祖時封皆列侯，未有鄉亭之爵，疑此封為不然。〉
entries.en: Pei Songzhi notes that eastern dialects used fu for “mother,” which may explain Kong Yan’s treating Xu Fu as a woman—yet Gaozu’s reign ennobled only full marquises, never mere village titles, so that fief is almost certainly wrong.
entries.literal: Your subject Songzhi considers that today eastern people call mother fu; Yan taking Xu Fu as a woman—if so there is resemblance; yet at Han Gaozu’s time enfeoffments were all full marquises, there were not village-hamlet ranks; I suspect this enfeoffment is incorrect.

entries.zh: 劉歆見圖讖之文則名字改易，終於不免其身，而慶鍾二主。
entries.en: Liu Xin changed his name after reading prognosticating texts, yet could not save himself, while the omen’s fulfillment fell instead upon two other sovereigns.
entries.literal: Liu Xin saw the texts of charts and prophecies then changed names and characters; in the end did not escape his own person, yet the auspice concentrated on two lords.

entries.zh: 此則神明不可虛要，天命不可妄冀，必然之驗也。
entries.en: So it is: the spirits cannot be coaxed with empty prayers, and the mandate of Heaven cannot be forced—that is the hard lesson of their fates.
entries.literal: This then is that the gods and numina cannot be emptily demanded; Heaven’s mandate cannot be recklessly hoped for—it is verification of necessity.

entries.zh: 而劉焉聞董扶之辭則心存益土，聽相者之言則求婚吳氏，遽造輿服，圖竊神器，其惑甚矣。
entries.en: Liu Yan took Dong Fu’s talk to heart and fixed his ambition on Yizhou, listened to a physiognomist and wed the Wu family, rushed out imperial-style carriages and robes, and angled for the throne—folly in its purest form.
entries.literal: But Liu Yan heard Dong Fu’s phrases then his heart lodged in Yi soil; heard the physiognomist’s words then sought marriage with the Wu clan; hastily made carriage and apparel, plotted to steal the sacred vessels—his delusion was extreme.

entries.zh: 璋才非人雄，而據土亂世，負乘致寇，自然之理，其見奪取，非不幸也。
entries.en: Liu Zhang was no champion of men, yet he clutched a rich province in an age of chaos—a lesser man in a high carriage invites robbers by nature. That he lost his domain was less misfortune than inevitability.
entries.literal: Zhang’s talents were not those of a human hero, yet he occupied territory in a chaotic age; bearing while riding brings bandits—it is natural principle; his being seen seized and taken is not misfortune.

entries.zh: 〈張璠曰：劉璋愚弱而守善言，斯亦宋襄公、徐偃王之徒，未為無道之主也。
entries.en: 〈Zhang Fan remarks: “Liu Zhang was dull and pliant yet clung to fine phrases—much like Duke Xiang of Song or King Yan of Xu; he hardly ranks among the truly lawless rulers.”
entries.literal: 〈Zhang Fan says: Liu Zhang was foolish and weak yet preserved good words; this also is of the class of Duke Xiang of Song, King Yan of Xu—not to be deemed a lord without the Way.

entries.zh: 張松、法正，雖有君臣之義不正，然固以委名附質，進不顯陳事勢，若韓嵩、
entries.en: Zhang Song and Fa Zheng broke the bond between lord and vassal, yet they had formally pledged themselves: they did not lay the strategic facts plainly before their master, as did Han Song,
entries.literal: Zhang Song, Fa Zheng—although the righteousness between ruler and minister was not correct, yet firmly they entrusted name and attached substance; advancing they did not openly set forth the situation of affairs, like Han Song,

entries.zh: （劉光）
entries.en: (Liu Guang)
entries.literal: (Liu Guang)

entries.zh: 劉先之說劉表，退不告絕奔亡，若陳平、韓信之去項羽，而兩端攜貳，為謀不忠，罪之次也。〉
entries.en: 〔Liu Xian〕 in counseling Liu Biao, or on retreating failed to announce a clean break before fleeing, as Chen Ping and Han Xin had done when they left Xiang Yu—yet they played both sides; such disloyal scheming is the lesser crime.
entries.literal: 〔Liu Xian〕’s persuading Liu Biao; withdrawing did not declare break and flee, like Chen Ping and Han Xin’s leaving Xiang Yu—yet wavering two ends, as planning not loyal, is the next grade of guilt.

entries.zh: 先主姓劉，諱備，字玄德，涿郡涿縣人，漢景帝子中山靖王勝之後也。
entries.en: The Former Lord was Liu Bei, courtesy Xuande, from Zhuo county in Zhuo commandery, a descendant of Han Prince Jing of Zhongshan, Prince Sheng, son of Emperor Jing.
entries.literal: The Former Lord’s surname was Liu, his taboo name was Bei, his courtesy name Xuande; he was a man of Zhuo County in Zhuo Commandery; he was a descendant of Prince Jing of Zhongshan Sheng, son of Han Emperor Jing.

entries.zh: 勝子貞，元狩六年封涿縣陸城亭侯，坐酎金失侯，因家焉。
entries.en: Sheng’s son Liu Zhen received the village fief of Lucheng at Zhuo in the sixth year of Yuanshou, lost his rank over the “ritual gold” affair, and the line then made its home there.
entries.literal: Sheng’s son Zhen, in the sixth year of Yuanshou, was enfeoffed village marquis of Lucheng in Zhuo County; he sat guilty of ritual gold and lost the marquisate; therefore the family settled there.

entries.zh: 〈典略曰：備本臨邑侯枝屬也。〉
entries.en: 〈The Compendium states that Liu Bei sprang from a collateral branch of the marquises of Linyi.〉
entries.literal: 〈The Compendium says: Bei was originally a cadet branch of the marquis of Linyi.〉

entries.zh: 先主祖雄，父弘，世仕州郡。
entries.en: His grandfather Liu Xiong and father Liu Hong had for generations held posts in local government.
entries.literal: The Former Lord’s grandfather was Xiong, his father was Hong; for generations they served in prefecture and commandery offices.

entries.zh: 雄舉孝廉，官至東郡範令。
entries.en: Liu Xiong rose as a filial and incorrupt candidate to magistrate of Fan in Dong commandery.
entries.literal: Xiong was recommended as filial and incorrupt; his office reached magistrate of Fan in Dong Commandery.

entries.zh: 二十五年，魏文帝稱尊號，改年曰黃初。
