entries.literal: In youth he and his younger cousin Shao were both famous, and together they had a reputation for judging men and ranking character, but in private feeling they were not harmonious.

entries.zh: 劭為郡功曹，排擯靖不得齒敘，以馬磨自給。
entries.en: When Shao served as the commandery’s merit assessor, he shut Xu Jing out of official placement altogether, and Xu was reduced to earning a living at a horse-driven mill.
entries.literal: Shao became merit assessor of the commandery, excluded Jing so that he could not be ranked in order, and Jing supported himself by grinding grain with a horse mill.

entries.zh: 颍川劉翊為汝南太守，乃舉靖計吏，察孝廉，除尚書郎，典選舉。
entries.en: Liu Yi of Yingchuan, as grand warden of Runan, nominated Xu Jing as accounts clerk, then recommended him on the filial-and-incorrupt roll; Xu was appointed gentleman of the Secretariat and given charge of personnel appointments.
entries.literal: Liu Yi of Yingchuan became grand warden of Runan, thereupon recommended Jing as clerk on the annual accounts, investigated him as filial and incorrupt, appointed him gentleman of the masters of writing, and put him in charge of selections.

entries.zh: 靈帝崩，董卓秉政，以漢陽周毖為吏部尚書，與靖共謀議，進退天下之士，沙汰穢濁，顯拔幽滯。
entries.en: After Emperor Ling’s death, Dong Zhuo took power. He named Zhou Bi of Hanyang director of personnel and had him work with Xu Jing to decide promotions and dismissals across the empire—purging the corrupt and raising men who had long languished in obscurity.
entries.literal: When Emperor Ling died, Dong Zhuo seized government, appointed Zhou Bi of Hanyang as director of the Ministry of Personnel, and with Jing together deliberated, advancing and retiring the gentlemen of the realm, washing away the foul and turbid, and manifestly elevating the secluded and blocked.

entries.zh: 進用颍川荀爽、韓融、陳紀等為公、卿、郡守，拜尚書韓馥為冀州牧，侍中劉岱為兗州剌史，颍川張咨為南陽太守，陳留孔伷為豫州剌史，東郡張邈為陳留太守，而遷靖巴郡太守，不就，補御史中丞。
entries.en: They brought in men such as Xun Shuang, Han Rong, and Chen Ji of Yingchuan to fill the highest civil posts and commandery governorships; Han Fu was made shepherd of Ji, Liu Dai inspector of Yan, Zhang Zi grand warden of Nanyang, Kong Zhou inspector of Yu, and Zhang Miao grand warden of Chenliu. Xu Jing was slated for Ba commandery, but he declined the post and was appointed assistant secretary of the imperial censorate instead.
entries.literal: They advanced and employed Xun Shuang, Han Rong, Chen Ji, and others of Yingchuan as dukes, ministers, and grand wardens; invested Masters of Writing Han Fu as shepherd of Ji province, Palace Attendant Liu Dai as inspector of Yan province, Zhang Zi of Yingchuan as grand warden of Nanyang, Kong Zhou of Chenliu as inspector of Yu province, Zhang Miao of Dong commandery as grand warden of Chenliu; and transferred Jing to be grand warden of Ba commandery, but he did not take up the post, and was instead supplemented as palace assistant secretary.

entries.zh: 馥等到官，各舉兵還向京都，欲以誅卓。
entries.en: Once Han Fu and his colleagues reached their assignments, they each mobilized forces and marched on the capital, aiming to destroy Dong Zhuo.
entries.literal: When Fu and the others reached their posts, each raised troops and turned back toward the capital, intending thereby to execute Zhuo.

entries.zh: 卓怒毖曰︰「諸君言當拔用善士，卓從諸君計，不欲違天下人心。
entries.en: Dong Zhuo rounded on Zhou Bi in fury: "You insisted we elevate worthy men. I followed your counsel because I would not set myself against the will of the realm.
entries.literal: Zhuo angrily said to Bi: "You gentlemen said one ought to promote and employ good gentlemen; Zhuo followed your gentlemen's plan and did not wish to go against the hearts of men under Heaven.

entries.zh: 而諸君所用人，至官之日，還來相圖。
entries.en: Yet the very men you placed in office turned their armies against me the moment they took up their posts.
entries.literal: Yet as for the men your gentlemen employed, on the day they reached office, they returned to plot against me.

entries.zh: 卓何用查負！」
entries.en: What have I done to deserve such treachery in return?"
entries.literal: What use has Zhuo for being betrayed!"

entries.zh: 叱毖令出，于外斬之。
entries.en: He had Zhou Bi hustled outside and executed him on the spot.
entries.literal: He shouted at Bi ordering him out, and outside beheaded him.

entries.zh: 靖從兄陳相玚，又與伷合規，靖懼誅，奔伷。
entries.en: Xu Jing’s cousin Xu Yang, who was chancellor of Chen, was also in league with Kong Zhou’s designs; fearing he would be put to death, Xu Jing fled to Kong Zhou’s camp.
entries.literal: Jing's elder cousin Yang, chancellor of Chen, again with Zhou joined in plotting; Jing feared execution and fled to Zhou.

entries.zh: 〈蜀記雲：靖後自表曰：「黨賊求生，情所不忍；
entries.en: 〈The Shu Ji records that Xu Jing later explained in a memorial: "To side with rebels merely to save my skin was more than conscience would allow;
entries.literal: 〈The Shu Ji states: Later Jing himself in a memorial said: "To cling to rebels to seek life, in feeling is what I cannot bear;

entries.zh: 守官自危，死不成義。
entries.en: to cling to an empty title while peril closed in would have been a death that accomplished no duty worth the name.
entries.literal: to guard office and endanger oneself, to die and not complete righteousness.

entries.zh: 竊念古人當難詭常，權以濟其道。」〉
entries.en: I recalled how the ancients, in extremity, bent the usual rules and used timely shifts of course to preserve what truly mattered."〉
entries.literal: I privately thought that the ancients, facing difficulty, altered the constant, and by expediency aided their way."〉

entries.zh: 伷卒，依揚州剌史陳祎。
entries.en: After Kong Zhou died, Xu Jing took refuge with Chen Yi, the inspector of Yang province.
entries.literal: When Zhou died, he relied on Chen Yi, inspector of Yang province.

entries.zh: 祎死，吳郡都尉許貢、會稽太守王朗素與靖有舊，故往保焉。
entries.en: When Chen Yi died, Wu’s commandant Xu Gong and Kuaiji’s grand warden Wang Lang—both old acquaintances—offered Xu Jing shelter.
entries.literal: When Yi died, Commandant of Wu Commandery Xu Gong and Grand Warden of Kuaiji Wang Lang, who from old had ties with Jing, therefore went to protect there.

entries.zh: 靖收恤親裡，經紀振贍，出于仁濃。
entries.en: Xu Jing gathered his kinsmen and neighbors, organized relief, and kept them fed—acts born of deep human kindness.
entries.literal: Jing gathered and comforted kin and neighborhood, managed and relieved and supported, coming from thick benevolence.

entries.zh: 巴復從交阯至蜀。
entries.en: From Jiaozhi Liu Ba eventually made his way into Shu.
entries.literal: Ba again went from Jiaozhi to Shu.

entries.zh: 〈零陵先賢傳曰：巴入交阯，更姓為張。
entries.en: 〈The Lingling tradition adds that after entering Jiaozhi he assumed the surname Zhang.
entries.literal: 〈The Traditions of Former Worthies of Lingling states: When Ba entered Jiaozhi, he changed his surname to Zhang.

entries.zh: 與交阯太守士谿計議不合，乃由牂牁道去。
entries.en: He quarreled with Jiaozhi Administrator Shi Xi and slipped away along the Zangke route.
entries.literal: He did not agree in planning and consultation with the Administrator of Jiaozhi, Shi Xi; therefore he departed by the Zangke road.

entries.zh: 為益州郡所拘留，太守欲殺之。
entries.en: Yi Province authorities seized him and the local prefect meant to execute him.
entries.literal: He was detained by Yi Province Commandery; the Administrator wished to kill him.

entries.zh: 主簿曰：「此非常人，不可殺也。」
entries.en: His chief clerk protested: "This is no ordinary captive—you must not kill him."
entries.literal: The chief clerk said: 'This is no ordinary man; he cannot be killed.'

entries.zh: 主簿請自送至州，見益州牧劉璋，璋父焉昔為巴父祥所舉孝廉，見巴驚喜，每大事輒以諮訪。
entries.en: The clerk offered to escort Liu Ba to provincial headquarters. Yi Governor Liu Zhang—whose father Liu Yan had once received a filial-and-incorrupt nomination from Liu Ba’s father—welcomed him warmly and consulted him on every major decision.
entries.literal: The chief clerk requested personally to escort him to the province and see the Governor of Yi Province, Liu Zhang; Zhang's father Yan in the past had been nominated Filial and Incorrupt by Ba's father Xiang; seeing Ba, [Zhang] was astonished and delighted; on every great matter he then took counsel and inquiry.

entries.zh: 臣松之案：劉焉在漢靈帝時已經宗正太常，出為益州牧，祥始以孫堅作長沙時為江夏太守，不得舉焉為孝廉，明也。〉
entries.en: Pei Songzhi notes: Liu Yan had already served as director of the imperial clan and grand master of ceremonies under Emperor Ling before he became Yi governor, whereas Liu Xiang became Jiangxia administrator only during Sun Jian’s tenure at Changsha—so he could not have nominated Liu Yan as filial and incorrupt; the anecdote cannot stand.〉
entries.literal: Your subject Songzhi examines: Liu Yan in Emperor Ling of Han's time had already passed through Director of the Imperial Clan and Grand Master of Ceremonies and gone out as Governor of Yi Province; Xiang only when Sun Jian was at Changsha became Administrator of Jiangxia—he could not have nominated Yan as Filial and Incorrupt—this is clear.〉

entries.zh: 俄而先主定益州，巴辭謝罪負，先主不責。
entries.en: When Liu Bei soon mastered Yi Province, Liu Ba offered a humble apology for his past opposition; Liu Bei did not punish him.
entries.literal: Soon the First Sovereign settled Yi Province; Ba apologized for guilt and burden; the First Sovereign did not blame him.

entries.zh: 〈零陵先賢傳曰：璋遣法正迎劉備，巴諫曰：「備，雄人也，入必為害，不可內也。」
entries.en: 〈The Lingling tradition says Liu Zhang sent Fa Zheng to welcome Liu Bei. Liu Ba warned: "Liu Bei is a formidable rival; letting him in courts disaster."
entries.literal: 〈The Traditions of Former Worthies of Lingling states: Zhang dispatched Fa Zheng to welcome Liu Bei; Ba remonstrated, saying: 'Bei is a heroic man; if he enters he will surely become a harm—he cannot be let in.'

entries.zh: 既入，巴复諫曰：「若使備討張魯，是放虎於山林也。」
entries.en: After Liu Bei entered Shu, Liu Ba protested again: "Sending him against Zhang Lu is like turning a tiger loose in the hills."
entries.literal: After [Bei] entered, Ba again remonstrated, saying: 'If you send Bei to campaign against Zhang Lu, this is releasing a tiger in mountain forests.'

entries.zh: 璋不聽。
entries.en: Liu Zhang ignored him.
entries.literal: Zhang did not listen.

entries.zh: 巴閉門稱疾。
entries.en: Liu Ba shut his doors and pleaded illness.
entries.literal: Ba closed his gate and claimed illness.

entries.zh: 備攻成都，令軍中曰：「其有害巴者，誅及三族。」
entries.en: During the siege of Chengdu Liu Bei ordered: "Anyone who harms Liu Ba will answer with the three-clan penalty."
entries.literal: When Bei attacked Chengdu, he ordered the army, saying: 'As for any who harm Ba, execution extends to three clans.'

entries.zh: 及得巴，甚喜。〉
entries.en: When Liu Ba finally came into his hands, Liu Bei was overjoyed.〉
entries.literal: When he obtained Ba, he was greatly pleased.〉

entries.zh: 而諸葛孔明數稱薦之，先主闢為左將軍西曹掾。
entries.en: Zhuge Liang spoke up for him repeatedly, and Liu Bei named him western bureau clerk on the Left General’s staff.
entries.literal: Moreover Zhuge Kongming repeatedly praised and recommended him; the First Sovereign appointed him as Western Bureau Clerk to the Left General.

entries.zh: 〈零陵先賢傳曰：張飛嘗就巴宿，巴不與語，飛遂忿恚。
entries.en: 〈The Lingling tradition recounts that Zhang Fei once tried to stay the night with Liu Ba; Liu Ba refused to speak to him, and Zhang Fei flared up.
entries.literal: 〈The Traditions of Former Worthies of Lingling states: Zhang Fei once went to lodge with Ba; Ba did not speak with him; Fei therefore was resentful and angry.

entries.zh: 諸葛亮謂巴曰：「張飛雖實武人，敬慕足下。
entries.en: Zhuge Liang urged Liu Ba: "Zhang Fei may be a soldier, but he admires you.
entries.literal: Zhuge Liang said to Ba: 'Although Zhang Fei is indeed a military man, he esteems and admires you.

entries.zh: 主公今方收合文武，以定大事；
entries.en: Our lord is knitting civil and military officers together for the great task ahead;
entries.literal: The lord now is just gathering civil and military to settle great affairs;

entries.zh: 足下雖天素高亮，宜少降意也。」
entries.en: you are rightly proud by nature, yet you might bend a little."
entries.literal: although you, sir, by Heaven's nature are lofty and bright, you ought slightly to lower your intent.'

entries.zh: 巴曰：「大丈夫處世，當交四海英雄，如何與兵子共語乎？」
entries.en: Liu Ba answered: "A gentleman should consort with heroes from every quarter—why should I waste words on a mere fighting man?"
entries.literal: Ba said: 'A great man in the world ought to associate with heroes within the Four Seas—how can he speak together with soldier lads?'

entries.zh: 備聞之，怒曰：「孤欲定天下，而子初專亂之。
entries.en: Liu Bei heard this and growled: "I mean to pacify the empire, yet Zichu keeps sowing discord.
entries.literal: When Bei heard it, he angrily said: 'I desire to settle the realm, yet Zichu specially throws it into disorder.

entries.zh: 其欲還北，假道於此，豈欲成孤事邪？」
entries.en: He wants to return north and is only borrowing a road here—does he mean to complete my enterprise?"
entries.literal: His desire is to return north, borrowing a road here—does he wish to complete my enterprise?'

entries.zh: 備又曰：「子初才智絕人，如孤，可任用之，非孤者難獨任也。」
entries.en: Then he added: "Zichu’s abilities tower above other men. A ruler like me can use him; anyone less would fail alone."
entries.literal: Bei also said: 'Zichu's talent and wisdom surpass others; one like me can employ him—those who are not like me will find it hard to employ him alone.'

entries.zh: 亮亦曰：「運籌策於帷幄之中，吾不如子初遠矣！
entries.en: Zhuge Liang said: "When it comes to planning behind the curtain, I am nowhere near Zichu.
entries.literal: Liang also said: 'In planning strategies within the tent, I am far inferior to Zichu!

entries.zh: 若提枹鼓，會軍門，使百姓喜勇，當與人議之耳。」
entries.en: But beat the war drums at the camp gate and fire the people’s courage—that is a topic for other advisers."
entries.literal: If [it is a matter of] grasping drumsticks and drum, assembling at the army gate, making the hundred surnames rejoice in bravery—then one ought to consult others about it.'

entries.zh: 初攻劉璋，備與士眾約：「若事定，府庫百物，孤無預焉。」
entries.en: At the outset of the war on Liu Zhang, Liu Bei had promised the army: "Once we win, the public stores are yours, not mine."
entries.literal: When they first attacked Liu Zhang, Bei made a pact with officers and troops: 'If the affair is settled, as for the granaries and treasuries and hundred goods—I have no part in them.'

entries.zh: 及拔成都，士眾皆舍干戈，赴諸藏競取寶物。
entries.en: Yet when Chengdu fell, the men threw down their arms and mobbed the treasuries for loot.
entries.literal: When they took Chengdu, officers and troops all cast aside weapons and hastened to the various storehouses, competing to seize precious goods.

entries.zh: 軍用不足，備甚憂之。
entries.en: Military funds ran dry, and Liu Bei was frantic.
entries.literal: Military supplies were insufficient; Bei was greatly worried about it.

entries.zh: 巴曰：「易耳，但當鑄直百錢，平諸物賈，令吏為官巿。」
entries.en: Liu Ba said: "Simple: mint high-value copper coins, stabilize prices, and let officials run public markets."
entries.literal: Ba said: 'It is easy; one need only cast hundred-value coins, level the prices of the various goods, and order clerks to make official markets.'

entries.zh: 備從之，數月之間，府庫充實。〉
entries.en: Liu Bei agreed; within months the treasuries were full again.〉
entries.literal: Bei followed this; within several months the granaries and treasuries were full and substantial.〉

entries.zh: 建安二十四年，先主為漢中王，巴為尚書，後代法正為尚書令。
entries.en: In 219, when Liu Bei became king of Hanzhong, Liu Ba was appointed minister and later succeeded Fa Zheng as director of the masters of writing.
entries.literal: In the twenty-fourth year of Jian'an, the First Sovereign became King of Hanzhong; Ba was Minister; afterward he replaced Fa Zheng as Director of the Masters of Writing.

entries.zh: 躬履清儉，不治產業，又自以歸附非素，懼見猜嫌，恭默守靜，退無私交，非公事不言。
entries.en: He lived plainly and built no private fortune; because he had joined Liu Bei late he feared suspicion, kept his head down, avoided private friendships, and spoke only on official business.
entries.literal: Personally he practiced purity and frugality; he did not manage estates; moreover he considered himself not long affiliated by nature and feared being suspected; he was respectful and silent, guarding quietude; in retirement he had no private associations; except for public affairs he did not speak.

entries.zh: 〈零陵先賢傳曰：是時中夏人情未一，聞備在蜀，四方延頸。
entries.en: 〈The Lingling tradition notes that the Central Plains were still divided, yet everywhere men craned their necks toward Liu Bei in Shu.
entries.literal: 〈The Traditions of Former Worthies of Lingling states: At this time hearts in central Xia were not yet one; hearing that Bei was in Shu, the four quarters stretched their necks.

entries.zh: 而備銳意欲即真，巴以為如此示天下不廣，且欲緩之。
entries.en: Liu Bei was impatient to declare himself emperor; Liu Ba argued that rushing would look petty to the world and urged delay.
entries.literal: Yet Bei keenly desired immediately to assume the true [throne]; Ba thought that in this way showing the realm was not broad-minded, and moreover wished to slow it.

entries.zh: 與主簿雍茂諫備，備以他事殺茂，由是遠人不復至矣。〉
entries.en: He and chief clerk Yong Mao spoke against it; Liu Bei executed Yong on another charge, and talent from afar stopped coming.〉
entries.literal: Together with chief clerk Yong Mao he remonstrated Bei; Bei on another matter killed Mao; from this men from afar did not again arrive.〉

entries.zh: 先主稱尊號，昭告於皇天上帝后土神祇，凡諸文誥策命，皆巴所作也。
entries.en: When Liu Bei took the imperial title and proclaimed it to Heaven and Earth, every proclamation and investiture document came from Liu Ba’s brush.
entries.literal: When the First Sovereign assumed the honored title, he proclaimed to August Heaven, Supreme Lord, Posterior Earth, and the spirits; all documents of edicts, commands, and patent appointments were composed by Ba.

entries.zh: 章武二年卒。
entries.en: He died in the second year of the Zhangwu era (222).
entries.literal: He died in the second year of Zhangwu.

entries.zh: 卒後，魏尚書僕射陳群與丞相諸葛亮書，問巴消息，稱曰劉君子初，甚敬重焉。
entries.en: After his death Wei’s supervisor of the masters of writing, Chen Qun, wrote Zhuge Liang asking after “Lord Liu Zichu,” a mark of deep respect.
entries.literal: After his death, Wei Supervisor of the Masters of Writing Chen Qun wrote to Chancellor Zhuge Liang, inquiring after Ba's news, addressing him as 'Lord Liu Zichu,' greatly esteeming and respecting him.

entries.zh: 〈零陵先賢傳曰：輔吳將軍張昭嘗對孫權論巴褊□厄，不當拒張飛太甚。
entries.en: 〈The tradition adds that Zhang Zhao once told Sun Quan Liu Ba had been too harsh—narrow-minded perhaps—in snubbing Zhang Fei.
entries.literal: 〈The Traditions of Former Worthies of Lingling states: General Who Aids Wu Zhang Zhao once spoke to Sun Quan discussing Ba's narrowness [text damaged] adversity—one ought not to have refused Zhang Fei too severely.

entries.zh: 權曰：「若令子初隨世沈浮，容悅玄德，交非其人，何足稱為高士乎？」〉
entries.en: Sun Quan replied: "Had Zichu bent with every fashion and flattered Liu Bei just to fit in, could we still call him a man of principle?"〉
entries.literal: Quan said: 'If one ordered Zichu to drift and sink with the age, ingratiating himself to Xuande, associating with unworthy persons—how could that suffice to be called a lofty gentleman?'〉

entries.zh: 九年，都護李平坐誣罔廢；
entries.en: In 231 Chief Protector Li Yan was stripped of office for deceit;
entries.literal: In the ninth year [231], Chief Protector Li Ping sat [was sentenced] for slanderous deceit and was dismissed;

entries.zh: 諸葛亮與長史蔣琬、侍中董允書曰：「孝起前臨至吳，為吾說正方腹中有鱗甲，鄉黨以為不可近。
entries.en: Zhuge Liang wrote Jiang Wan and Dong Yun: “When Xiaoqi went east he warned me Li Yan was armored inside—his neighbors had long kept their distance.
entries.literal: Zhuge Liang wrote to Chief Clerk Jiang Wan and Palace Attendant Dong Yun, saying: 'When Xiaoqi previously went forth to Wu, he told me Zhengfang [Li Ping's style] had fish scales inside his belly—his village fellows considered him untouchable.

entries.zh: 吾以為鱗甲者但不當犯之耳，不圖復有蘇、張之事出於不意。
entries.en: I assumed that meant merely “don’t provoke him”—I never expected another Su–Zhang intrigue.
entries.literal: I thought that "fish scales" meant only that one ought not offend him—I did not scheme that again there would be Su[-Qin] and Zhang [Yi] affairs arising beyond expectation.

entries.zh: 可使孝起知之。」
entries.en: Let Xiaoqi hear of it.”
entries.literal: You may cause Xiaoqi to know this.'

entries.zh: 十三年，震卒。
entries.en: Chen Zhen died in 235.
entries.literal: In the thirteenth year, Zhen died.

entries.zh: 子濟嗣。
entries.en: His son Chen Ji inherited the title.
entries.literal: His son Ji succeeded.

entries.zh: 祗字奉宗，汝南人，許靖兄之外孫也。
entries.en: Chen Zhi, styled Fengzong, came from Runan and was the maternal grandson of Xu Jing's elder brother.
entries.literal: Zhi, courtesy name Fengzong, was a man of Runan; he was the maternal grandson of Xu Jing's elder brother.

entries.zh: 少孤，長於靖家。
entries.en: Orphaned young, he was raised in Xu Jing's household.
entries.literal: Orphaned young, he was raised in Jing's household.

entries.zh: 弱冠知名，稍遷至選曹郎，矜厲有威容。
entries.en: He was already known at capping age and was gradually promoted to gentleman of the selection bureau, stern and imposing in bearing.
entries.literal: At capping age he was already known; he was gradually promoted to Gentleman of the Selection Bureau, stern and imposing in bearing.

entries.zh: 多技藝，挾數術，費禕甚異之，故超繼允內侍。
entries.en: Skilled in many arts and versed in divination, he greatly impressed Fei Yi, who therefore had him leapfrog Dong Yun into inner court service.
entries.literal: Skilled in many arts and versed in numerology, Fei Yi greatly regarded him as extraordinary; therefore he was promoted ahead of Yun into inner service.

entries.zh: 呂乂卒，祗又以侍中守尚書令，加鎮軍將軍，大將軍姜維雖班在祗上，常率眾在外，希親朝政。
entries.en: When Lü Yi died, Chen Zhi again served as palace attendant while acting as director of the masters of writing and was further named general who stabilizes the army. Grand General Jiang Wei, though ranking above him, usually led troops in the field and seldom attended to court governance.
entries.literal: When Lü Yi died, Zhi again served as palace attendant while acting as Director of the Masters of Writing, and was further given the title General Who Stabilizes the Army; Grand General Jiang Wei, though ranking above Zhi, usually led troops outside and seldom attended to court governance.

entries.zh: 祗上承主指，下接閹豎，深見信愛，權重於維。
entries.en: Chen Zhi carried out the sovereign's intent above and cultivated ties with eunuch attendants below; he was deeply trusted and favored, and his authority outweighed Jiang Wei's.
entries.literal: Zhi carried out the sovereign's intent above and cultivated ties with eunuch attendants below; he was deeply trusted and favored, and his authority outweighed Wei's.

entries.zh: 景耀元年卒，後主痛惜，發言流涕，乃下詔曰：「祗統職一紀，柔嘉惟則，幹肅有章，和義利物，庶績允明。
entries.en: He died in the first year of the Jingyao era. The Later Lord grieved deeply, wept as he spoke, and issued an edict: "Zhi held office for a full twelve years; gentle and good, he was a model; dignified and orderly, his conduct was manifest; harmonious and righteous, he benefited things and men; his many achievements were clear and bright.
entries.literal: In the first year of Jingyao he died; the Later Lord grieved deeply, wept as he spoke, and issued an edict saying: "Zhi held office for a full twelve years; gentle and good, he was a model; dignified and orderly, his conduct was manifest; harmonious and righteous, he benefited things and men; his many achievements were bright and clear.

entries.zh: 命不融遠，朕用悼焉。
entries.en: Fate did not grant him long life, and We mourn him.
entries.literal: Fate did not grant him long life; We mourn him.

entries.zh: 夫存有令問，則亡加美諡，諡曰忠侯。」
entries.en: When one in life has a fine reputation, in death an honorable posthumous title is added; his posthumous title is Loyal Marquis."
entries.literal: When one in life has a fine reputation, in death an honorable posthumous title is added; his posthumous title is Loyal Marquis."

entries.zh: 賜子粲爵關內侯，拔次子裕為黃門侍郎。
entries.en: He enfeoffed Chen Zhi's son Can as marquis within the passes and promoted his second son Yu to gentleman attendant at the yellow gates.
entries.literal: He granted Zhi's son Can noble rank as marquis within the passes and promoted his second son Yu to Gentleman Attendant at the Yellow Gates.

entries.zh: 自祗之有寵，後主追怨允日深，謂為自輕，由祗媚茲一人，皓構間浸潤故耳。
entries.en: From the time Chen Zhi gained favor, the Later Lord's resentment toward Dong Yun grew daily deeper; he thought himself undervalued—because Chen Zhi flattered this one man and Huang Hao wove intrigues and gradually poisoned his ear.
entries.literal: From the time Zhi gained favor, the Later Lord's resentment toward Yun grew daily deeper; he thought himself undervalued—because Zhi flattered this one man and Hao wove intrigues and gradually poisoned his ear.

entries.zh: 允孫宏，晉巴西太守。
entries.en: Dong Yun's grandson Hong served Jin as administrator of Brazil.
entries.literal: Yun's grandson Hong, under Jin, was Administrator of Brazil.

entries.zh: 臣松之以為陳群子泰，陸遜子抗，傳皆以子系父，不別載姓，及王肅、杜恕、張承、顧劭之流，莫不皆然，惟董允獨否，未詳其意，當以允名位優重，事蹟逾父故邪？
entries.en: Pei Songzhi notes that for Chen Qun's son Tai, Lu Xun's son Kang, and others, the biographies all attach sons under fathers without separately recording the surname; Wang Su, Du Shu, Zhang Cheng, Gu Shao, and the like all follow this pattern—only Dong Yun does not. The reason is unclear; perhaps because Yun's name and rank were exalted and his achievements surpassed his father's?
entries.literal: Pei Songzhi considers that for Chen Qun's son Tai, Lu Xun's son Kang, and others, the biographies all treat sons under fathers without separately recording the surname; Wang Su, Du Shu, Zhang Cheng, Gu Shao, and the like were all the same—only Dong Yun was not. The reason is unclear; perhaps because Yun's name and rank were exalted and his achievements surpassed his father's?

entries.zh: 夏侯玄、陳表並有騂角之美，而亦如泰者，《魏書》總名此卷云《諸夏侯曹傳》，故不復稍加品藻。
entries.en: Both Xiahou Xuan and Chen Biao had the brilliance of young prodigies, and cases like Tai's—the Wei shu titles this whole scroll "Biographies of the Xiahous, Cao clan, and others," so no further comment is added.
entries.literal: Both Xiahou Xuan and Chen Biao had the brilliance of young prodigies, and cases like Tai's—the Wei shu titles this whole scroll "Biographies of the Xiahous, Cao clan, and others," so no further elaboration is added.

entries.zh: 陳武與表俱至偏將軍，以位不相過故也。
entries.en: Chen Wu and Biao both reached the rank of lieutenant general because their ranks did not surpass each other's.
entries.literal: Chen Wu and Biao both reached the rank of lieutenant general; because their ranks did not surpass each other's.

entries.zh: 呂乂字季陽，南陽人也。
entries.en: Lü Yi, styled Jiyang, came from Nanyang.
entries.literal: Lü Yi, courtesy name Jiyang, was a man of Nanyang.

entries.zh: 父常，送故將
entries.en: His father Lü Chang escorted a former general
entries.literal: His father Chang escorted a former general

entries.en: (text damaged; likely ‘general of the army’ or similar)
entries.literal: (army)

entries.zh: 劉焉入蜀，值王路隔塞，遂不得還。
entries.en: Liu Yan’s march into Shu cut Lü Chang off from home—he never got back.
entries.literal: When Liu Yan entered Shu, it happened that royal roads were blocked and sealed; therefore [Chang] could not return.

entries.zh: 乂少孤，好讀書鼓琴。
entries.en: Orphaned young, Lü Yi loved books and the qin.
entries.literal: Yi was orphaned young; he loved reading books and strumming the qin.

entries.zh: 初，先主定益州，置鹽府校尉，較鹽鐵之利，後校尉王連請乂及南陽杜祺、南鄉劉幹等並為典曹都尉。
entries.en: After Liu Bei took Yi Province he set up a salt monopoly to manage iron and salt revenues; Colonel Wang Lian later named Lü Yi, Du Qi of Nanyang, Liu Gan of Nanxiang, and others capital bureau commandants.
entries.literal: At first, when the First Sovereign settled Yi Province, he established a Salt Office Colonel to compare the profits of salt and iron; afterward Colonel Wang Lian requested Yi together with Du Qi of Nanyang, Liu Gan of Nanxiang, and others concurrently as Capital Bureau Commandants.

entries.zh: 乂遷新都、綿竹令，乃心隱卹，百姓稱之，為一州諸城之首。
entries.en: As magistrate of Xindu and Mianzhu he governed with genuine compassion; people acclaimed him the finest administrator in the province.
entries.literal: Yi was transferred to be magistrate of Xindu and Mianzhu; he applied his heart to hidden sympathy; the hundred surnames praised him; he was first among the various cities of one province.

entries.zh: 遷巴西太守。
entries.en: He was promoted to administrator of Ba-Xi.
entries.literal: He was promoted to Administrator of Ba-Xi.

entries.zh: 丞相諸葛亮連年出軍，調發諸郡，多不相救，乂募取兵五千人詣亮，慰喻檢制，無逃竄者。
entries.en: Zhuge Liang’s endless campaigns strained county levies until few answered the call. Lü Yi raised five thousand men, delivered them to the front, and through careful encouragement and discipline lost not one deserter.
entries.literal: Chancellor Zhuge Liang for successive years led armies forth; requisitions were issued to the various commanderies—many did not mutually aid one another; Yi recruited and took five thousand soldiers and went to Liang; comforting, instructing, inspecting, and regulating—there were none who fled.

entries.zh: 徙為漢中太守，兼領督農，供繼軍糧。
entries.en: Transferred to Hanzhong administrator, he doubled as agriculture intendant and kept the northern armies fed.
entries.literal: He was shifted to Administrator of Hanzhong, concurrently supervising agriculture, supplying successive military grain.

entries.zh: 亮卒，累遷廣漢、蜀郡太守。
entries.en: After Zhuge Liang’s death he rose through posts as Guanghan and Shu administrators.
entries.literal: When Liang died, [Yi] was progressively promoted to Administrator of Guanghan and Shu Commandery.

entries.zh: 蜀郡一都之會，戶口眾多，又亮卒之後，士伍亡命，更相重冒，姦巧非一。
entries.en: Shu Commandery, centered on the capital, swarmed with people; after Zhuge Liang’s death deserters multiplied identities and fraud flourished in countless forms.
entries.literal: Shu Commandery was the meeting place of the capital region; households were numerous; moreover after Liang died, soldiers fled service; they mutually doubled and falsely assumed [identities]; crafty deceit was not of one kind.

entries.zh: 乂到官，為之防禁，開喻勸導，數年之中，漏脫自出者萬馀口。
entries.en: Lü Yi tightened regulations, explained the law, and within a few years coaxed more than ten thousand ghosts back onto the rolls.
entries.literal: When Yi arrived at office, for these matters he set prevention and prohibition; opening explanation and urging guidance—within several years, those who had leaked away and fled came forth of themselves—more than ten thousand persons.

entries.zh: 後入為尚書，代董允為尚書令，眾事無留，門無停賓。
entries.en: Called to court as minister, he succeeded Dong Yun as director of the masters of writing—paperwork never piled up and callers never cooled their heels.
entries.literal: Later he entered court as Minister; replacing Dong Yun he became Director of the Masters of Writing; numerous affairs had no backlog; at his gate there were no stalled guests.

entries.zh: 乂歷職內外，治身儉約，謙靖少言，為政簡而不煩，號為清能；
entries.en: Serving both in the field and at court Lü Yi lived plainly, spoke little, and governed with lean efficiency—men called him honest and able;
entries.literal: Yi served in posts inner and outer; he cultivated himself frugally and restrained; humble and quiet, seldom speaking; in governance concise and not vexing—he was styled pure and capable;

entries.zh: 然持法刻深，好用文俗吏，故居大官，名聲損於郡縣。
entries.en: yet his legalism ran harsh and he favored petty clerks, so high rank actually tarnished the reputation he had earned in the provinces.
entries.literal: yet he held the law harsh and deep; he loved to employ clerical vulgar clerks—therefore although he dwelt in high office, his reputation suffered compared to [his time in] commanderies and counties.

entries.zh: 延熙十四年卒。
entries.en: He died in 251.
entries.literal: He died in the fourteenth year of Yanxi [251].

entries.zh: 子辰，景耀中為成都令。
entries.en: His son Lü Chen became Chengdu magistrate during the Jingyao era.
entries.literal: His son Chen, during Jingyao [258–263], was magistrate of Chengdu.

entries.zh: 辰弟雅，謁者。
entries.en: Lü Chen’s younger brother Lü Ya served as court herald.
entries.literal: Chen's younger brother Ya was a herald.

entries.zh: 雅清厲有文才，著格論十五篇。
entries.en: Lü Ya was austere and literary; he wrote fifteen chapters of “Discourses on Standards.”
entries.literal: Ya was pure and stern and had literary talent; he composed fifteen chapters of Discourses on Standards.

entries.zh: 董和字幼宰，南郡枝江人也，其先本巴郡江州人。
entries.en: Dong He, styled Youzai, came from Zhijiang in Nan Commandery, though his family was originally from Jiangzhou in Ba Commandery.
entries.literal: Dong He, courtesy name Youzai, was a man of Zhijiang in Nan Commandery; his ancestors had originally been people of Jiangzhou in Ba Commandery.

entries.zh: 漢末，和率宗族西遷，益州牧劉璋以為牛鞞、
entries.en: Near the end of the Han, Dong He moved west at the head of his kin, and Yi Province Governor Liu Zhang named him magistrate of Niubi and
entries.literal: At the end of the Han, He led his clan west in migration, and the Governor of Yi Province, Liu Zhang, appointed him [magistrate of] Niubi and

entries.zh: 〈音髀。〉
entries.en: 〈The place name is read bi, homophonous with the word for 'thigh'.〉
entries.literal: 〈Pronounced bi (like 'thigh').〉

entries.zh: 江原長、成都令。
entries.en: later chief of Jiangyuan and magistrate of Chengdu.
entries.literal: [magistrate of] Jiangyuan and prefect of Chengdu.

entries.zh: 蜀土富實，時俗奢侈，貨殖之家，侯服玉食，婚姻葬送，傾家竭產。
entries.en: Shu was prosperous, and the fashion of the time ran to extravagance: merchant houses dressed like nobles and feasted like kings, while weddings and funerals could ruin a household outright.
entries.literal: Shu soil was rich and substantial; the customs of the day were extravagant; households that traded and accumulated wealth wore lordly robes and ate fine food; marriages and burials utterly depleted families and exhausted their property.

entries.zh: 和躬率以儉，惡衣蔬食，防遏逾僭，為之軌制，所在皆移風變善，畏而不犯。
entries.en: Dong He set the example himself—plain dress and simple fare—checked ostentation and overreach, and laid down clear rules. Wherever he served, manners improved; people stepped carefully and stayed within the law.
entries.literal: He personally led by frugality, wearing coarse clothes and eating plain vegetables; he guarded against and stopped excess and usurpation, and for these things made norms and regulations; wherever he was, customs shifted and improved for the better; people feared him and did not transgress.

entries.zh: 然縣界豪強憚和嚴法，說璋轉和為巴東屬國都尉。
entries.en: Local magnates, chafing under his stern rule, pressed Liu Zhang to transfer him out as commandant of the dependent state of Badong.
entries.literal: Yet powerful families within the county borders feared He's strict laws and persuaded Zhang to transfer He to be Commandant of the Dependent State of Badong.

entries.zh: 吏民老弱相攜乞留和者數千人，璋聽留二年，還遷益州太守，其清約如前。
entries.en: Thousands of clerks and townsfolk, young and old together, pleaded that Dong He stay; Liu Zhang let him remain two years more, then promoted him again to Yi Province administrator. His austerity never slackened.
entries.literal: Officials and commoners, old and weak, supporting one another, begged to retain He—several thousand persons; Zhang listened and allowed him to remain two years, then again promoted him to Administrator of Yi Province; his purity and restraint were as before.

entries.zh: 與蠻夷從事，務推誠心，南土愛而信之。
entries.en: In dealing with the southern tribes he dealt in good faith, and the region came to love and trust him.
entries.literal: In conducting affairs with the Man and Yi tribes, he strove to extend sincere heart; the southern lands loved and trusted him.

entries.zh: 初，劉璋遣扶風孟達副法正，各將兵二千人，使迎先主，先主因令達並領其眾，留屯江陵。
entries.en: At first Liu Zhang sent Meng Da of Fufeng to assist Fa Zheng; each brought two thousand men to greet Liu Bei, who then put Meng Da in charge of both contingents and left them holding Jiangling.
entries.literal: At first Liu Zhang sent Fufeng’s Meng Da as deputy to Fa Zheng; each led two thousand troops to welcome the Former Lord; the Former Lord then ordered Da also to command their hosts and left them garrisoned at Jiangling.

entries.zh: 蜀平後，以達為宜都太守。
entries.en: After the conquest he named Meng Da governor of Yidu.
entries.literal: After Shu was pacified, Da was made Governor of Yidu.

entries.zh: 建安二十四年，命達從秭歸北攻房陵，房陵太守蒯祺為達兵所害。
entries.en: In 219 Meng Da was ordered north from Zigui against Fangling; Governor Kuai Qi fell to his attack.
entries.literal: In the twenty-fourth year of Jian’an he ordered Da from Zigui to attack Fangling to the north; Fangling Governor Kuai Qi was killed by Da’s troops.

entries.zh: 達將進攻上庸，先主陰恐達難獨任，乃遣封自漢中乘沔水下統達軍，與達會上庸。
entries.en: Fearing Meng Da could not take Shangyong alone, Liu Bei sent Liu Feng from Hanzhong down the Han River to assume command of his troops and link up at Shangyong.
entries.literal: As Da was about to advance on Shangyong, the Former Lord secretly feared Da could not shoulder the task alone; he therefore sent Feng from Hanzhong down the Mian River to take command of Da’s army and join Da at Shangyong.

entries.zh: 上庸太守申耽舉眾降，遣妻子及宗族詣成都。
entries.en: Shen Dan of Shangyong capitulated with his entire command and sent his family and kin to Chengdu.
entries.literal: Shangyong Governor Shen Dan surrendered with his whole force, sending wife, children, and clan members to Chengdu.

entries.zh: 先主加耽征北將軍，領上庸太守員鄉侯如故，以耽弟儀為建信將軍、西城太守，遷封為副軍將軍。
entries.en: Liu Bei named Shen Dan general who conquers the north and left him marquis of Yuan Village as governor of Shangyong; Shen Yi became general who establishes trust and governor of Xicheng; Liu Feng rose to deputy army commander.
entries.literal: The Former Lord added Dan as General Who Conquers the North, continuing as before as Governor of Shangyong and Marquis of Yuan Village; he made Dan’s younger brother Yi General Who Establishes Trust and Governor of Xicheng, and promoted Feng to General of the Army, Deputy.

entries.zh: 自關羽圍樊城、襄陽，連呼封、達，令發兵自助。
entries.en: While Guan Yu besieged Fancheng and Xiangyang he repeatedly called on Liu Feng and Meng Da to send reinforcements.
entries.literal: From when Guan Yu besieged Fancheng and Xiangyang, he repeatedly summoned Feng and Da, ordering them to raise troops to assist himself.

entries.zh: 封、達辭以山郡初附，未可動搖，不承羽命。
entries.en: They refused, pleading that the hill country had only just submitted and could not be risked, and ignored Guan Yu’s command.
entries.literal: Feng and Da declined on the grounds that the mountain commanderies had newly submitted and could not be disturbed; they did not obey Yu’s order.

entries.zh: 會羽覆敗，先主恨之。
entries.en: When Guan Yu was destroyed, Liu Bei blamed them both.
entries.literal: It happened that Yu was utterly defeated; the Former Lord resented them.

entries.zh: 又封與達忿爭不和，封尋奪達鼓吹。
entries.en: Liu Feng also feuded with Meng Da and soon stripped him of his ceremonial musicians.
entries.literal: Moreover Feng quarrelled with Da and they did not get along; Feng shortly seized Da’s ceremonial band.

entries.zh: 達既懼罪，又忿恚封，遂表辭先主，率所領降魏。
entries.en: Meng Da, fearing execution and furious at Liu Feng, submitted a resignation to Liu Bei and defected to Wei with his troops.
entries.literal: Da both feared punishment and resented Feng; he then memorialized his farewell to the Former Lord and led his command to surrender to Wei.

entries.zh: 〈《魏略》載達辭先主表曰：「伏惟殿下將建伊、呂之業，追桓、文之功，大事草創，假勢吳、楚，是以有為之士深睹歸趣。
entries.en: 〈The Wei Summary preserves Meng Da’s memorial: “Your Highness pursues the legacies of Yi Yin and Lü Wang and the hegemony of Huan and Wen; the enterprise is still young and leans on Wu and Chu—men of ambition know where to turn.
entries.literal: 〈The Wei Summary carries Da’s memorial of farewell to the Former Lord, saying, “I humbly consider that Your Highness will establish the enterprises of Yi Yin and Lü Shang and pursue the achievements of Huan and Wen; the great task is newly begun; borrowing strength from Wu and Chu—therefore men of purpose deeply see where allegiance lies.

entries.zh: 臣委質已來，愆戾山積，臣猶自知，況於君乎！
entries.en: Since I pledged my service, my offenses have stacked high—I know it, and how much more must you!
entries.literal: Since I pledged myself, faults have piled like mountains—I know this myself; how much more my lord!

entries.zh: 今王朝以興，英俊鱗集，臣內無輔佐之器，外無將領之才，列次功臣，誠自愧也。
entries.en: Now the court flourishes and talent crowds in; I have neither administrative gifts nor martial gifts among your servants—I blush to stand even on the roll of honour.
entries.literal: Now the royal court rises; heroes gather like scales; I lack inner capacity to assist and outer talent to command—ranked among meritorious ministers, I am truly ashamed.

entries.zh: 臣聞范蠡識微，浮於五湖；
entries.en: Fan Li read the signs and sailed the Five Lakes;
entries.literal: Your servant has heard that Fan Li sensed the subtlety and floated on the Five Lakes;

entries.zh: 咎犯謝罪，逡巡於河上。
entries.en: Jiu Fan waited his lord’s pardon by the Yellow River.
entries.literal: Jiu Fan apologized for crime and hesitated on the river.

entries.zh: 夫際會之間，請命乞身。
entries.en: At such turning points wise men beg leave to withdraw.
entries.literal: At meetings of circumstance they begged their lives and bodies.

entries.zh: 何則？
entries.en: Why?
entries.literal: Why?

entries.zh: 欲絜去就之分也。
entries.en: They wished to keep honour whole when staying or leaving.
entries.literal: They wished to clarify the boundary between going and staying.

entries.zh: 況臣卑鄙，無元功巨勳，自系於時，竊慕前賢，早思遠恥。
entries.en: I am mean and small, with no great merit to my name; bound by events, I emulate the ancients and flee humiliation early.
entries.literal: Moreover your servant is base and mean, without founding merit or great deed; tied by circumstance, I secretly admire former worthies and long ago ponder distant shame.

entries.zh: 昔申生至孝見疑於親，子胥至忠見誅於君，蒙恬拓境而被大刑，樂毅破齊而遭讒佞，臣每讀其書，未嘗不慷慨流涕，而親當其事，益以傷絕。
entries.en: Shensheng’s filial piety earned suspicion; Wu Zixu’s loyalty brought death; Meng Tian died after conquering new lands; Yue Yi fell to calumny after crushing Qi—I have always wept over such stories; to live them myself is worse still.
entries.literal: Of old Shensheng was supremely filial yet suspected by kin; Wu Zixu supremely loyal yet executed by his lord; Meng Tian expanded the borders yet suffered great punishment; Yue Yi broke Qi yet met slander—each time I read their tales I never fail to weep with passion; now I face the matter myself and am all the more broken-hearted.

entries.zh: 何者？
entries.en: Why?
entries.literal: Why?

entries.zh: 荊州覆敗，大臣失節，百無一還。
entries.en: Jing fell; not one defector in a hundred kept his honour.
entries.literal: Jing Province was overturned and defeated; great ministers lost their integrity—of a hundred not one returned.

entries.zh: 惟臣尋事，自致房陵、上庸，而復乞身，自放於外。
entries.en: I alone carved out Fangling and Shangyong, then asked to step aside and live at the margin.
entries.literal: Only your servant pursued affairs and brought himself to Fangling and Shangyong, then again begged his person and released himself abroad.

entries.zh: 伏想殿下聖恩感悟，愍臣之心，悼臣之舉。
entries.en: I trust Your Highness’s kindness will pity my heart and regret my choice.
entries.literal: I humbly imagine Your Highness’s sacred grace will awaken to pity your servant’s heart and mourn your servant’s act.

entries.zh: 臣誠小人，不能始終，知而為之，敢謂非罪！
entries.en: I am a small man who could not see things through; I knew the risk and took it—how can I claim innocence!
entries.literal: Your servant is truly a petty man, unable to finish what he began—knowing yet doing it, how dare I call it no crime!

entries.zh: 臣每間交絕無惡聲，去臣無怨辭，臣過奉教於君子，原君王勉之也。」〉
entries.en: Partings need no bitter words, banishment no grudge—I have heard gentlemen teach thus; I pray you take it to heart.”〉”
entries.literal: Whenever ties break, let there be no angry words; when I depart, let there be no resentful speech—I have received instruction from gentlemen; I beg my lord to understand.”〉"

entries.zh: 魏文帝善達之姿才容觀，以為散騎常侍、建武將軍，封平陽亭侯。
entries.en: Cao Pi admired Meng Da’s presence and ability, named him palace attendant and general who establishes martial might, and made him village marquis of Pingyang.
entries.literal: Wei Wendi approved Da’s bearing, talent, and appearance; he made him Regular Attendant of the Scattered Cavalry, General Who Establishes Martial Might, and enfeoffed him Marquis of Pingyang village.

entries.zh: 合房陵、上庸、西城三郡為新城郡，以達領新城太守。
entries.en: He merged Fangling, Shangyong, and Xicheng into New City commandery and put Meng Da in charge.
entries.literal: He merged the three commanderies of Fangling, Shangyong, and Xicheng into New City commandery and made Da concurrent Governor of New City.

entries.zh: 遣征南將軍夏侯尚、右將軍徐晃與達共襲封。
entries.en: He dispatched Xiahou Shang and Xu Huang with Meng Da against Liu Feng.
entries.literal: He sent General Who Conquers the South Xiahou Shang and General of the Right Xu Huang together with Da to strike Feng.

entries.zh: 達與封書曰：
entries.en: Meng Da wrote to Liu Feng:
entries.literal: Da wrote a letter to Feng, saying:

entries.zh: 古人有言：『疏不間親，新不加舊。』
entries.en: The ancients said: “Outsiders cannot divide kin; newcomers cannot supplant old retainers.”
entries.literal: The ancients said: “The distant do not come between the close; the new does not rank above the old.”

entries.zh: 此謂上明下直，讒慝不行也。
entries.en: That holds when the sovereign is clear-sighted and ministers straightforward—slander then finds no foothold.
entries.literal: This means when the ruler is enlightened and subordinates upright, slander and evil cannot operate.

entries.zh: 若乃權君譎主，賢父慈親，猶有忠臣蹈功以罹禍，孝子抱仁以陷難，種、商、白起、孝己、伯奇，皆其類也。
entries.en: Even under capricious fathers and sage parents, loyal servants still died for their deeds and filial sons for their love—Wen Zhong, Lord Shang, Bai Qi, Xiao Ji, and Boyi all belong to that tale.
entries.literal: Yet twisted rulers and deceitful lords, worthy fathers and loving parents, still had loyal ministers who followed merit and met disaster, filial sons who embraced benevolence and fell into hardship—Wen Zhong, Bai Qi, filial Ji, Boyi—their kind.

entries.zh: 其所以然，非骨肉好離，親親樂患也。
entries.en: It is not that kin love estrangement or welcome ruin.
entries.literal: The reason is not that flesh and blood love separation or that kinfolk delight in calamity.

entries.zh: 或有恩移愛易，亦有讒間其間，雖忠臣不能移之於君，孝子不能變之於父者也。
entries.en: Favour shifts, love turns, and whisperers slip between—even loyal ministers cannot sway every ruler, nor filial sons every father.
entries.literal: Sometimes favour shifts and love changes; sometimes slander drives in between—though a loyal minister cannot move his lord, a filial son cannot alter his father.

entries.zh: 勢利所加，改親為讎，況非親親乎！
entries.en: Interest turns kin into enemies—what of mere adoption?
entries.literal: When power and profit bear down, kin become foes—how much more when there is no blood tie!

entries.zh: 故申生、衛伋、禦寇、楚建禀受形之氣，當嗣立之正，而猶如此。
entries.en: Shensheng, Ji of Wei, Yu Kou, and Jian of Chu were lawful heirs—yet each met doom.
entries.literal: Therefore Shensheng, Wei Ji, Yu Kou, and Chu Jian received their bodily qi with rightful claim to succession, yet still came to this.

entries.zh: 今足下與漢中王，道路之人耳，親非骨血而據勢權，義非君臣而處上位，徵則有偏任之威，居則有副軍之號，遠近所聞也。
entries.en: You and the King of Hanzhong are strangers by blood yet you wield real power; you are no true minister yet stand high; in the field you hold disproportionate authority, at court the title of deputy commander—the whole realm knows it.
entries.literal: Now you and the King of Hanzhong are but fellow travellers on the road—not bone and blood yet holding power and rank; not lord and minister by duty yet occupying high station; when campaigning you wield favoritism’s weight, at rest you bear the deputy army’s title—far and near have heard it.

entries.zh: 自立阿斗為太子已來，有識之人相為寒心。
entries.en: Since Liu Shan was named heir, thinking men have trembled.
entries.literal: From the day Adou was established heir, every thoughtful man has shivered.

entries.zh: 如使申生從子輿之言，必為太伯；
entries.en: Had Shensheng heeded his tutor he might have become another Taibo;
entries.literal: Had Shensheng followed Ziyu’s words, he would surely have become Taibo;

entries.zh: 衛伋聽其弟之謀，無彰父之譏也。
entries.en: had Ji of Wei trusted his brother’s counsel, his father would not have been shamed.
entries.literal: had Wei Ji listened to his younger brother’s plan, there would have been no reproach that shamed the father.

entries.zh: 且小白出奔，入而為霸；
entries.en: Duke Huan fled Qi yet returned to lead the alliance;
entries.literal: Moreover Little Bai fled out and entered to become hegemon;

entries.zh: 重耳踰垣，卒以克復。
entries.en: Chong’er scaled the wall and won his state back.
entries.literal: Chong’er climbed the wall and in the end recovered all.

entries.zh: 自古有之，非獨今也。
entries.en: Such turns are old news, not news from our age alone.
entries.literal: Since antiquity it has been thus—not only today.

entries.zh: 夫智貴免禍，明尚夙達，僕揆漢中王慮定於內，疑生於外矣；
entries.en: The wise flee disaster and foresee trouble early—I believe the King of Hanzhong has made his decision within while doubt gathers without;
entries.literal: Wisdom prizes escaping calamity; insight esteems foresight early—I gauge that the King of Hanzhong has settled his mind within and suspicion arises without;

entries.zh: 慮定則心固，疑生則心懼，亂禍之興作，未曾不由廢立之間也。
entries.en: resolve breeds confidence, suspicion breeds fear—every throne struggle proves it.
entries.literal: when the mind is settled the heart is firm; when suspicion arises the heart fears—turmoil and disaster never fail to spring from the interval of deposing and establishing.

entries.zh: 私怨人情，不能不見，恐左右必有以間於漢中王矣。
entries.en: Men nurse private grudges—I fear someone whispers against you in Chengdu.
entries.literal: Private resentment is human feeling—it cannot help but show; I fear those about him surely speak against you to the King of Hanzhong.

entries.zh: 然則疑成怨聞，其發若踐機耳。
entries.en: Once suspicion hardens, the trap springs like a sprung crossbow.
entries.literal: Then suspicion forms and resentment is heard—its release is like treading a trigger.

entries.zh: 今足下在遠，尚可假息一時；
entries.en: Distance still buys you a little time;
entries.literal: Now you are far away—you may still catch your breath for a while;

entries.zh: 若大軍遂進，足下失據而還，竊相為危之。
entries.en: when our hosts close in and you retreat stripped of position, I tremble for you.
entries.literal: but if the great army advances and you lose footing and return, I privately think danger for you.

entries.zh: 昔微子去殷，智果別族，違難背禍，猶皆如斯。
entries.en: Weizi fled Yin; Zhiguo split his lineage—wise men dodge ruin this way.
entries.literal: Of old Weizi left Yin; Zhiguo split his clan—fleeing hardship and turning from disaster, all were thus.

entries.zh: 〈國語曰：智宣子將以瑤為後，智果曰：「不如霄也。」
entries.en: 〈The Discourses of the States tells how Lord Xuan of Zhi meant to choose Yao until Zhiguo urged Xia instead.”
entries.literal: 〈The Discourses of the States says: Lord Xuan of Zhi was about to make Yao his heir; Zhiguo said, “Better Xia.”

entries.zh: 宣子曰：「霄也佷。」
entries.en: “Xia is brutal,” said Lord Xuan.
entries.literal: Lord Xuan said, “Xia is brutal.”

entries.zh: 對曰：「霄也佷在面，瑤之賢於人者五，其不逮者一也。
entries.en: Zhiguo answered: “Xia’s cruelty shows on his skin; Yao excels in five talents yet lacks humaneness.
entries.literal: He replied, “Xia’s brutality shows on his face; Yao surpasses men in five ways—what he lacks is one.

entries.zh: 美須長大則賢，射禦足力則賢，技藝畢給則賢，巧文辯惠則賢，強毅果敢則賢，如是而甚不仁；
entries.en: Long beard and tall frame, shooting and riding, every craft, fluent speech, iron nerve—all marks of talent—yet wholly ruthless;
entries.literal: Fine beard and tall stature counts as worthy; archery and charioteering and foot strength counts as worthy; skills fully supplied counts as worthy; clever writing and eloquent wit counts as worthy; strength and resolve and daring counts as worthy—thus yet deeply inhumane;

entries.zh: 以五者賢陵人，而不仁行之，其誰能待之！
entries.en: five virtues deployed without mercy will destroy everyone around him!
entries.literal: with five kinds of excellence he overrides others and acts without benevolence—who can endure him!

entries.zh: 若果立瑤也。
entries.en: If you raise Yao,
entries.literal: If indeed Yao is established.

entries.zh: 智宗必滅。」
entries.en: the house of Zhi will fall.”
entries.literal: The Zhi lineage will surely perish.”

entries.zh: 不聽。
entries.en: Lord Xuan refused to listen.
entries.literal: He did not listen.

entries.zh: 智果別族於太史氏為輔氏。
entries.en: Zhiguo registered his line separately as the Fu clan.
entries.literal: Zhiguo split his clan from the Grand Scribe’s house and became the Fu clan.

entries.zh: 及智氏亡，惟輔果在焉。〉
entries.en: When Zhi fell, only Fuguo remained.〉
entries.literal: When the Zhi clan perished, only Fuguo survived.〉

entries.zh: 今足下棄父母而為人後，非禮也；
entries.en: You turned your back on your birth parents to be adopted—against propriety;
entries.literal: Now you abandon parents to become another’s heir—it is not ritual;

entries.zh: 知禍將至而留之，非智也；
entries.en: to see disaster coming yet linger—not wisdom;
entries.literal: knowing disaster will come yet staying—not wisdom;

entries.zh: 見正不從而疑之，非義也。
entries.en: to hear sound counsel and doubt it—not honour.
entries.literal: seeing the right and not following yet doubting—not righteousness.

entries.zh: 自號為丈夫，為此三者，何所貴乎？
entries.en: You style yourself a hero yet break three cardinal virtues—what remains to respect?
entries.literal: Calling yourself a man while doing these three—what is there to honour?

entries.zh: 以足下之才，棄身來東，繼嗣羅侯，不為背親也；
entries.en: Come east with your gifts and resume the Luo marquisate—you would not betray your blood;
entries.literal: With your talent, leave yourself and come east, inherit Marquis Luo—it is not betraying kin;

entries.zh: 北面事君，以正綱紀，不為棄舊也；
entries.en: serve the Son of Heaven and restore order—you would not cast off the past;
entries.literal: face north and serve a lord, rectifying the norms—not abandoning the old;

entries.zh: 怒不致亂，以免危亡，不為徒行也。
entries.en: withdraw without sparking revolt and save your skin—that is no idle gesture.
entries.literal: anger not reaching chaos, thereby escaping peril—not empty motion.

entries.zh: 加陛下新受禪命，虛心側席，以德懷遠，若足下翻然內向，非但與僕為倫，受三百戶封，繼統羅國而已，當更剖符大邦，為始封之君。
entries.en: Our new emperor hungers for loyal talent: return and you will rank beside me, keep your three-hundred-household fief and the Luo succession, and likely gain a great province with bronze tallies.
entries.literal: Moreover Your Majesty has newly received the abdication mandate, empties his heart and leaves the mat aside, embracing the distant with virtue—if you turn about toward the inner court, you will not only match your servant, receive a three-hundred-household fief, and continue the Luo state—you will further split tallies in a great region and be its first enfeoffed lord.

entries.zh: 陛下大軍，金鼓以震，當轉都宛、鄧；
entries.en: The imperial host will soon roll toward Wan and Deng;
entries.literal: Your Majesty’s great army, drums and gongs shaking, will shift the capital toward Wan and Deng;

entries.zh: 若二敵不平，軍無還期。
entries.en: until Shu and Wu yield, there will be no going home.
entries.literal: if the two foes are not pacified, the army has no date of return.

entries.zh: 足下宜因此時早定良計。
entries.en: Choose your course before it is chosen for you.
entries.literal: You ought at this time early settle a good plan.

entries.zh: 易有『利見大人』，詩有『自求多福』，行矣。
entries.en: The Zhou yi promises blessing for those who approach greatness; the Odes urge men to win their own fortune—act.
entries.literal: The Changes has ‘It furthers one to see the great man’; the Odes has ‘Seek much blessing for yourself’—go.

entries.zh: 今足下勉之，無使狐突閉門不出。
entries.en: Move now—do not die like Hutu, who never ventured forth again.
entries.literal: Now strive, sir—do not make Hutu shut his gate and never come out.

entries.zh: 九年春，亮軍祁山，平催督運事。
entries.en: In the spring of 231 Zhuge Liang was at Qishan; Li Ping oversaw supply runs.
entries.literal: In the spring of the ninth year, Liang’s army was at Qishan; Ping urged and supervised transport affairs.

entries.zh: 秋夏之際，值天霖雨，運糧不繼，平遣參軍狐忠、督軍成籓喻指，呼亮來還；
entries.en: Autumn rains cut the supply line; Li Ping sent Hu Zhong and Cheng Fan with orders for Zhuge Liang to pull back;
entries.literal: Between autumn and summer it happened that Heaven sent continuous rain; grain transport did not continue; Ping sent staff adviser Hu Zhong and supervisor Cheng Fan with instructions, summoning Liang to return;

entries.zh: 亮承以退軍。
entries.en: Zhuge Liang obeyed and withdrew.
entries.literal: Liang accepted and withdrew the army.

entries.zh: 平聞軍退，乃更陽驚，說「軍糧饒足，何以便歸」！
entries.en: Then Li Ping feigned shock: “We have plenty of grain—why retreat?”
entries.literal: When Ping heard the army had withdrawn, then feigned surprise, saying “Army grain is abundant—why return so soon!”

entries.zh: 欲以解己不辦之責，顯亮不進之愆也。
entries.en: He meant to blame Zhuge Liang for timidity and cover his own logistics failure.
entries.literal: He wished thereby to excuse his own failure to deliver and display Liang’s fault for not advancing.

entries.zh: 又表後主，說「軍偽退，欲以誘賊與戰」。
entries.en: He also memorialized the Later Lord, saying “The army feigned retreat, wishing thereby to lure the bandits to battle.”
entries.literal: He also memorialized the Later Lord, saying “The army feigned retreat, wishing thereby to lure the bandits to battle.”

entries.zh: 亮具出其前後手筆書疏本末，平違錯章灼。
entries.en: Zhuge Liang produced their correspondence; Li Ping’s lies stood exposed.
entries.literal: Liang produced in full his earlier and later handwritten letters and memorials’ beginning and end—Ping’s violation and error were manifestly clear.

entries.zh: 平辭窮情竭，首謝罪負。
entries.en: Cornered, Li Ping confessed.
entries.literal: Ping’s words were exhausted and feeling spent; he bowed and confessed guilt.

entries.zh: 於是亮表平曰：「自先帝崩後，平所在治家，尚為小惠，安身求名，無憂國之事。
entries.en: Zhuge Liang wrote: “Since the late emperor died Li Ping has tended his private affairs, traded petty favours for reputation, and ignored the state.
entries.literal: Thereupon Liang memorialized Ping, saying: “Since the Former Lord’s passing, wherever Ping has been he has managed his household, still doing petty kindnesses, securing himself and seeking fame—there are no affairs of worrying for the state.

entries.zh: 臣當北出，欲得平兵以鎮漢中，平窮難縱橫，無有來意，而求以五郡為巴州刺史。
entries.en: When I marched north I asked him to hold Hanzhong; he stalled and demanded to be inspector over five commanderies as Ba province.
entries.literal: When your servant should go north, I wished to obtain Ping’s troops to garrison Hanzhong; Ping raised difficulties in every direction and had no intent to come, yet sought to make five commanderies into Inspector of Ba Province.

entries.zh: 去年臣欲西征，欲令平主督漢中，平說司馬懿等開府闢召。
entries.en: Last year I meant to leave him Hanzhong; he answered that Sima Yi was recruiting worthies.
entries.literal: Last year your servant wished to campaign west and wished to order Ping to take charge of Hanzhong; Ping spoke of Sima Yi and others opening offices and summoning recruits.

entries.zh: 臣知平鄙情，欲因行之際偪臣取利也，是以表平子豐督主江州，隆崇其遇，以取一時之務。
entries.en: I knew he meant to profit from my absence, so I honoured his son Li Feng in Jiangzhou to keep him quiet.
entries.literal: Your servant knew Ping’s base intent—wishing on the march’s occasion to coerce your servant for profit; therefore your servant memorialized Ping’s son Feng to supervise Jiangzhou, greatly honouring his treatment, to settle the moment’s tasks.

entries.zh: 平至之日，都委諸事，群臣上下皆怪臣待平之厚也。
entries.en: When he arrived I gave him full trust—the court marvelled at my generosity.
entries.literal: When Ping arrived, all affairs were entrusted to him; host of ministers above and below all marvelled at how thickly your servant treated Ping.

entries.zh: 正以大事未定，漢室傾危，伐平之短，莫若褒之。
entries.en: The realm still hung in the balance—praise worked better than blame.
entries.literal: Just because the great task was not settled and the Han house leaned toward peril—to attack Ping’s shortcomings was not as good as praising him.

entries.zh: 然謂平情在於榮利而已，不意平心顛倒乃爾。
entries.en: I thought he only cranked rank and wealth—I never dreamed he would sink this low.
entries.literal: Yet your servant thought Ping’s intent lay only in glory and profit—did not expect Ping’s heart to be upside-down thus.

entries.zh: 若事稽留，將致禍敗，是臣不敏，言多增咎。」
entries.en: If delay ruins the campaign, the fault is mine for trusting him too long.”
entries.literal: If affairs drag and delay, will bring calamity and defeat—this is your servant’s dullness; words add more fault.”

entries.zh: 〈亮公文上尚書曰：「平為大臣，受恩過量，不思忠報，橫造無端，危恥不辦，迷罔上下，論獄棄科，導人為奸，
entries.en: 〈Zhuge Liang’s official document to the Ministry says: “As a great minister, Li Ping received favor beyond measure, yet he gave no thought to repaying it with loyalty. He recklessly invented groundless claims, failed to deal with danger and disgrace, deceived superiors and subordinates alike, discarded legal standards in judging cases, and led others into wrongdoing,
entries.literal: 〈Liang’s official document to the Ministry says: “Ping as great minister received favour beyond measure; did not think to repay with loyalty; recklessly created without cause; peril and shame unmet; deluded above and below; argued lawsuits abandoning statute; led men to wickedness,

entries.zh: （狹情）
entries.en: 〈variant: narrow sentiment〉
entries.literal: (narrow feeling)

entries.zh: 情狹志狂，若無天地。
entries.en: petty, arrogant, as though heaven and earth did not exist.
entries.literal: narrow of temper ambition mad, as if without Heaven and Earth.

entries.zh: 自度姦露，嫌心遂生，聞軍臨至，西鄉託疾還沮、漳，軍臨至沮，復還江陽，平參軍狐忠勤諫乃止。
entries.en: Sensing exposure he fled west toward Ju and Zhang, doubled back to Jiangyang, until his aide Hu Zhong stopped him.
entries.literal: Estimating himself exposed in treachery, suspicious heart then arose; hearing the army drew near, westward feigned illness returning to Ju and Zhang; when army drew near Ju, returned again to Jiangyang—Ping’s staff adviser Hu Zhong earnestly remonstrated and only then stopped.

entries.zh: 今篡賊未滅，社稷多難，國事惟和，可以克捷，不可苞含，以危大業。
entries.en: Wei still stands; national crisis demands unity—we cannot shelter traitors and risk the realm.
entries.literal: Now the usurping bandit is not yet destroyed; altars and grain face many hardships—state affairs rely on harmony to achieve victory; cannot wrap and contain to endanger the great enterprise.

entries.zh: 輒與行中軍師車騎將軍都鄉侯臣劉琰，使持節前軍師征西大將軍領涼州刺史南鄭侯臣魏延、前將軍都亭侯臣袁綝、左將軍領荊州刺史高陽鄉侯臣吳壹、督前部右將軍玄鄉侯臣高翔、督後部後將軍安樂亭侯臣吳班、領長史綏軍將軍臣楊儀、督左部行中監軍揚武將軍臣鄧芝、行前監軍征南將軍臣劉巴、行中護軍偏將軍臣費禕、行前護軍偏將軍漢成亭侯臣許允、行左護軍篤信中郎將臣丁咸、行右護軍偏將軍臣劉敏、行護軍征南將軍當陽亭侯臣姜維、行中典軍討虜將軍臣上官雝、行中參軍昭武中郎將臣胡濟、行參軍建義將軍臣閻晏、行參軍偏將軍臣爨習、行參軍裨將軍臣杜義、行參軍武略中郎將臣杜祺、行參軍綏戎都尉盛勃、領從事中郎武略中郎將臣樊岐等議，輒解平任，免官祿、節傳、印綬、符策，削其爵土。」〉
entries.en: I therefore deliberated with Liu Yan, acting Central Army Adviser, General of Chariots and Cavalry, and Marquis of Duxiang; Wei Yan, bearer of the tally, Former Army Adviser, Grand General Who Conquers the West, acting Inspector of Liang Province, and Marquis of Nanzheng; Yuan Lin, Former General and Marquis of Duting; Wu Yi, General of the Left, acting Inspector of Jing Province, and Marquis of Gaoyangxiang; Gao Xiang, commander of the front division, General of the Right, and Marquis of Xuanxiang; Wu Ban, commander of the rear division, General of the Rear, and Marquis of Anleting; Yang Yi, chief clerk and General Who Pacifies the Army; Deng Zhi, commander of the left division, acting Central Army Supervisor, and General Who Displays Might; Liu Ba, acting front supervisor and General Who Conquers the South; Fei Yi, acting Central Protector of the Army and lieutenant general; Xu Yun, acting Front Protector of the Army, lieutenant general, and Marquis of Hanchengting; Ding Xian, acting Left Protector of the Army and Gentleman General of Earnest Trust; Liu Min, acting Right Protector of the Army and lieutenant general; Jiang Wei, acting Protector of the Army, General Who Conquers the South, and Marquis of Dangyangting; Shangguan Yong, acting Central Army Director and General Who Punishes Caitiffs; Hu Ji, acting Central Staff Adviser and Gentleman General of Brilliant Might; Yan Yan, acting Staff Adviser and General Who Establishes Righteousness; Cuan Xi, acting Staff Adviser and lieutenant general; Du Yi, acting Staff Adviser and assistant general; Du Qi, acting Staff Adviser and Gentleman General of Martial Strategy; Sheng Bo, acting Staff Adviser and Commandant Who Pacifies the Rong; Fan Qi, acting Attendant Clerk and Gentleman General of Martial Strategy; and the others. We have removed Li Ping from his post, stripped him of office, salary, tally, travel credential, seals, ribbons, patents, and warrants, and cut away his noble lands.”〉
entries.literal: Thereupon together with Acting Army Adviser General of Chariots and Cavalry Marquis of Dou Village Liu Yan, Bearer of Insignia Former Army Adviser Grand General Who Conquers the West Concurrent Inspector of Liang Province Marquis of Nan Zheng Wei Yan, Former General Marquis of Du Village Yuan Yi, Left General Concurrent Inspector of Jing Province Marquis of Gaoyang Village Wu Yi, Supervisor of Front Section General of the Right Marquis of Xuan Village Gao Xiang, Supervisor of Rear Section General of the Rear Marquis of Anle Village Wu Ban, Chief Clerk General Who Pacifies the Army Yang Yi, Supervisor of Left Section Acting Central Army Supervisor General Who Displays Might Deng Zhi, Acting Former Supervisor General Who Conquers the South Liu Ba, Acting Central Protector of the Army Lieutenant General Fei Yi, Acting Former Protector of the Army Lieutenant General Marquis of Hancheng Village Xu Yun, Acting Left Protector of the Army Faithful General of the Household Ding Xian, Acting Right Protector of the Army Lieutenant General Liu Min, Acting Protector of the Army General Who Conquers the South Marquis of Dangyang Village Jiang Wei, Acting Central Army Director General Who Punishes Barbarians Shangguan Yong, Acting Central Staff Adviser General of Brilliant Might Hu Ji, Acting Staff Adviser General Who Establishes Righteousness Yan Yan, Acting Staff Adviser Lieutenant General Cuan Xi, Acting Staff Adviser General of the Household Du Yi, Acting Staff Adviser General of Martial Stratagem Du Qi, Acting Staff Adviser Pacification Commandant of the Rong Sheng Bo, Concurrent Attendant Clerk General of Martial Stratagem Fan Qi, and others deliberated—thereupon removed Ping from office, stripped official salary, insignia courier, seals and ribbons, tallies and patents, and cut his noble lands.”〉

entries.zh: 乃廢平為民，徙梓潼郡。
entries.en: Li Ping was reduced to commoner status and exiled to Zitong.
entries.literal: Thereupon Ping was reduced to commoner and moved to Zitong Commandery.

entries.zh: 〈諸葛亮又與平子豐教曰：「吾與君父子戮力以獎漢室，此神明所聞，非但人知之也。
entries.en: 〈Zhuge Liang wrote Li Feng: “Your father and I laboured for Han—Heaven knows it.
entries.literal: 〈Zhuge Liang again instructed Ping’s son Feng, saying: “I with you, father and son, joined strength to aid the Han house—this the spirits have heard, not only men know it.

entries.zh: 表都護典漢中，委君於東關者，不與人議也。
entries.en: I meant to give him Hanzhong and you the eastern gate without debate.
entries.literal: Memorializing the Director of Retainers to govern Hanzhong, entrusting you at the eastern pass—not consulted with others.

entries.zh: 謂至心感動，終始可保，何圖中乖乎！
entries.en: I trusted hearts would stay true—who foresaw this breach?
entries.literal: I thought utmost hearts would move each other—beginning and end could be kept—who plotted mid-course betrayal!

entries.zh: 昔楚卿屢絀，亦乃克復，思道則福，應自然之數也。
entries.en: Great ministers fall and rise again—virtue brings restoration.
entries.literal: Formerly Chu ministers were repeatedly dismissed—yet could recover; pondering the Way brings blessing—it answers nature’s reckoning.

entries.zh: 原寬慰都護，勤追前闕。
entries.en: Comfort your father and help him atone.
entries.literal: I beg you comfort the Director of Retainers and diligently pursue remedying former faults.

entries.zh: 今雖解任，形業失故，奴婢賓客百數十人，君以中郎參軍居府，方之氣類，猶為上家。
entries.en: Though dismissed he keeps scores of servants; you remain an attendant at headquarters—still a great house.
entries.literal: Now although office is removed, form and estate lose their old state—yet slaves, maids, and guests number over a hundred; you as Gentleman of the Household staff adviser dwell at headquarters—compared to peers of your kind, still count as upper households.

entries.zh: 若都護思負一意，君與公琰推心從事者，否可複通，逝可複還也。
entries.en: If he owns his fault and you and Jiang Wan work in good faith, doors can reopen.
entries.literal: If the Director of Retainers ponders fault with single mind, you and Gongyan push hearts and serve affairs—blocked can again open; departed can again return.

entries.zh: 詳思斯戒，明吾用心，臨書長嘆，涕泣而已。」〉
entries.en: Read this and know my heart—I sign in tears.”〉"
entries.literal: Think carefully on this warning; clarify my intent—facing the letter I sigh long; tears only.”〉"

entries.zh: 劉封者，本羅侯寇氏之子，長沙劉氏之甥也。
entries.en: Liu Feng was born to the Kou house of Marquis Luo and was the nephew of the Liu clan of Changsha.
entries.literal: Liu Feng was originally the son of Marquis Luo of the Kou clan and the nephew of the Liu family of Changsha.

entries.zh: 先主至荊州，以未有繼嗣，養封為子。
entries.en: When Liu Bei reached Jing Province he still had no heir, so he adopted Liu Feng as his son.
entries.literal: When the Former Lord arrived in Jing Province, because he had yet no heir, he adopted Feng as a son.

entries.zh: 及先主入蜀，自葭萌還攻劉璋，時封年二十馀，有武藝，氣力過人，將兵俱與諸葛亮、張飛等溯流西上，所在戰克。
entries.en: When Liu Bei marched into Shu from Jiameng against Liu Zhang, Liu Feng was already in his twenties—strong, skilled in arms, and bold enough to lead men beside Zhuge Liang and Zhang Fei upriver into the west, victorious at every turn.
entries.literal: When the Former Lord entered Shu and turned back from Jiameng to attack Liu Zhang, at that time Feng was over twenty, had martial skill, and strength surpassing others; he led troops together with Zhuge Liang, Zhang Fei, and others up the river westward, winning victory wherever they fought.

entries.zh: 益州既定，以封為副軍中郎將。
entries.en: Once Yi Province was secured, Liu Feng became a general of the household serving as deputy to the army.
entries.literal: After Yi Province was settled, Feng was appointed General of the Household, Deputy to the Army.

entries.zh: 《襄阳记》曰：罗宪字令则。
entries.en: The Xiangyang ji gives Luo Xian’s style as Lingze.
entries.literal: The Xiangyang ji states: Luo Xian, courtesy name Lingze.

entries.zh: 父蒙，避乱於蜀，官至广汉太守。
entries.en: His father Luo Meng had fled the turmoil into Shu and rose to governor of Guanghan.
entries.literal: His father Meng, fleeing disorder, went to Shu, and his office reached Administrator of Guanghan.

entries.zh: 宪少以才学知名，年十三能属文。
entries.en: Even as a boy he was known for literary talent and could write polished essays at thirteen.
entries.literal: Xian in youth was known for talent and learning; at thirteen sui he could compose texts.

entries.zh: 后主立太子，为太子舍人，迁庶子、尚书吏部郎，以宣信校尉再使於吴，吴人称美焉。
entries.en: After the crown prince was named, he served as gentleman attendant, then as palace attendant and personnel director at the secretariat, and twice went to Wu as envoy with the rank of colonel who spreads trust, winning praise in the eastern court.
entries.literal: When the Later Sovereign established the heir apparent, he became gentleman attendant at the heir's palace, was promoted attendant and gentleman of the Ministry of Personnel of the Masters of Writing, and as Colonel Who Spreads Trust twice was sent on mission to Wu; the men of Wu praised him.

entries.zh: 时黄皓预政，众多附之，宪独不与同，皓恚，左迁巴东太守。
entries.en: When the eunuch Huang Hao dominated politics, most officials curried favor, but Luo Xian held aloof; Huang Hao exiled him to the governorship of Badong.
entries.literal: At the time Huang Hao intervened in government, the multitude attached to him; Xian alone did not join with him; Hao was resentful and demoted him to Administrator of Badong.

entries.zh: 时右大将军阎宇都督巴东，为领军，后主拜宪为宇副贰。
entries.en: General Yan Yu of the right commanded east of Ba while also leading the central army; the emperor named Luo Xian his second-in-command there.
entries.literal: At the time the General of the Right Yan Yu supervised Badong as commander-in-chief and was commander of the army; the Later Sovereign appointed Xian as Yu's deputy.

entries.zh: 魏之伐蜀，召宇西还，留宇二千人，令宪守永安城。
entries.en: When Wei invaded Shu, Yan Yu was recalled westward, leaving two thousand men under Luo Xian to hold Yong’an.
entries.literal: When Wei attacked Shu, Yu was summoned to return west, two thousand of Yu's men were left, and Xian was ordered to defend Yong'an city.

entries.zh: 寻闻成都败，城中扰动，江边长吏皆弃城走，宪斩称成都乱者一人，百姓乃定。
entries.en: News of Chengdu’s fall threw the town into panic; riverfront magistrates bolted, but Luo Xian executed a man who spread false rumors of riot, and the people calmed down.
entries.literal: Soon hearing of Chengdu's defeat, there was disturbance in the city; the senior officials along the river all abandoned the cities and fled; Xian beheaded one who claimed Chengdu was in chaos, and the hundred surnames then settled.

entries.zh: 得后主委质问至，乃帅所统临于都亭三日。
entries.en: When the emperor’s formal surrender order reached him, he led his troops to the metropolitan pavilion and kept mourning rites for three days.
entries.literal: Having received the Later Sovereign's order to submit credentials, he thereupon led those he commanded to attend at the metropolitan pavilion three days.

entries.zh: 吴闻蜀败，起兵西上，外讬救援，内欲袭宪。
entries.en: Wu, learning of Shu’s collapse, marched west on the pretext of rescue while intending to seize Luo Xian’s position.
entries.literal: Wu heard Shu was defeated, raised troops westward, outwardly pretending relief, inwardly wishing to strike Xian.

entries.zh: 宪曰：“本朝倾覆，吴为脣齿，不恤我难而徼其利，背盟违约。
entries.en: Luo Xian said, "My dynasty had fallen and Wu, supposedly a close ally, was profiting from Shu’s ruin instead of helping—breaking faith and the treaty.
entries.literal: Xian said, "This court has overturned; Wu is lip and teeth; it does not pity our difficulty but seeks its profit, betraying the alliance and violating the covenant.

entries.zh: 且汉已亡，吴何得久，宁能为吴降虏乎！”
entries.en: Han was gone, he argued, and Wu could not last; he would never surrender to become Wu’s prisoner."
entries.literal: Moreover Han is already gone; how can Wu long endure—how could I become a surrendered captive for Wu!

entries.zh: 保城缮甲，告誓将士，厉以节义，莫不用命。
entries.en: He strengthened the walls and arms, rallied his officers on their honor, and every man obeyed.
entries.literal: He protected the city, repaired armor, announced oath to generals and soldiers, exhorted them with integrity and righteousness; none did not obey orders.

entries.zh: 吴闻锺、邓败，百城无主，有兼蜀之志，而巴东固守，兵不得过，使步协率众而西。
entries.en: After Zhong Hui and Deng Ai fell, Wu saw a chance to swallow Shu, but Luo Xian’s grip on Badong blocked the route, so Wu sent Bu Xie west with an army.
entries.literal: Wu heard Zhong and Deng were defeated, a hundred cities had no master, and had the intention to annex Shu, but Badong firmly held and troops could not pass, so they sent Bu Xie to lead the host westward.

entries.zh: 宪临江拒射，不能御，遣参军杨宗突围北出，告急安东将军陈骞，又送文武印绶、任子诣晋王。
entries.en: Luo Xian’s bowmen along the river could not hold the line; he sent Yang Zong through the encirclement to Chen Qian and forwarded seals and hostages to the king of Jin.
entries.literal: Xian along the river resisted with archery, could not withstand it, sent aide-de-camp Yang Zong to break the encirclement northward, report emergency to General Who Pacifies the East Chen Qian, and also sent civil and military seals and cords and hostage sons to the King of Jin.

entries.zh: 协攻城，宪出与战，大破其军。
entries.en: When Bu Xie assaulted the walls, Luo Xian sallied out and shattered his force.
entries.literal: Xie attacked the city; Xian went out and fought with him, greatly smashing his army.

entries.zh: 孙休怒，复遣陆抗等帅众三万人增宪之围。
entries.en: Sun Xiu, furious, sent Lu Kang with thirty thousand more men to tighten the siege.
entries.literal: Sun Xiu was angry and again sent Lu Kang and others to lead thirty thousand men to increase the siege of Xian.

entries.zh: 被攻凡六月日而救援不到，城中疾病大半。
entries.en: The siege ran half a year without relief, and disease laid low most of the garrison.
entries.literal: Being attacked in all six months and relief not arriving, in the city sickness was more than half.

entries.zh: 或说宪奔走之计，宪曰：“夫为人主，百姓所仰，危不能安，急而弃之，君子不为也，毕命於此矣。”
entries.en: When someone urged retreat, he replied that a leader owed the people steadiness in danger; to bolt in a crisis was unworthy of a gentleman, and he would see the defense through here.
entries.literal: Someone urged Xian on a plan of flight; Xian said, "Now as a people's lord, what the hundred surnames look up to, in peril unable to secure, in urgency abandoning them—a gentleman does not do this; I complete my life here."

entries.zh: 陈骞言於晋王，遣荆州刺史胡烈救宪，抗等引退。
entries.en: Chen Qian persuaded the king of Jin to send Hu Lie from Jingzhou; Lu Kang then lifted the siege.
entries.literal: Chen Qian spoke to the King of Jin, who sent the Inspector of Jing Province Hu Lie to rescue Xian; Kang and others drew back.

entries.zh: 晋王即委前任，拜宪凌江将军，封万年亭侯。
entries.en: The king confirmed him in office, named him general who crosses the river, and enfeoffed him as village marquis of Wannian.
entries.literal: The King of Jin thereupon entrusted his former post, appointed Xian General Who Crosses the River, and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Wannian village.

entries.zh: 会武陵四县举众叛吴，以宪为武陵太守巴东监军。
entries.en: When four Wuling counties rose against Wu, he was appointed governor of Wuling and army supervisor for east of Ba.
entries.literal: It happened that four counties of Wuling raised hosts and rebelled against Wu; Xian was made Administrator of Wuling and army supervisor of Badong.

entries.zh: 泰始元年改封西鄂县侯。
entries.en: In 265 his title was transferred to marquis of Xi'e county.
entries.literal: In the first year of Taishi his fief was changed to Marquis of Xi'e county.

entries.zh: 宪遣妻子居洛阳，武帝以子袭为给事中。
entries.en: He moved his family to Luoyang, and Emperor Wu of Jin gave his son Luo Xi a post as palace attendant.
entries.literal: Xian sent wife and children to dwell at Luoyang; Emperor Wu appointed his son Xi as palace attendant.

entries.zh: 三年冬，入朝，进位冠军将军、假节。
entries.en: In the winter of 267 he attended court and was promoted to general who vanquishes champions with ceremonial credentials.
entries.literal: In the third year, winter, he entered court, was advanced in rank to General Who Vanquishes Champions, and granted credentials.

entries.zh: 四年三月，从帝宴于华林园，诏问蜀大臣子弟，后问先辈宜时叙用者，宪荐蜀郡常忌、杜轸、寿良、巴西陈寿、南郡高轨、南阳吕雅、许国、江夏费恭、琅邪诸葛京、汝南陈裕，即皆叙用，咸显於世。
entries.en: In the third month of the fourth year, he attended the emperor’s banquet in Hualin Park. An edict asked about the sons and younger brothers of Shu’s great ministers, and then about senior men of the previous generation who ought now to be appointed. Luo Xian recommended Chang Ji of Shu Commandery, Du Zhen, Shou Liang, Chen Shou of Baxi, Gao Gui of Nan Commandery, Lü Ya and Xu Guo of Nanyang, Fei Gong of Jiangxia, Zhuge Jing of Langye, and Chen Yu of Runan; all were appointed and all became prominent in their time.
entries.literal: In the fourth year, third month, he followed the Emperor feasting in Hualin Garden; an edict asked about sons and younger brothers of Shu great ministers, afterward asking which elders of former times should be employed in due season; Xian recommended Chang Ji of Shu commandery, Du Zhen, Shou Liang, Chen Shou of Baxi, Gao Gui of Nan commandery, Lü Ya, Xu Guo, Fei Gong of Jiangxia, Zhuge Jing of Langye, Chen Yu of Runan; all were at once employed in order, all illustrious in the age.

entries.zh: 宪还，袭取吴之巫城，因上伐吴之策。
entries.en: When he came back he struck east, captured the Wu outpost at Wucheng, and followed with a memorial urging a campaign against Wu.
