entries.en: Though those who knew me cleared my name, in these troubled times calumny wins and doubt lingers; I live in dread of sudden injustice, my heart torn as between ice and fire.
entries.literal: Although those who knew the truth vouched for his heart, in a chaotic age slander prevailed and lingering suspicion remained; he constantly feared suddenly suffering innocence by violence—his heart deeply afflicted, as if overturned between ice and fire.

entries.zh: 昔樂毅為燕昭王立功於齊，惠王即位，疑奪其任，遂去燕之趙，休烈不虧。
entries.en: Once Yue Yi served King Zhao of Yan against Qi; when King Hui came to the throne he was suspected and stripped of command, left Yan for Zhao, and lost none of his renown.
entries.literal: Formerly Yue Yi for King Zhao of Yan achieved merit in Qi; when King Hui ascended, suspecting him he removed his charge, whereupon he left Yan for Zhao—his splendid fame undiminished.

entries.zh: 彼豈欲二三其德，蓋畏功名不建，而懼禍之將及也。
entries.en: Was he fickle in loyalty? He feared his achievements would come to nothing and ruin was closing in.
entries.literal: Did he wish to double his virtue? He feared merit and fame would not be established and disaster was about to reach him.

entries.zh: 昔遣魏郡周光以賈販為名，托叛南詣，宣達密計。
entries.en: I once sent Zhou Guang of Wei commandery south disguised as a peddler, pretending to defect, to convey a secret design.
entries.literal: Formerly he dispatched Zhou Guang of Wei commandery under the name of a merchant-trader, feigning defection to go south and declare the secret plan.

entries.zh: 時以倉卒，未敢便有章表，使光口傳而已。
entries.en: In the rush I dared not send a formal memorial and had Guang speak the message orally.
entries.literal: At the time, because of haste, he dared not at once submit a formal memorial and had Guang transmit it by word alone.

entries.zh: 以為天下大歸可見，天意所在，非吳復誰?此方之民，思為臣妾，延頸舉踵，惟恐兵來之遲耳。
entries.en: I believed the realm's great allegiance was plain and Heaven's choice obvious—if not Wu, then who? The folk here long to submit, craning their necks and rising on tiptoe, dreading only that your armies arrive too late.
entries.literal: He considered that the great return of All under Heaven was visible and Heaven's intent lay elsewhere—if not Wu, then who? The people of this region wish to become subjects; they stretch necks and lift heels, fearing only that troops come too late.

entries.zh: 若使聖恩少加信納，當以河北承望王師，疑心赤實，天日是鑒。
entries.en: If Your Majesty would grant a little trust, I would hold Hebei open for your host—my loyal heart is true; Heaven and sun bear witness.
entries.literal: If Your sacred grace would slightly add trust and acceptance, he would from Hebei await the royal host—his loyal heart true red; sun and Heaven are witness.

entries.zh: 而光去經年，不聞咳唾，未審此意竟得達不?瞻望長歎，日月以幾，魯望高子，何足以喻!又臣今日見待稍薄，蒼蠅之聲，綿綿不絕，必受此禍，遲速事耳。
entries.en: Yet Guang left a year ago and not a word has returned—did my message ever reach you? I gaze south and sigh as the months pass; even Lu’s longing for Gaozi scarcely matches this! And now I am treated coldly; slander never stops—I am sure to suffer for it, only sooner or later.
entries.literal: Yet Guang departed a year ago and no cough or spit has been heard—does this intent in the end reach you? Gazing afar he sighs long; days and months pile up—Lu Wang and Gao Zi are not enough as likeness! Moreover your subject today is treated somewhat thinly; the buzz of flies is unending—he is sure to suffer this calamity; it is only a matter of sooner or later.

entries.zh: 臣私度陛下未垂明慰者，必以臣質貫穿仁義之道，不行若此之事，謂光所傳，多虛少實，或謂比中有他消息，不知臣質構讒見疑，恐受大害也。
entries.en: I suppose Your Majesty has not yet reassured me because you take me for a man steeped in righteousness who would never act thus—thinking Guang's tale mostly false, or that some other intrigue is afoot—unaware that I am slandered and in peril.
entries.literal: Your subject privately surmises that if Your Majesty has not yet extended clear comfort, it must be because your subject Zhi is thought to pierce through the Way of benevolence and righteousness and would not do such a thing—deeming what Guang transmitted mostly empty and little real, or that among these matters there is other news—not knowing your subject Zhi is framed by slander and suspected, fearing great harm.

entries.zh: 且臣質著有罪之日，自當奔赴鼎鑊，束身待罪，此蓋人臣之宜也。
entries.en: And if I were truly guilty I would go bound to the executioner's cauldron—that is a subject's duty.
entries.literal: Moreover, on a day when your subject Zhi is clearly guilty, he ought of himself to rush to the tripod and the cauldron, binding his body to await punishment—this is what a minister should do.

entries.zh: 今日無罪，橫見譖毀，將有商鞅、白起之禍。
entries.en: Today, innocent, I am suddenly defamed and face the fate of Shang Yang or Bai Qi.
entries.literal: Today without guilt he is suddenly slandered and will meet the calamity of Shang Yang and Bai Qi.

entries.zh: 尋惟事勢，去亦直也。
entries.en: Weighing the situation, departure is the honest course.
entries.literal: Reflecting on the situation, to leave is also straight.

entries.zh: 死而弗義，不去何為!樂毅之出，吳起之走，君子傷其不遇，未有非之者也。
entries.en: To die without justice—why not leave? When Yue Yi left and Wu Qi fled, gentlemen mourned their ill treatment; none blamed them.
entries.literal: To die without righteousness—if he does not leave, what is he to do! Yue Yi's departure, Wu Qi's flight—gentlemen grieve their lack of recognition; none have condemned them.

entries.zh: 願陛下推古況今，不疑怪於臣質也。
entries.en: I beg Your Majesty to weigh antiquity against today and not find me strange.
entries.literal: May Your Majesty extend ancient examples to judge the present and not be suspicious or strange toward your subject Zhi.

entries.zh: 又念人臣獲罪，當如伍員奉己自效，不當繞幸因事為利。
entries.en: I know a guilty minister should, like Wu Zixu, offer himself in loyal service—not twist events for private gain.
entries.literal: He also reflects that when a minister receives guilt, he ought like Wu Yuan to offer himself in service, not seek advantage by circling fortune and using events for profit.

entries.zh: 然今與古，厥勢不同，南北悠遠。
entries.en: Yet today differs from antiquity; north and south are far apart.
entries.literal: Yet now and antiquity—their situations differ; north and south are vast and far.

entries.zh: 江湖隔絕，自不舉事，何得濟免!是以忘志士之節，而思立功之義也之也。
entries.en: Rivers and lakes stand between us—without acting myself, how could I escape? So I set aside pure integrity and think instead of earning merit by service.
entries.literal: Rivers and lakes cut off—if he himself does not act, how can he cross to safety! Therefore forgetting the integrity of a resolute man, he thinks instead of the righteousness of establishing merit.

entries.zh: 且臣質又以曹氏之嗣，非天命所在，政弱刑亂，柄奪於臣，諸將專威於外，各自為政，莫或同心，士卒衰耗，帑藏空虛，綱紀毀廢，上下並昏，想前後數得降叛，具聞此問，兼弱攻昧，宜應天時，此實陛下進取之秋。
entries.en: I also judge the Cao heir not Heaven's choice—weak rule, chaotic law, power held by ministers; generals rule their own domains abroad without unity; troops waste away and coffers stand empty; order is broken and court and country are blind. Your Majesty has heard this from many deserters: strike the weak while fortune favors you—this is your moment to advance.
entries.literal: Moreover your subject Zhi also considers that the Cao successor is not where Heaven's mandate lies—government weak, punishments chaotic, the handle seized by ministers; generals wield sole might abroad, each governing on his own, none of one heart; soldiers decline and waste; treasury stores are empty; statutes and discipline are ruined and abandoned; high and low alike are benighted. He thinks that from front and back you have repeatedly received defectors and rebels and fully heard this inquiry—attack the weak and strike the dim, fit Heaven's season—this is truly the season for Your Majesty's advance.

entries.zh: 是以區區敢獻其計。
entries.en: In my small way I dare offer this plan.
entries.literal: Therefore in his slight way he dares offer this plan.

entries.zh: 今若內兵淮、泗，據有下邳，荊、揚二州，聞聲響應，臣從河北席眷而南，形勢一連，根牙永固。
entries.en: If you march on the Huai and Si and seize Xiapi, Jing and Yang will answer at once; I will roll south from Hebei, our positions will link, and the foundation will hold.
entries.literal: Now if inner troops move on the Huai and Si, hold Xiapi, and the two provinces Jing and Yang respond at the sound, your subject from Hebei rolls up his mat-rug and goes south—the situation links as one, root and branch forever firm.

entries.zh: 關西之兵繫於所衛，青、徐二州不敢徹守，許，洛余兵眾不滿萬，誰能來東與陛下爭者?此城千載一會之期，可不深思而熟計乎!及臣所在，既自多馬，加以羌、胡常以三四月中美草時，驅馬來出，隱度今者，可得三千餘匹。
entries.en: Guansi's armies are pinned to their posts; Qing and Xu dare not strip their garrisons; fewer than ten thousand men remain at Xu and Luoyang—who could march east against you? This is a once-in-a-millennium chance—will you not weigh it carefully? Where I am we already have many horses; in the third and fourth months, when grass is rich, the Qiang and Hu drive herds out—I estimate three thousand mounts could be gathered now.
entries.literal: The troops of Guanxi are tied to what they guard; the two provinces Qing and Xu dare not fully withdraw garrisons; at Xu and Luo the remaining soldiers number less than ten thousand—who can come east to contend with Your Majesty? This is a once-in-a-thousand-years meeting—can you not deeply ponder and carefully plan! As to where your subject is, he already has many horses; moreover the Qiang and Hu often in the third and fourth months, when grass is lush, drive horses out—privately estimating the present, he could obtain more than three thousand head.

entries.zh: 陛下出軍，當投此時，多將騎士來就馬耳。
entries.en: Your Majesty should march at that season and send many horsemen to collect the mounts.
entries.literal: When Your Majesty sends out the army, you should strike at this time, bringing many knights to come take the horses.

entries.zh: 此皆先定所一二知。
entries.en: These points I know well in advance.
entries.literal: These are matters he knows beforehand one or two in advance.

entries.zh: 凡兩軍不能相究虛實，今此間實羸，易可克定，陛下舉動，應者必多。
entries.en: Armies cannot always probe each other's strength; this region is truly weak and easily taken—when you move, many will join you.
entries.literal: In general two armies cannot investigate each other's emptiness and fullness; now this region is truly weak and easily conquered and settled—when Your Majesty acts, responders will surely be many.

entries.zh: 上定洪業，使普天一統，下令臣質建非常之功，此乃天也。
entries.en: To settle the great enterprise and unify the realm, and to let me win extraordinary merit—that is Heaven's will.
entries.literal: Above, settling the great enterprise and making all under Heaven one—ordering your subject Zhi to establish extraordinary merit—this is Heaven.

entries.zh: 若不見納，此亦天也。
entries.en: If you refuse, that too is Heaven's decree.
entries.literal: If not accepted, this too is Heaven.

entries.zh: 願陛下思之，不復多陳。”
entries.en: I beg Your Majesty to consider it; I will say no more."
entries.literal: May Your Majesty ponder it; he will not further elaborate much."

entries.zh: 是儀字子羽，北海營陵人也。
entries.en: Shi Yi (courtesy Ziyu) came from Yingling in Beihai commandery.
entries.literal: Shi Yi, courtesy name Ziyu, was a man of Yingling in Beihai.

entries.zh: 本姓氏，初為縣吏，後仕郡。
entries.en: His clan name had been Shi; he began as a county clerk and later entered commandery service.
entries.literal: Originally his surname was Shi; at first he was a county clerk, afterward he served the commandery.

entries.zh: 郡相孔融嘲儀，言"氏"字"民"無上，可改為"是"，乃遂改焉。
entries.en: Commandery chief Kong Rong teased him that the graph for his surname looked like the people radical with nothing sovereign above it, and jokingly suggested he adopt the homophone meaning "yes"—so he did.
entries.literal: The commandery administrator Kong Rong mocked Yi, saying the character shi written as "clan" has "people" without a "ruler" above—it could be changed to shi meaning "yes"—thereupon he changed it.

entries.zh: 〈徐众评曰：古之建姓，或以所生，或以官号，或以祖名，皆有义体，以明氏族。
entries.en: 〈Commentator Xu Zhong remarks that ancient surnames were coined from birth tokens, offices, or forebears' names—each carried meaning that bound a lineage together.
entries.literal: 〈Xu Zhong's appraisal states: In ancient times in establishing surnames, some by what was born, some by office titles, some by ancestors' names—all had meaningful forms to clarify clan families.

entries.zh: 故曰胙之以土而命之氏，此先王之典也，所以明本重始，彰示功德，子孙不忘也。
entries.en: Hence the ritual formula: grant land and bestow the clan name—former kings used that to mark origins, celebrate merit, and keep descendants mindful of their roots.
entries.literal: Therefore it is said they enfeoffed them with soil and thereby commanded their clan name—this is the canon of former kings, whereby to clarify the root and honor beginnings, display merit and virtue, so descendants do not forget.

entries.zh: 今离文析字，横生忌讳，使仪易姓，忘本诬祖，不亦谬哉！
entries.en: To split characters for superstitious puns and make a man discard his surname is to sever him from his ancestors—surely that is folly.
entries.literal: Now splitting graphs and analyzing characters, recklessly producing taboos, causing Yi to change surname, forgetting the root and slandering ancestors—is this not erroneous!

entries.zh: 教人易姓，从人改族，融既失之，仪又不得也。〉
entries.en: To urge another to change his lineage was Kong Rong's mistake; Shi Yi ought not to have complied.〉
entries.literal: Teaching people to change surname, following others in altering clan—Kong Rong already missed the mark, and Yi too did not get it right.〉

entries.zh: 後依劉繇，避亂江東。
entries.en: He then joined Liu Yao and crossed south to escape the wars.
entries.literal: Afterward he attached himself to Liu Yao, fleeing turmoil to the east of the Yangzi.

entries.zh: 繇軍改，儀徙會稽。
entries.en: After Liu Yao's defeat he resettled in Kuaiji.
entries.literal: When Yao's army was defeated, Yi moved to Kuaiji.

entries.zh: 孫權承攝大業，優文征儀。
entries.en: Sun Quan, taking charge of Wu's destiny, sent him a warm letter of invitation.
entries.literal: When Sun Quan assumed regency of the great enterprise, he issued a gracious summons recruiting Yi.

entries.zh: 到見親任，專典機密，拜騎都尉。
entries.en: Once he arrived he won Sun Quan's confidence, handled confidential affairs, and was named chief of the capitals grooms.
entries.literal: When he arrived he was treated as intimate and trusted, exclusively managing secret matters, and was appointed Chief of the Capitals Grooms.

entries.zh: 呂蒙圖襲關羽，權以問儀，儀善其計，勸權聽之。
entries.en: When Lü Meng planned the strike on Guan Yu, Sun Quan consulted Shi Yi, who endorsed the scheme and urged him to act.
entries.literal: Lü Meng plotted a surprise attack on Guan Yu; Quan asked Yi about it; Yi approved the plan and urged Quan to heed it.

entries.zh: 從討羽，拜忠義校尉。
entries.en: He accompanied the campaign against Guan Yu and received the rank of colonel of loyalty and righteousness.
entries.literal: He followed in the punitive expedition against Yu and was appointed Colonel of Loyalty and Righteousness.

entries.zh: 儀陳謝，權令曰："孤雖非趙簡子，卿安得不自屈為周捨邪？
entries.en: Shi Yi tried to decline; Sun Quan told him, "I may not be Zhao Jianzi, but will you not humble yourself as Zhou She did for him?"
entries.literal: Yi offered thanks in declination; Quan issued an order saying: "Although I am not Zhao Jianzi, how can you refuse to humble yourself and be my Zhou She?"

entries.zh: "既定荊州，都武昌，拜裨將軍，後封都亭侯，守侍中。
entries.en: After Jingzhou fell the court moved to Wuchang, where Shi Yi became a subordinate general (pi jiangjun), then village marquis of the capital precinct, while remaining palace attendant.
entries.literal: "After Jingzhou was settled, the capital was established at Wuchang; he was appointed General of the Rear Guard, later enfeoffed as village marquis of the capital precinct, and kept as palace attendant.

entries.zh: 欲復授兵，儀自以非材，固辭不受。
entries.en: Sun Quan later offered him a military command; Shi Yi, judging himself no soldier, refused firmly.
entries.literal: When Quan wished again to confer troops, Yi considered himself without martial talent and firmly declined and did not accept.

entries.zh: 黃武中，遣儀之皖就將軍劉邵，欲誘致曹休。
entries.en: During Huangwu he sent Shi Yi to Wan to work with General Liu Shao on the ruse to draw Cao Xiu forward.
entries.literal: In the Huangwu period he dispatched Yi to Wan to join General Liu Shao, intending to lure Cao Xiu to come.

entries.zh: 休到，大破之，遷偏將軍，入闕省尚書事，外總平諸官，兼領辭訟，又令都諸公於書學。
entries.en: Cao Xiu walked into the trap and was crushed; Shi Yi rose to lieutenant general, took charge of Secretariat review, coordinated civil offices, heard lawsuits, and oversaw the palace school of writing.
entries.literal: When Xiu arrived, he was greatly defeated; Yi was promoted to lieutenant general, entered the court to inspect Secretariat business, outwardly oversaw the leveling of all offices, concurrently managed litigation, and was also ordered to supervise the gentlemen in calligraphy study.

entries.zh: 初，孫權行師征伐，每令達有所推步，皆如其言。
entries.en: Whenever Sun Quan marched he made Zhao Da cast ahead—and each forecast hit.
entries.literal: At first when Sun Quan campaigned he always ordered Da to forecast events—they always matched his words.

entries.zh: 權問其法，達終不語，由此見薄，祿位不至。
entries.en: Sun Quan demanded the technique; Zhao Da stayed mute—so courtiers snubbed him and promotions stopped.
entries.literal: Quan asked his method—Da never spoke—therefore he was slighted and salary and rank never rose.

entries.zh: 〈吴书曰：初，权即尊号，令达算作天子之后，当复几年？
entries.en: 〈The Book of Wu adds that after Sun Quan took the throne he asked Zhao Da how long his mandate would run.
entries.literal: 〈The Wu shu says: When Quan first assumed the imperial title he ordered Da to reckon how many years remained under Heaven after the Son of Heaven—how many years until repetition?

entries.zh: 达曰：“高祖建元十二年，陛下倍之。”
entries.en: Zhao Da answered, “Gaozu's reign-era ran twelve years—Your Majesty will double that.”
entries.literal: Da said: “Gaozu founded his reign-name in the twelfth year—Your Majesty doubles it.”

entries.zh: 权大喜，左右称万岁。
entries.en: Sun Quan cheered; the hall cried long life.
entries.literal: Quan rejoiced greatly; attendants shouted “Ten thousand years!”

entries.zh: 果如达言。〉
entries.en: Events matched Zhao Da’s reckoning.〉
entries.literal: It indeed happened as Da said.〉

entries.zh: 達常笑謂諸星氣風術者曰："當回算帷幕，不出戶牖以知天道，而反晝夜暴露以望氣樣，不亦難乎!"閒居無為，引算自校，乃歎曰："吾算訖盡某年月日，其終矣。
entries.en: Zhao Da mocked outdoor astrologers—true skill needed no sky-gazing—then computed his own death date and sighed it aloud.
entries.literal: Da often laughed at star-and-wind diviners: “You ought to reckon behind curtain and screen, know Heaven’s way without leaving doors and windows—yet you expose yourselves day and night watching qi—is it not painful!” Dwelling idle he pushed tallies and checked himself, then sighed: “My reckoning exhausts itself on such year month day—that is my end.

entries.zh: "達妻數見達效，聞而哭泣。
entries.en: His wife had seen his arts work—she wept at the sentence.
entries.literal: Da’s wife had often witnessed Da’s efficacy—hearing this she wept.

entries.zh: 達欲弭妻意，乃更步算，言："向者謬誤耳，尚未也。
entries.en: To calm her he recast the figures: “I miscalculated—the hour has not come.”
entries.literal: Da wished to soothe his wife—he paced calculations again and said: “Earlier I erred—not yet.”

entries.zh: "後如期死。
entries.en: He died exactly when first predicted.
entries.literal: Later he died on that date.

entries.zh: 權聞達有書，求之不得，乃錄問其女，及發棺無所得，法術絕焉。
entries.en: Sun Quan hunted Zhao Da’s manuscripts—questioned his daughter—opened the tomb—found nothing—the lineage of lore died.
entries.literal: Hearing Da had writings Quan sought them without success—then interrogated his daughter—opening the coffin found nothing—the arts were extinguished.

entries.zh: 〈吴录曰：皇象字休明，广陵江都人。
entries.en: 〈The Record of Wu names calligrapher Huang Xiang (style Xiuming) from Jiangdu.
entries.literal: 〈The Wu lu says: Huang Xiang, courtesy Xiuming, was a man of Jiangdu in Guangling.

entries.zh: 幼工书。
entries.en: He practiced brushwork from boyhood.
entries.literal: Skilled in writing from youth.

entries.zh: 时有张子并、陈梁甫能书。
entries.en: Zhang Zibing and Chen Liangfu were rivals in script.
entries.literal: At the time Zhang Zibing and Chen Liangfu could write.

entries.zh: 甫恨逋，并恨峻，象斟酌其间，甚得其妙，中国善书者不能及也。
entries.en: Huang Xiang balanced their styles and surpassed both—northern masters fell short.
entries.literal: Liangfu resented Bu, Zibing resented Jun—Xiang mediated between them and grasped the exquisite point—calligraphers of the Central Plains could not equal him.

entries.zh: 严武字子卿，卫尉畯再从子也，围釭莫与为辈。
entries.en: Yan Wu (Ziqing), great-grandson of Wei officer Yan Jun, stood alone in bronze-seal carving.
entries.literal: Yan Wu, courtesy Ziqing—grand-nephew twice removed of Commandant of the Guards Jun—none matched him in seal-ring engraving.

entries.zh: 宋寿占梦，十不失一。
entries.en: Song Shuo dream-divined with ninety-percent accuracy.
entries.literal: Song Shou interpreted dreams—missed one in ten.

entries.zh: 曹不兴善画，权使画屏风，误落笔点素，因就以作蝇。
entries.en: Ordered to paint a screen Cao Buxing smeared ink—turned the blot into a fly.
entries.literal: Cao Buxing excelled at painting—Quan had him paint a screen—by mistake ink dropped on silk—thereupon he turned it into a fly.

entries.zh: 既进御，权以为生蝇，举手弹之。
entries.en: Sun Quan tried to swat the painted fly.
entries.literal: When presented Quan thought it a living fly and raised his hand to flick it.

entries.zh: 孤城郑妪能相人，及范、惇、达八人，世皆称妙，谓之八绝云。
entries.en: Physiognomist Mother Zheng of lone-walled Gucheng joined Wu Fan, Liu Dun, Zhao Da, and five talents hailed as the Eight Wonders.
entries.literal: Old woman Zheng of Gucheng could read faces—with Fan, Dun, Da and five others the age called them the Eight Marvels.

entries.zh: 《晋阳秋曰：吴有葛衡字思真，明达天官，能为几巧，作浑天，使地居于中，以机动之，天转而地止，以上应晷度。〉
entries.en: The Jin Yang Qiu credits Ge Heng with a geared cosmos-model matching celestial arcs.〉
entries.literal: The Jin Yang Qiu says: Wu had Ge Heng, courtesy Sizhen—understood celestial offices—crafted ingenious devices—made an armillary sphere with earth at the center moved by gears—heaven turned while earth stood still—matching sundial degrees.〉

entries.zh: 評曰：三子各於其術精矣，其用思妙矣，然君子等役心神，宜於大者遠者，是以有識之士，捨彼而取此也。
entries.en: The historian concludes: technical genius tempts petty wonders; thoughtful men aim higher.
entries.literal: The appraisal says: Each of the three men mastered his craft—their application of mind was subtle—yet the gentleman employs spirit on great and distant aims—therefore discerning scholars forsake the former and embrace the latter.

entries.zh: 〈孙盛曰：夫玄览未然，逆鉴来事，虽裨灶、梓慎其犹病诸，况术之下此者乎？
entries.en: 〈Sun Sheng notes even canonical astrologers stumbled—lesser tricks merit doubt.
entries.literal: 〈Sun Sheng said: To survey the unseen and mirror coming events—even Pi Zao and Zi Shen struggled—how much more arts beneath theirs?

entries.zh: 吴史书达知东南当有王气，故轻举济江。
entries.en: Wu records say Zhao Da crossed south chasing imperial vapors.
entries.literal: The Wu history says Da knew kingly qi would rise in the southeast—therefore he lightly crossed the Yangzi.

entries.zh: 魏承汉绪，受命中畿，达不能豫睹兆萌，而流窜吴越。
entries.en: Wei held the Central Plain—yet Zhao Da missed Wei’s rise and wandered eastern marshes.
entries.literal: Wei inherited Han’s thread and received mandate in the heartland—Da failed to foresee the budding sign beforehand and drifted among Wu and Yue.

entries.zh: 又不知吝术之鄙，见薄於时，安在其能逆睹天道而审帝王之符瑞哉？
entries.en: Sun Sheng asks how a stingy technician could read dynastic fate.
entries.literal: Again ignorant how base it is to hoard arts—slighted by the age—where lies ability to foresee Heaven’s way and discern imperial portents?

entries.zh: 昔圣王观天地之文，以画八卦之象，故亹亹成於蓍策，变化形乎六爻，是以三易虽殊，卦繇理一，安有回转一筹，可以钩深测隐，意对逆占，而能遂知来物者乎？
entries.en: The classics unified oracle logic—no single abacus replaces the Changes.
entries.literal: Ancient sage kings observed Heaven and Earth’s patterns to fashion the eight trigrams—thus abundant wisdom arose from milfoil and transformation took form in six lines—therefore though three Changes differ hexagram principle is one—how could rotating one tally hook depths and probe concealments or invert divination face-to-face and thereby know future things?

entries.zh: 流俗好异，妄设神奇，不幸之中，仲尼所弃，是以君子志其大者，无所取诸。
entries.en: Fashion craves miracles—Confucius spurned fortune-telling—the gentleman thinks bigger.
entries.literal: Common fashion loves the strange and vainly fabricates marvels—among ill omens Confucius discarded these—therefore the gentleman sets his aim on greatness and takes nothing from such.

entries.zh: 臣松之以为盛云“君子志其大者，无所取诸”，故评家之旨，非新声也。
entries.en: Pei Songzhi notes Sun Sheng echoes the official appraisal.
entries.literal: Pei Songzhi considers: When Sheng says “the gentleman aims at greatness and takes nothing from such”—the appraiser’s meaning is no novelty.

entries.zh: 其餘所讥，则皆为非理。
entries.en: Pei rejects Sun Sheng’s other barbs.
entries.literal: His remaining ridicule is altogether unreasonable.

entries.zh: 自中原酷乱，至于建安，数十年间，生民殆尽，比至小康，皆百死之餘耳。
entries.en: Decades of northern slaughter left few survivors—peace meant beating overwhelming odds.
entries.literal: From central plains cruel chaos until Jian’an—within several decades the living nearly vanished—by modest peace all were survivors of hundred deaths.

entries.zh: 江左虽有兵革，不能如中国之甚也，焉知达不算其安危，知祸有多少，利在东南，以全其身乎？
entries.en: The south suffered less—Zhao Da may simply have sought safer ground.
entries.literal: Though east of the river knew warfare it could not match China’s severity—how know Da did not reckon safety and danger, weigh harm’s measure, and judge profit lay in the southeast to preserve himself?

entries.zh: 而责不知魏氏将兴，流播吴越，在京房之筹，犹不能自免刑戮，况达但以秘术见薄，在悔吝之间乎！
entries.en: Pinning prophets for politics ignores worse failures—even masters died under suspicion.
entries.literal: Yet blame him for not foreknowing Wei’s rise and drifting Wu-Yue—even Jing Fang’s reckonings could not spare execution—how much more Da slighted only for secret arts—between regret and miserliness!

entries.zh: 古之道术，盖非一方，探赜之功，岂惟六爻，苟得其要，则可以易而知之矣，回转一筹，胡足怪哉？
entries.en: Many roads led to insight—the Changes were broader than one chip.
entries.literal: Ancient arts were not one path—work plumbing mysteries used not only six lines—grasp the essentials and you know through Change—rotating one tally—what is strange?

entries.zh: 达之推算，穷其要妙以知幽测隐，何愧于古！
entries.en: Zhao Da plumbed secrets as well as ancients.
entries.literal: Da’s reckonings exhausted subtle essentials to probe depths—what shame before antiquity?

entries.zh: 而以裨、梓限之，谓达为妄，非笃论也。
entries.en: Equating him with Pi Zao sells Zhao Da short.
entries.literal: Yet limiting him with Pi and Zi—calling Da deluded—is not serious judgment.

entries.zh: 《抱朴子》曰：时有葛仙公者，每饮酒醉，常入人家门前陂水中卧，竟日乃出。
entries.en: Ge Hong tells how Immortal Ge dozed in roadside ponds.
entries.literal: The Baopuzi says: Immortal Lord Ge when drunk would lie in pond water before people’s gates all day before emerging.

entries.zh: 曾从吴主别，到洌州，还遇大风，百官船多没，仙公船亦沉沦，吴主甚怅恨。
entries.en: Once, after taking leave of the Wu ruler and reaching Liezhou, he was caught on the return journey in a great gale. Many officials' boats went down, the Immortal Lord's boat sank as well, and the Wu ruler was deeply distressed.
entries.literal: Once bidding farewell to the Wu lord and reaching Liezhou, he met a great wind; many officials' boats sank, and the Immortal Lord's boat also went under; the Wu lord deeply regretted it.

entries.zh: 明日使人钩求公船，而登高以望焉。
entries.en: Next day crews dragged for wreckage from the heights.
entries.literal: Next day men grappled for the boat while watchers climbed high to scan.

entries.zh: 久之，见公步从水上来，衣履不沾，而有酒色。
entries.en: He walked ashore dry and tipsy.
entries.literal: After long delay they saw him walking from the water—clothes dry—with wine-flushed face.

entries.zh: 既见而言曰：“臣昨侍从而伍子胥见请，暂过设酒，忽忽不得，即委之。”
entries.en: He blamed a banquet with Wu Zixu’s ghost for his delay.
entries.literal: Seeing him he said: “Yesterday my attendant Wu Zixu invited me—I stopped for wine—could not linger—had to leave.”

entries.zh: 又有姚光者，有火术。
entries.en: Yao Guang commanded flame.
entries.literal: Also Yao Guang practiced fire arts.

entries.zh: 吴主身临试之，积荻数千束，使光坐其上，又以数千束荻裹之，因猛风而燔之。
entries.en: Sun Quan piled reeds, seated Yao Guang, torched the heap.
entries.literal: The Wu lord personally tested—stacked thousands of reed bundles—had Guang sit atop—wrapped thousands more—blazed them with fierce wind.

entries.zh: 荻了尽，谓光当以化为烬，而光端坐灰中，振衣而起，把一卷书。
entries.en: Ash fell away—Yao Guang stood untouched with a book.
entries.literal: When reeds burned out they expected Guang reduced to ash—yet Guang sat upright in ashes—shook his robes and rose—holding a scroll.

entries.zh: 吴主取其书视之，不能解也。
entries.en: Sun Quan could not read the script.
entries.literal: The Wu lord took the book—could not decipher it.

entries.zh: 又曰：吴景帝有疾，求觋视者，得一人。
entries.en: Emperor Jing of Wu sought healers—found a medium.
entries.literal: Also: Wu Jingdi fell ill—sought a spirit medium—found one.

entries.zh: 景帝欲试之，乃杀鹅而埋於苑中，架小屋，施床几，以妇人屐履服物著其上，乃使觋视之。
entries.en: He staged a fake tomb with goose remains and women’s gear.
entries.literal: Jingdi wished to test—killed a goose buried in the garden—built a hut—bed and desk—placed woman’s shoes and garments atop—sent the medium to view.

entries.zh: 告曰：“若能说此冢中鬼妇人形状者，当加赏而即信矣。”
entries.en: Success meant reward—describe the ghost woman.
entries.literal: Told him: “If you can describe this tomb ghost woman’s shape—you shall be rewarded and trusted.”

entries.zh: 竟日尽夕无言，帝推问之急，乃曰：“实不见有鬼，但见一头白鹅立墓上，所以不即白之，疑是鬼神变化作此相，当候其真形而定。
entries.en: Pressed hard, the medium finally said, “I truly saw no ghost—only a white goose standing on the tomb. I did not report at once because I suspected spirits had disguised themselves thus—I waited to determine the true form.
entries.literal: All day to evening no word—the emperor pressed urgently—then said: “Truly saw no ghost—only a white goose on the tomb—did not report immediately—suspected spirit disguise—waited for true form.

entries.zh: 无复移易，不知何故，不敢不以实上闻。”
entries.en: There was no further change; I know not why—but I dared not report anything but the truth.”
entries.literal: No further change—know not why—dare report only truth.”

entries.zh: 景帝乃厚赐之。
entries.en: The emperor paid him well.
entries.literal: Jingdi richly rewarded.

entries.zh: 然则鹅死亦有鬼也。
entries.en: Pei wonders whether geese have ghosts.
entries.literal: Thus even a dead goose has a ghost?

entries.zh: 葛洪《神仙传》曰：仙人介象，字元则，会稽人，有诸方术。
entries.en: Ge Hong’s hagiography introduces Jie Xiang of Kuaiji.
entries.literal: Ge Hong’s Traditions of Immortals says: Immortal Jie Xiang, courtesy Yuanze—Kuaiji—commanded many arts.

entries.zh: 吴主闻之，徵象到武昌，甚敬贵之，称为介君，为起宅，以御帐给之，赐遗前后累千金，从象学蔽形之术。
entries.en: Sun Quan housed him in luxury and studied concealment.
entries.literal: The Wu lord summoned him to Wuchang—honored him—styled Lord Jie—built a mansion—granted imperial curtains—gifts piled to thousand gold—studied invisibility from Xiang.

entries.zh: 试还后宫，及出殿门，莫有见者。
entries.en: He vanished crossing palace gates.
entries.literal: Tested returning through rear palace—exiting hall gate—none saw him.

entries.zh: 又使象作变化，种瓜菜百果，皆立生可食。
entries.en: He sprouted melons and fruits on command.
entries.literal: Also had Xiang perform transformations—plant melons vegetables hundred fruits—all sprouted instantly edible.

entries.zh: 吴主共论鲙鱼何者最美，象曰：“鯔鱼为上。”
entries.en: Asked about sashimi, Jie Xiang praised zi fish.
entries.literal: The Wu lord debated which sliced fish excelled—Xiang said: “Zi fish ranks highest.

entries.zh: 吴主曰：“论近道鱼耳，此出海中，安可得邪？”
entries.en: Sun Quan called sea fish unattainable inland.
entries.literal: The Wu lord said: “Speaking of nearby river fish—this comes from the sea—how obtain?”

entries.zh: 象曰：“可得耳。”
entries.en: Jie Xiang promised delivery.
entries.literal: Xiang said: “Can obtain.”

entries.zh: 乃令人於殿庭中作方埳，汲水满之，并求钩。
entries.en: Servants dug a pool and fetched tackle.
entries.literal: Thereupon ordered a square pit dug in the courtyard—filled with water—and sought hooks.

entries.zh: 象起饵之，垂纶於埳中。
entries.en: He angled in the courtyard pool.
entries.literal: Xiang baited—cast line into the pit.

entries.zh: 须臾，果得鯔鱼。
entries.en: He landed a zi fish.
entries.literal: Presently obtained zi fish.

entries.zh: 吴主惊喜，问象曰：“可食不？”
entries.en: Sun Quan asked if it was safe to eat.
entries.literal: The Wu lord delighted—asked: “Edible?”

entries.zh: 象曰：“故为陛下取以作生鲙，安敢取不可食之物！”
entries.en: Jie Xiang swore it suited sashimi.
entries.literal: Xiang said: “Fetched for Your Majesty as raw slices—how dare bring inedible!”

entries.zh: 乃使厨下切之。
entries.en: Chefs carved the fish.
entries.literal: Ordered the kitchen to slice.

entries.zh: 吴主曰：“闻蜀使来，得蜀姜作韲甚好，恨尔时无此。”
entries.en: Sun Quan said, “I heard Shu envoys came and that Shu ginger made into pickles was excellent—I regret we did not have it then.”
entries.literal: The Wu lord said: “Heard Shu envoys came and brought Shu ginger made into pickles—it was excellent; regret none then.”

entries.zh: 象曰：“蜀姜岂不易得，愿差所使者，并付直。”
entries.en: Jie Xiang said, “Shu ginger is not hard to obtain—I wish to send the messenger along and pay for it.”
entries.literal: Xiang said: “Shu ginger is not hard to obtain—I wish to send the messenger along and pay the price.”

entries.zh: 吴主指左右一人，以钱五十付之。
entries.en: Sun Quan picked a runner and fifty coins.
entries.literal: The Wu lord pointed to an attendant—gave fifty cash.

entries.zh: 象书一符，以著青竹杖中，使行人闭目骑杖，杖止，便买姜讫，复闭目。
entries.en: He charmed a bamboo rod for blind teleport shopping.
entries.literal: Xiang wrote a charm—placed it in a green bamboo staff—had the traveler close eyes and ride the staff—when the staff stopped buy ginger—close eyes again.

entries.zh: 此人承其言骑杖，须臾止，已至成都，不知是何处，问人，人言是蜀市中，乃买姜。
entries.en: The courier opened his eyes in Chengdu’s market.
entries.literal: The man obeyed—presently stopped—already at Chengdu—did not know where—asked—people said Shu market—bought ginger.

entries.zh: 于时吴使张温先在蜀，既於市中相识，甚惊，便作书寄其家。
entries.en: He met Zhang Wen and sent mail east.
entries.literal: At that time Wu envoy Zhang Wen was in Shu—recognized him in the market—startled—wrote a letter home.

entries.zh: 此人买姜毕，捉书负姜，骑杖闭目，须臾已还到吴，厨下切鲙适了。
entries.en: He finished buying ginger, took the letter and carried the ginger, rode the staff with eyes closed, and in an instant was back in Wu—the kitchen had just finished slicing the fish.
entries.literal: The man finished buying ginger—took letter carried ginger—rode staff eyes closed—instantly back in Wu—the kitchen had just finished slicing fish.

entries.zh: 臣松之以为葛洪所记，近为惑众，其书文颇行世，故撮取数事，载之篇末也。
entries.en: Pei cites Ge Hong to show wonder-tales entertained readers—not sober history.
entries.literal: Pei Songzhi considers Ge Hong’s records approach deluding masses—the text circulates widely—therefore excerpt several matters at chapter end.

entries.zh: 神仙之术，讵可测量，臣之臆断，以为惑众，所谓夏虫不知冷冰耳。〉
entries.en: Pei dismisses miracle lore as summer worms denying winter—closing the gloss.
entries.literal: Immortal arts—how measure—my opinion judges them deluding masses—the so-called summer insects knowing nothing of ice—end quote.

entries.zh: 吳范字文則，會稽上虞人也。
entries.en: Wu Fan, whose courtesy name was Wenze, came from Shangyu in Kuaiji Commandery.
entries.literal: Wu Fan, courtesy name Wenze, was a man of Shangyu in Kuaiji.

entries.zh: 以治歷數知風氣聞於郡中。
entries.en: He earned local renown for calendar science, numerology, and interpreting weather signs.
entries.literal: He became known in the commandery for mastering calendars and reckoning and reading winds and qi.

entries.zh: 舉有道，詣京都，世亂不行。
entries.en: Recommended for the “Abundant in the Way” candidacy and called to the capital, he stayed home because the realm was in chaos.
entries.literal: Recommended as Abundant in the Way, he was summoned to the capital, but with the age in turmoil he did not go.

entries.zh: 會孫權起於東南，范委身服事，每有災祥，輒推數言狀。
entries.en: After Sun Quan rose in the southeast Wu Fan entered his service—whenever heaven sent prodigies he cast figures and explained what they meant.
entries.literal: When Sun Quan arose in the southeast Fan devoted himself to service; whenever omens of fortune or disaster appeared he always reckoned by numbers and stated their forms.

entries.zh: 其術多效，遂以顯名。
entries.en: Again and again his calculations held, and his name spread.
entries.literal: His arts proved effective many times, and so he became famous.

entries.zh: 赤烏中，魏司馬宣王謀欲攻恪。
entries.en: In the Chiwu years Sima Yi of Wei laid plans to crush Zhuge Ke.
entries.literal: During the Chiwu reign-period, Sima Yi (King Xuan of Wei) planned an offensive against Ke.

entries.zh: 權方發兵應之，望氣者以為不利，於是徒恪屯於柴桑。
entries.en: Wu was mobilizing to meet the threat when court diviners called the stars hostile, so Ke’s corps was redeployed to Chaisang.
entries.literal: Sun Quan was on the point of raising troops to counter him when specialists in reading vapors pronounced the omens ill; thereupon Ke’s command was shifted to garrison Chaisang.

entries.zh: 與丞相陸遜書曰：
entries.en: He sent Chancellor Lu Xun a letter that ran:
entries.literal: He wrote to Chancellor Lu Xun, saying:

entries.zh: 夫天無二日，土無二王，王者不務兼併天下而欲垂祚後世，古今未之有也。
entries.en: Two suns cannot share the sky; two kings cannot share the soil—no emperor ever secured his line without conquering all beneath it.
entries.literal: Heaven admits no second sun; earth bears no second king—never in antiquity or today has a true king aimed to pass down fortune without striving to swallow the realm.

entries.zh: 昔戰國之時，諸候自恃兵強地廣，互有救援，謂此足以傳世，人莫能危。
entries.en: Warring States princes trusted mutual rescue and vast domains to live forever safe.
entries.literal: In the Warring States age each lord trusted his strong armies and broad lands, lent aid across borders, deemed such enough to preserve his line forever beyond peril.

entries.zh: 恣情從懷，憚於勞苦，使秦漸得自大，遂以並之，此既然矣。
entries.en: They lounged while Qin grew—then swallowed them whole.
entries.literal: They indulged whim and shrank from toil until Qin-by degrees grew paramount and annexed them—so it proved.

entries.zh: 近者劉景昇在荊州，有眾十萬，財谷如山。
entries.en: Liu Biao once held Jingzhou—hosts in six figures, granaries like mountains.
entries.literal: Recently Liu Jingsheng held Jingzhou with a hundred thousand men and grain piled like hills.

entries.zh: 不及曹操尚微，與之力競，坐觀其強大，吞滅諸袁，北方都定之後，操率三十萬眾來向荊州，當時雖有吞智者，不能復為畫計，於是景升兒子，交臂請降，遂為囚虜。
entries.en: He refused to strike Cao while Cao was small, watched him crush the Yuans and pacify the north—then three hundred thousand Wei troops rolled south; even clever advisers could plot nothing; Biao’s sons surrendered shackled.
entries.literal: Before Cao Cao was still weak he declined to wrestle him, sat watching him swell, swallow the Yuans, settle the north—then Cao led three hundred thousand south toward Jingzhou; though wise men remained, none could sketch further counsel; Jingsheng’s sons folded arms and sued for surrender, ending prisoners.

entries.zh: 凡敵國欲相吞，即仇雠欲相除也，有仇而長之，禍不在己，則在後人，不可不為遠慮也。
entries.en: States that would eat each other are feuds that must be killed—feed your foe and your heirs pay.
entries.literal: Whenever rival states mean to devour each other it is as mortal foes meaning to erase each other—if you nurse an enemy you grow it; the calamity falls not on you then on those after—long sight cannot be neglected.

entries.zh: 昔伍子胥曰：『越十年生聚，十年教訓，二十年之外，吳其為沼乎！』
entries.en: Wu Zixu warned: “Ten years Yue breeds men, ten years schools them—twenty years on, Wu becomes swamp!”
entries.literal: Wu Zixu said of old: “Yue will breed men ten years and train them ten years—twenty years hence Wu shall be marsh!”

entries.zh: 夫差自恃強大，聞此邈然，是以誅子胥而無備越之心，至於臨敗悔之，豈有及乎？
entries.en: Fucha trusted strength, sneered, slew Zixu, ignored Yue—too late he repented at the water’s edge.
entries.literal: Fucha trusted his might, heard this with lofty dismissiveness—therefore he executed Zixu and never prepared against Yue; only when ruin closed in did he repent—could that avail?

entries.zh: 越小於吳，尚為吳禍，況其強大者邪？
entries.en: Lesser Yue ruined Wu—what of a stronger foe?
entries.literal: Yue was smaller than Wu yet became Wu’s scourge—how much more a greater power?

entries.zh: 昔秦但得關西耳，尚以併吞六國，今賊皆得秦趙、韓、魏、燕齊九州之地，地悉戎馬之鄉，士林之藪。
entries.en: Classic Qin held only the western march yet devoured six states; Wei now owns Guanzhong and the Zhao-Han-Wei-Yan-Qi heartland—nine provinces of cavaliers and lettered men.
entries.literal: Antiquity’s Qin possessed only the ground west of the passes yet swallowed the six kingdoms; today’s rebels hold Guanzhong and the old domains of Zhao, Han, Wei, Yan, and Qi—the nine heartland provinces where every vale breeds chargers and every dell hides scholars.

entries.zh: 今以魏比古之秦，土地數倍；
entries.en: Wei beside classic Qin spans several times the ground.
entries.literal: Compare Wei to antique Qin—their territory multiples several fold.

entries.zh: 以吳與蜀比古穴國，不能半之。
entries.en: Wu and Shu together are not half that footprint.
entries.literal: Compare Wu and Shu to ancient cave-minnow states—they do not reach half.

entries.zh: 然所以能敵之，但以操時兵眾於今適盡，而後生者未悉長大，正是賊衰少未盛之時。
entries.en: We endure because Cao’s cohort died off and boys still train—the enemy trough before the crest.
entries.literal: Yet we can oppose them only because Cao Cao’s veterans are largely spent while replacements have not yet grown—this is precisely the foe’s thinning hour before his zenith.

entries.zh: 加司馬懿先誅王淩，續自隕斃，其子幼弱，而專彼大任，雖有智計之士，未得施用。
entries.en: Sima Yi slew Wang Ling then died; weak sons hold supreme command—brains stay bottled.
entries.literal: Add that Sima Yi first executed Wang Ling then himself perished; his sons are young yet clutch supreme command—though strategists exist they cannot be employed.

entries.zh: 當今伐之，是其厄會。
entries.en: Strike now and you hit the hinge moment.
entries.literal: To strike now is to catch their crisis.

entries.zh: 聖人急於趨時，誠謂今日。
entries.en: The sage races time—I say that hour is today.
entries.literal: Sages hurry to ride the moment—I declare today that hour.

entries.zh: 若順眾人之情，懷偷安之計，以為長江之險可以傳世；
entries.en: Follow the crowd, cling to false peace, trust the Long River as eternal shield—
entries.literal: If we follow the multitude’s mood and hug a policy of stolen ease, reckoning the Yangzi’s barrier enough to pass down generations —

entries.zh: 不論魏之終始，而以今日遂輕其後。
entries.en: —ignore Wei’s arc yet shrug at tomorrow—
entries.literal: without weighing Wei’s beginning and end yet lightly dismissing what follows today —

entries.zh: 此吾所以長歎息者也。
entries.en: that is why I groan aloud.
entries.literal: that is why I sigh long.

entries.zh: 自本以來，務在產育，今者賊民歲月繁滋，但以尚小，未可得用耳。
entries.en: Since dynastic founding we bred people; Wei’s peasants swell each year—they are young but not yet spear fodder.
entries.literal: From our founders day we have urged breeding population; now enemy folk multiply yearly—they are still young and not yet usable.

entries.zh: 若復十數年後，其眾必倍於今，而國家勁兵之地，皆已空盡，唯有此見眾可以定事。
entries.en: Another decade doubles their ranks while our crack districts hollow—only today’s soldiers can decide it.
entries.literal: Wait another dozen years and their numbers must double today’s while our elite regions already stand emptied—only these present troops can settle the matter.

entries.zh: 若不早用之，端坐使老，復十數年，略當損半，而見子弟數不足言。
entries.en: Idle them till old age and ten years cuts our hosts in half while heirs thin to nothing.
entries.literal: If we do not use them early but sit until they age, another decade will roughly halve them while our sons barely merit mention.

entries.zh: 若賊眾一倍，而我兵損半，雖復使伊、管圖之，未可如何。
entries.en: Double them and halve us—even Yi Yin and Guan Zhong could not save us.
entries.literal: If enemy strength doubles while ours halves, though Yi Yin and Guan Zhong plotted, nothing could be done.

entries.zh: 今不達遠慮者，必以此言為迂。
entries.en: Short thinkers will call this preachy.
entries.literal: Men lacking far sight must deem such words pedantic.

entries.zh: 夫禍難未至而豫憂慮，此固眾人之所迂也。
entries.en: Worry before disaster looks foolish—crowds always sneer.
entries.literal: Calamity not yet arrived yet anxiety beforehand—this is what common minds dismiss as pedantic.

entries.zh: 及於難至，然後頓顙，雖有智者，又不能圖。
entries.en: Disaster lands and they beat their brows—too late for even wise heads.
entries.literal: When disaster strikes they knock foreheads in vain—though wise men remain, nothing can be plotted.

entries.zh: 此乃古今所病，非獨一時。
entries.en: That folly spans every age—not ours alone.
entries.literal: This sickness runs through ages—not one moment alone.

entries.zh: 昔吳始以伍員為迂，故難至而不可救。
entries.en: Wu once mocked Wu Zixu as alarmist—when doom came there was no remedy.
entries.literal: Long ago Wu first deemed Wu Yuan pedantic—hence when calamity arrived they could not be saved.

entries.zh: 劉景升不能慮十年之後，故無以治其子孫。
entries.en: Liu Biao never looked past the decade—so he left no shelter for his heirs.
entries.literal: Liu Jingsheng could not plan ten years ahead—therefore he had no way to govern his sons and grandsons.

entries.zh: 今恪無具臣之才，而受大吳蕭、霍之任，智與眾同思不經遠，若不及今日為國斥境，俯仰年老，而仇敵更強。
entries.en: I lack common bureaucratic polish yet carry a Xiao-Huo burden for Wu; my wit is ordinary—if I fail to widen our borders now, old age will creep in while enemies swell.
entries.literal: Now Ke lacks the talent of a mere competent minister yet bears Great Wu’s charge such as fell to Xiao He and Huo Guang; his wisdom matches the crowd’s and his thought does not reach far—if he does not today for the state push the frontier, in the blink of an eye he will age while foes grow stronger.

entries.zh: 欲刎頸謝責，寧有補邪？
entries.en: Would slitting my throat then undo the stain?
entries.literal: Wishing then to cut one’s throat and apologize for fault—would that avail?

entries.zh: 今聞眾人或以百姓尚貧，欲務閒息，此不右其慮其大危而其小勤者也。
entries.en: Some plead poverty and urge repose—they fret over small fatigue while ignoring existential peril.
entries.literal: Now I hear some argue that because the common people remain poor they wish to pursue ease and rest—this fails to weigh supreme peril against petty hardship.

entries.zh: 昔漢祖幸已自有三秦之地，何不閉關守險以自娛樂，空出攻楚，身被創痍，介冑生蟣蝨，將士厭困苦，豈甘鋒刃而忘安寧哉？
entries.en: Gaozu held Guanzhong—why not bolt Hangu and feast? He chose war: wounds, lice in his armor, troops pushed past endurance—not because they loved steel over peace.
entries.literal: Of old the Han Founding Emperor already possessed the Three Qins—why did he not bar the passes and guard the defiles for private pleasure, instead marching out empty-handed against Chu, his body scarred, lice breeding in helm and mail, officers sick of misery—did they relish naked blades and forget quiet?

entries.zh: 慮於長久不得兩存者耳！
entries.en: They knew two dragons cannot share one pool.
entries.literal: They reckoned that long-term survival allowed no two powers side by side!

entries.zh: 每覽荊邯說公孫述以進取之圖，近風家叔父表陳與賊爭競之計，未嘗不喟然歎息也。
entries.en: Each time I read Jing Han’s brief to Gongsun Shu or my uncle’s essay on tackling Wei, I groan with recognition.
entries.literal: Whenever I read how Jing Han urged Gongsun Shu with plans of advance, or lately my uncle’s memorial laying out how to vie with the foe, never do I fail to sigh aloud.

entries.zh: 夙夜反側，所慮如此，故聊疏愚言，以達二三君子之末。
entries.en: These worries cost me sleep—so I sketch this crude plea for you few who judge.
entries.literal: Night and day I toss with such cares—therefore I loosely set forth these blunt words to reach the ears of you gentlemen.

entries.zh: 若一朝隕歿志畫不立，貴令來世知我所憂，可思於後。
entries.en: If I die before the plan is laid, let posterity read my fear and learn.
entries.literal: If one morning I fall dead before designs are fixed, may later generations know what gnawed me and ponder it after.

entries.zh: 於是亮、峻聽恪故吏斂葬，遂求之於石子岡。
entries.en: The regents let old aides recover Ke from Shizi Gang.
entries.literal: Thereupon Liang and Jun allowed Ke’s former clerks to wrap him for burial and sought the corpse at Shizi Ridge.

entries.zh: 〈《江表傳》曰：朝臣有乞為恪立碑以銘其勳績者，博士盛衝以為不應。
entries.en: 〈Some wanted a monument—Doctor Sheng Chong refused.
entries.literal: 〈The Jiang Biao Zhuan says: Courtiers petitioned to raise a stele engraving Ke’s deeds—Doctor Sheng Chong argued against.

entries.zh: 孫休曰：「盛夏出軍，士卒傷損，無尺寸之功，不可謂能；
entries.en: Sun Xiu judged: “Summer war without gain is not skill;
entries.literal: Sun Xiu said: “To march midsummer wounding troops without inch-wide merit—cannot be called able;

entries.zh: 受託孤之任，死於豎子之手，不可謂智。
entries.en: to die regent at a stripling’s blade is not wisdom.
entries.literal: to bear orphan-entrustment yet die at a boy’s hand—cannot be called wise.

entries.zh: 衝議為是。」
entries.en: Sheng Chong had the right of it."
entries.literal: Chong’s opinion was correct."

entries.zh: 遂寢。〉
entries.en: The stele died unraised.〉
entries.literal: Thereupon the matter slept.〉

entries.zh: 孫綝字子通，與峻同祖。
entries.en: Sun Lin (Zitong)—Jun’s cousin.
entries.literal: Sun Lin, courtesy name Zitong, shared ancestors with Jun.

entries.zh: 綝父綽為安民都尉。
entries.en: Father Sun Chuo held pacification command.
entries.literal: Lin’s father Chuo was Commandant Who Pacifies the People.

entries.zh: 綝始為偏將軍，及峻死，為待中武衛將軍，領中外諸軍事，代知朝政。
entries.en: Major to regent—Jun’s death made Lin armed chamberlain of all hosts.
entries.literal: Lin began as Major-General—when Jun died he became Palace Attendant, General Who Guards the Martial, commanding inner and outer armies, replacing him in managing court.

entries.zh: 呂據聞之大恐，與諸督將連名，共表薦滕胤為丞相，綝以胤為大司馬，代呂岱駐武昌。
entries.en: Lü Ju petitioned Yin as chancellor—Lin banished Yin to Grand Marshal at Wuchang instead.
entries.literal: Lü Ju heard and panicked—jointly with commanders memorialized recommending Teng Yin as Chancellor—Lin made Yin Grand Marshal replacing Lü Dai at Wuchang.

entries.zh: 據引兵還，使人報胤，欲共廢綝。
entries.en: Lü Ju reversed course and urged Teng Yin to sack Sun Lin together.
entries.literal: Ju led troops back and sent word to Yin—they meant jointly to depose Lin.

entries.zh: 綝聞之，遣從兄慮將兵逆據於江都，使中使敕文欽、劉纂、唐諮等合眾擊據，遣侍中左將軍華融、中書丞丁晏告胤取據，並喻胤宜速去意，胤自以禍及，因留融、晏，勒兵自衛，召典軍揚崇、將軍孫諮，告以綝為亂，迫融等使有書難綝。
entries.en: Lin bottled Ju at Jiangdu while envoys pressured Yin; Yin held Hua Rong hostage, armed his household, and denounced Lin.
entries.literal: Hearing this Lin dispatched his cousin Sun Lü with troops to intercept Ju at Jiangdu; sent inner envoys ordering Wen Qin, Liu Zuan, Tang Zi and others to unite hosts and strike Ju; dispatched Palace Attendant General of the Left Hua Rong and Secretariat Deputy Ding Yan to notify Yin to seize Ju while instructing Yin he must flee swiftly—Yin judged calamity had reached him—thereupon detained Rong and Yan, mobilized troops for self-defense, summoned Army Clerk Yang Chong and general Sun Zi, declared Lin rebel, forced Rong and others to draft letters challenging Lin.

entries.zh: 綝不聽，表言胤反，許將軍劉丞以封爵，使率兵騎急攻圍胤。
entries.en: Lin branded Yin traitor and threw Liu Cheng’s riders at his compound.
entries.literal: Lin refused listening—memorialized that Yin rebelled—promised general Liu Cheng enfeoffment—had him lead horse troops to storm and besiege Yin.

entries.zh: 胤又劫融等使詐詔發兵。
entries.en: He tried to fake an outbreak order through Hua Rong.
entries.literal: Yin again coerced Rong and others to forge edict raising troops.

entries.zh: 融等不從，胤皆殺之。
entries.en: When they balked he cut them down.
entries.literal: Rong and others refused—Yin slew them all.

entries.zh: 〈文士傳曰：華融字德蕤，廣陵江都人。
entries.en: 〈Literary tradition: Hua Rong (Derui) of Jiangdu.
entries.literal: 〈The Wen shi zhuan states: Hua Rong, courtesy name Derui, was a man of Jiangdu in Guangling.

entries.zh: 祖父避亂，居山陰蕊山下。
entries.en: Ancestors fled war to Shanyin hills.
entries.literal: His grandfather fled turmoil and dwelt beneath Ruirui Mountain in Shanyin.

entries.zh: 時皇象亦寓居山陰，吳郡張溫來就像學，欲得所舍。
entries.en: Calligrapher Huang Xiang shared the hamlet—Zhang Wen studied there.
entries.literal: At the time Huang Xiang also lodged in Shanyin—Zhang Wen of Wu commandery came to Xiang for study and sought lodging.

entries.zh: 或告溫曰：「蕊山下有華德蕤者，雖年少，美有令志，可舍也。」
entries.en: Someone told Wen: “Below Ruirui Mountain dwells Hua Derui—young yet fine in aspiration—lodging may be had there.”
entries.literal: Someone told Wen: “Below Ruirui Mountain dwells Hua Derui—young yet fine in aspiration—lodging may be had there.”

entries.zh: 溫遂止融家，朝夕談講。
entries.en: Zhang Wen roomed with Hua Rong and talked night and day.
entries.literal: Wen therefore lodged at Rong’s house—morning and evening they conversed.

entries.zh: 俄而溫為選部尚書，乃擢融為太子庶子，遂知名顯達。
entries.en: When Zhang Wen ran appointments he lifted Hua Rong to tutor staff—fame followed.
entries.literal: Soon Wen became Director of Selection—thereupon promoted Rong to Palace Attendant to the Heir—thus he rose famed.

entries.zh: 融子諝，黃門郎，與融並見害。
entries.en: Son Hua Xu died beside him.
entries.literal: Rong’s son Xu was Gentleman at the Yellow Gates—perished with Rong.

entries.zh: 次子譚，以才辯稱，晉秘書監。〉
entries.en: Younger son Tan won Jin office as library chief.〉
entries.literal: Second son Tan famed for eloquence—became Jin Palace Library Director.〉

entries.zh: 胤顏色不變，談笑若常。
entries.en: Teng Yin faced death smiling.
entries.literal: Yin’s color never changed—talked and laughed as usual.

entries.zh: 或勸胤引兵至蒼龍門，「將士見公出，必皆委綝就公」。
entries.en: Some urged Yin to lead troops to Azure Dragon Gate—“when soldiers see Your Excellency emerge they will surely abandon Lin for you.”
entries.literal: Some urged Yin to lead troops to Azure Dragon Gate—“when soldiers see Your Excellency emerge they will surely abandon Lin for you.”

entries.zh: 時夜已半，胤恃與據期。
entries.en: Midnight—Yin still waited for Lü Ju.
entries.literal: Night was already half spent—Yin relied on his rendezvous with Ju.

entries.zh: 又難舉兵向富，乃約令部曲，說呂侯以在近道，故皆為胤盡死，無離散者。
entries.en: He told his men Ju was close—hold the line—but Ju never came.
entries.literal: Again finding it hard to raise arms toward the palaces (the transmitted graph here is corrupt)—thereupon instructed retainers—explaining Marquis Lü was on nearby roads—therefore all fought to death for Yin without scattering.

entries.zh: 時大風，比曉，據不至。
entries.en: Gale till dawn—no Ju.
entries.literal: Great wind blew—by dawn Ju had not arrived.

entries.zh: 綝兵大會，遂殺及將士數十人，夷胤三族。
entries.en: Sun Lin stormed in—slaughtered Yin’s clan to the third degree.
entries.literal: Lin’s troops massacred—thereupon slew Yin and several tens of officers—extinguished Yin’s three clans.

entries.zh: 〈臣松之以為孫綝雖凶虐，與滕胤宿無嫌隙，胤若且順綝意，出鎮武昌，豈徒免當時之禍，仍將永保元吉，而犯機觸害，自取夷滅，悲夫！〉
entries.en: 〈Pei Songzhi: Yin could have taken Wuchang and lived—instead he chose martyrdom.〉
entries.literal: 〈Your servant Pei Songzhi judges that though Sun Lin was cruel and violent he bore Yin no old grudge—had Yin temporized with Lin’s will and gone out to garrison Wuchang—not only would he have escaped immediate calamity—he might long have kept supreme good fortune—yet he brushed hazard and courted ruin—self-inviting extinction—how tragic!〉

entries.zh: 綝遷大將軍，假節，封永寧侯，負貴倨傲，多行無禮。
entries.en: Sun Lin grabbed Yongning marquisate and swaggered.
entries.literal: Lin advanced to Grand General—credential insignia—enfeoffed marquis of Yongning—bearing rank proud and rude—acting ceaselessly without courtesy.

entries.zh: 初，峻從弟慮與諸葛恪之謀，峻厚之，至右將軍、無難督，授節蓋，平九官事。
entries.en: Sun Lü had backed Ke—Jun raised him to right general and inner-court fixer.
entries.literal: Earlier Jun’s cousin Lü had joined Zhuge Ke’s plot—Jun favored him—to General of the Right, Chief of “No Difficulty,” granting insignia and canopy, adjudicating nine palaces’ affairs.

entries.zh: 綝遇慮薄於峻時，慮怒，與將軍王惇謀殺綝。
entries.en: Lin snubbed Sun Lü—Lü plotted with Wang Dun.
entries.literal: Lin treated Lü more coldly than Jun had—Lü grew angry—conspired with general Wang Dun to murder Lin.

entries.zh: 綝殺惇。
entries.en: Lin executed Wang Dun.
entries.literal: Lin slew Dun.

entries.zh: 慮服藥死。
entries.en: Sun Lü swallowed poison.
entries.literal: Lü took poison and died.

entries.zh: 典軍施正勸綝徵立琅邪王休，綝從之。
entries.en: Shi Zheng talked Lin into king Huima—Sun Xiu.
entries.literal: Army Clerk Shi Zheng urged Lin summon and enthrone Prince Langye Xiu—Lin followed.

entries.zh: 遣宗正楷奉書於休曰：
entries.en: Sun Kai carried summons to Xiu:
entries.literal: Dispatched Director of Imperial Clan Kai bearing letter to Xiu saying:

entries.zh: 綝以薄才，見授大任，不能輔導陛下。
entries.en: The indictment opens with Lin’s sham confession that he failed as regent.
entries.literal: Lin by slender talent received great charge—unable to tutor guidance Your Majesty.

entries.zh: 頃月以來，多所造立。
entries.en: It lists Liang’s alleged novelty-building excesses.
entries.literal: These recent months—many creations established.

entries.zh: 親近劉承，悅於美色；
entries.en: Charges dalliance with Liu Cheng and palace women.
entries.literal: Favored Liu Cheng—delighted in beauty;

entries.zh: 發吏民婦女，料其好者，留於宮內，取兵弟十八已下三千餘人，習之苑中，連日續夜，大小呼嗟，敗壞藏中矛戈五千餘枚，以作戲具。
entries.en: Monstrous catalog of Liang’s alleged orgies and toy navy.
entries.literal: Drafted civilian women—grading fairest—detained inside palace—recruited soldier youths eighteen and below over three thousand—drilled them in park—days linked nights—great and small wailed—ruined armory spears and halberds over five thousand—fashioned play gear.

entries.zh: 朱據先帝舊臣，子男熊、損皆承父之基，以忠議自立，昔殺小主。
entries.en: Claims Zhu heirs murdered princess—distorts truth.
entries.literal: Zhu Ju prior emperor old minister—sons Xiong and Sun both inherited father base—stood by loyal counsel—yet killed junior lord.

entries.zh: 自是大主所創，帝不復精其本未，便殺熊、損，諫不見用。
entries.en: Blames Liang for Zhu executions without hearing Lin’s guilt.
entries.literal: Since then Great Princess authored affair—emperor never examined root tip—then slew Xiong and Sun—remonstrance unused.

entries.zh: 諸下莫不側息。
entries.en: Court terrified into silence.
entries.literal: Underlings none failed to hold breath.

entries.zh: 帝於宮中作小船三百餘艘，成以金銀，師工晝夜不息。
entries.en: Accuses toy fleet waste.
entries.literal: Emperor inside palace built small boats over three hundred—gold and silver clad—artisans day night ceaseless.

entries.zh: 太常全尚，累世受恩，不能督諸宗親，而全端等委城就魏。
entries.en: Smears Quan clan treason.
entries.literal: Chamberlain Quan Shang—generations receiving grace—unable to supervise clan kin—while Quan Duan and others surrendered cities to Wei.

entries.zh: 尚位過重，曾無一言以諫陛下，而與敵往來，使傳國消息，懼必傾危社稷。
entries.en: Claims Quan Shang spied for Wei.
entries.literal: Shang rank overly weighty—never one word remonstrating Majesty—yet trafficked with foe—transmitting state messages—I fear certain overturn of altars.

entries.zh: 推案舊典，運集大王，輒以今月二十七日擒尚斬承。
entries.en: Announces staged arrests— date fixed.
entries.literal: Pushing investigation old precedent—fortune gathers Great King—therefore twenty-seventh of this month seized Shang executed Cheng.

entries.zh: 以帝為會稽王，遣楷牽迎。
entries.en: Deposes Liang to Kuaiji prince—sends escort for Xiu.
entries.literal: Demoting emperor Prince of Kuaiji—dispatching Kai escorting welcome.

entries.zh: 百寮喁喁。
entries.en: Bureaucracy voiced obedience.
entries.literal: Hundred officials murmured assent.

entries.zh: 立任道側。
entries.en: They lined the route for new sovereign.
entries.literal: Stood waiting along roadway.

entries.zh: 綝奉牛酒詣休，休不受，齎詣左將軍張布。
entries.en: Sun Lin’s peace gifts went to Zhang Bu—Xiu declined face-to-face.
entries.literal: Lin carried cattle wine visiting Xiu—Xiu refused—had them forwarded to General of the Left Zhang Bu.

entries.zh: 酒酣，出怨言曰：「徹廢少主時，多勸吾自為之者。
entries.en: Wine heated—bitter words emerged—“When we utterly deposed young sovereign—many urged me take throne myself.
entries.literal: Wine heated—bitter words emerged—“When we utterly deposed young sovereign—many urged me take throne myself.

entries.zh: 吾以陛下賢明，故迎之。
entries.en: Claims he chose Xiu for virtue.
entries.literal: I deemed Your Majesty sagely enlightened—therefore welcomed you.

entries.zh: 帝非我不立，今上禮見拒，是與凡臣無異，當復改圖耳。」
entries.en: Emperor without me would not stand—now courtesy visit refused—no different from common minister—must scheme anew.”
entries.literal: Emperor without me would not stand—now courtesy visit refused—no different from common minister—must scheme anew.”

entries.zh: 布以言聞休，休銜之。
entries.en: Zhang Bu warned Xiu—resentment seeded.
entries.literal: Bu reported speech to Xiu—Xiu nursed grudge.

entries.zh: 鞏其有變，數加賞賜，又復加恩侍中，與綝分省文書。
entries.en: Emperor Xiu feared Lin would bolt—showered honors and busywork to watch him.
entries.literal: Fearing he might stir change—the received character here is probably a scribal error for fear—repeatedly piled rewards—again extended grace as Palace Attendant—sharing Lin province over documents.

entries.zh: 或有告綝懷怨侮上欲圖反者，休執以付綝，綝殺之。
entries.en: Xiu fed Lin a false informer—Lin killed him—proving brutality.
entries.literal: Someone reported Lin nursed grievance insulting superior plotting revolt—Xiu seized accuser handing to Lin—Lin slew him.

entries.zh: 由是愈懼，因孟宗求出屯武昌，休許焉，盡敕所督中營精兵萬餘人，皆令裝載，所取武庫兵器，咸令給與。
entries.en: Lin fled toward Wuchang with elite ten thousand—throne armed him freely.
entries.literal: Thereby Lin grew more fearful—through Meng Zong begged posting garrison Wuchang—Xiu permitted—full order to crack troops over ten thousand he commanded—all directed loaded—armory weapons requested—all granted.

entries.zh: 〈《吳曆》曰：綝求中書兩郎，典知荊州諸軍事，主者奏中書不應外出，休特聽之，其所請求，一皆給與。〉
entries.en: 〈Wu li: Xiu let Lin pick secretaries for Jingzhou staff.〉
entries.literal: 〈Wu li states: Lin begged two Secretariat gentlemen managing Jingzhou military affairs—chief memorialized Secretariat ought not post outward—Xiu specially permitted—all requests granted.〉

entries.zh: 將軍魏邈說休曰「綝居外必有變」，武衛士施朔又告「綝欲反有徵」休密問張布，布與丁奉謀於會殺綝。
entries.en: General Wei Miao advised Sun Xiu, “If Lin remains outside, there will surely be trouble.” Palace guardsman Shi Shuo also reported, “There are signs that Lin intends rebellion.” Xiu secretly questioned Zhang Bu, and Bu plotted with Ding Feng to kill Lin at the banquet.
entries.literal: General Wei Mi advised Xiu—“Lin abroad certain brings mutiny”—Palace guardsman Shi Shuo again reported—“Lin plots revolt with signs”—Xiu secretly questioned Zhang Bu—Bu with Ding Feng plotted banquet killing Lin.

entries.zh: 濮陽興字子元，陳留人也。
entries.en: Puyang Xing, styled Ziyuan, came from Chenliu.
entries.literal: Puyang Xing, courtesy name Ziyuan, was a man of Chenliu.

entries.zh: 父逸，漢末避亂江東，官至長沙太守。
entries.en: His father Yi fled the late-Han turmoil to Jiangdong and became administrator of Changsha.
entries.literal: His father Yi, fleeing chaos at the end of Han, crossed to Jiangdong and rose to Administrator of Changsha.

entries.zh: 逸事見《陸瑁傳》。
entries.en: Yi's career is recorded in the biography of Lu Mao.
entries.literal: Yi's career appears in the biography of Lu Mao.

entries.zh: 興少有士名，孫權時除上虞令，稍遷至尚書左曹，以五官中郎將使蜀，還為會稽太守。
entries.en: Puyang Xing won early fame as a gentleman; under Sun Quan he served as magistrate of Shangyu, rose through the secretariat, went to Shu as envoy, and returned as administrator of Kuaiji.
entries.literal: Xing early gained a scholar's reputation; under Sun Quan he was appointed magistrate of Shangyu, gradually rose to the left bureau of the Masters of Writing, served as General of the Five Offices as envoy to Shu, and on return became Administrator of Kuaiji.

entries.zh: 時琅邪王休居會稽，興深與相結。
entries.en: While Prince Xiu of Langye lived in Kuaiji, Puyang Xing became his close ally.
entries.literal: At that time Prince of Langye Xiu resided in Kuaiji, and Xing formed a deep bond with him.

entries.zh: 及休即位，徵興為太常衛將軍、平軍國事，封外黃侯。
entries.en: When Emperor Xiu ascended the throne, Xing was made chamberlain for ceremonies and guard general, charged with military affairs, and enfeoffed as marquis of Waihuang.
entries.literal: When Xiu took the throne, Xing was summoned as Chamberlain for Ceremonies and Guard General and charged with settling military affairs, enfeoffed as Marquis of Waihuang.

entries.zh: 永安三年260年，都尉嚴密建丹楊湖田，作浦裡塘。
entries.en: Yongan 3 (260): Commandant Yan Mi proposed the Danyang lake-field project and the Puli reclamation.
entries.literal: In the third year of Yongan, 260 CE, Commandant Yan Mi proposed Danyang lake-field works, building Puli Pool.

entries.zh: 綝遣將軍孫耽送亮之國，徙尚於零陵，遷公主於豫章。
entries.en: Sun Lin sent Sun Dan to escort Sun Liang to his fief, banished Quan Shang to Lingling, and moved the princess to Yuzhang.
entries.literal: Lin sent General Sun Dan to escort Liang to his fief, moved Shang to Lingling, and transferred the princess to Yuzhang.

entries.zh: 綝意彌溢，侮慢民神，遂燒大橋頭伍子胥廟，又壞浮屠祠，斬道人。
entries.en: Sun Lin grew ever more arrogant, insulted gods and people, burned the Wu Zixu temple at Daqiao, wrecked Buddhist shrines, and executed Daoist clergy.
entries.literal: Lin's arrogance overflowed; he insulted folk spirits, burned the Wu Zixu temple at Daqiao, destroyed Buddhist shrines, and executed Daoist clergy.

entries.zh: 休既即位，稱草莽臣。
entries.en: Once Emperor Xiu reigned, Sun Lin called himself a rustic subject.
entries.literal: After Xiu took the throne, Lin styled himself a rustic subject.

entries.zh: 詣闕上書曰：「臣伏自省，才非干國，因緣肺腑，位極人臣，傷錦敗駕，罪負彰露，尋愆惟闕，夙夜憂懼。
entries.en: He went to court and wrote, "I reflect that my talent cannot sustain the state, yet kinship raised me to the summit of power; I have torn brocade and wrecked the carriage, and guilt stands clear; day and night I fear my faults.
entries.literal: He went to court and submitted a memorial saying, "Your subject reflects in humility: talent unfit to sustain the state, yet through kinship rose to the summit of ministers; I have torn brocade and wrecked the carriage—guilt stands revealed; reviewing faults I fear day and night.

entries.zh: 臣聞天命棐諶，必就有德，是以幽、厲失度，閡宣中興，陛下聖德，纂承大統，宜得良輔；
entries.en: Heaven aids the sincere and settles on virtue; You and Li lost the way yet Xuan restored the house; Your Majesty inherits the great succession and deserves worthy assistants;
entries.literal: Your subject has heard that Heaven's mandate is aided and sincere and must settle on the virtuous; thus You and Li lost measure yet Xuan restored the house; Your Majesty's sagely virtue inherits the great succession and deserves worthy assistants;

entries.zh: 以協雍熙，雖堯之盛，猶求稷契之佐；
entries.en: to harmonize peace; even Yao sought men like Ji and Qi;
entries.literal: to harmonize peace and glory; even in Yao's greatness he still sought assistants like Ji and Qi;

entries.zh: 以協明聖之德。
entries.en: to match enlightened and sagely virtue.
entries.literal: to harmonize with enlightened and sagely virtue.

entries.zh: 古人有言：『陳力就列，不能者止。』
entries.en: The ancients said, "Offer strength and take your place; if unable, withdraw."
entries.literal: The ancients said, "Offer strength and take your place; if unable, withdraw."

entries.zh: 臣雖自展竭，無益庶政，謹上印綬節鉞，退還田裡，以避賢路。」
entries.en: Though I have exhausted myself I benefit no governance; I return seals, ribbons, and the staff of authority, withdraw to my fields, and yield the path for the worthy."
entries.literal: Though your subject has exhausted himself, he benefits no common governance; I respectfully return seals, ribbons, and credential staff, withdraw to fields and hamlets, and yield the path for the worthy."

entries.zh: 休引見慰喻。
entries.en: Emperor Xiu received him in audience and comforted him.
entries.literal: Xiu received him in audience and comforted him.

entries.zh: 又下詔曰：「朕以不德，守藩於外，值茲際會，群公卿士，暨於朕躬，以奉宗廟。
entries.en: He also issued an edict: "Lacking virtue I guarded a fief abroad until this juncture, when lords and ministers with me uphold the ancestral temple.
entries.literal: He also issued an edict saying, "We lack virtue, guarded a fief abroad, met this juncture, and lords, ministers, and scholars together with Our person uphold the ancestral temple.

entries.zh: 朕用撫然，若涉淵冰。
entries.en: I am apprehensive, as if treading deep ice.
entries.literal: We are apprehensive, as if treading deep ice.

entries.zh: 大將軍忠計內發，扶危定傾，安康社稷，功勳赫然。
entries.en: The grand general's loyal counsel braced peril, steadied the state, and his merit blazed bright.
entries.literal: The Grand General's loyal plan arose within, braced peril and steadied the tipping, brought peace to altars and state, and his merit blazed bright.

entries.zh: 昔漢孝宣踐阼，霍光尊顯，褒德賞功，古今之通義也。
entries.en: When Emperor Xuan of Han took the throne he honored Huo Guang—praising merit is the constant way of past and present.
entries.literal: Formerly when Han's Emperor Xuan ascended the throne, Huo Guang was honored and exalted—praising virtue and rewarding merit is the constant principle of past and present.

entries.zh: 其以大將軍為丞相、荊州牧，食五縣。」
entries.en: Let the grand general be chancellor and governor of Jing with income from five counties."
entries.literal: Let the Grand General be Chancellor and Governor of Jing Province with income from five counties."

entries.zh: 恩為禦史大夫、衛將軍，據右將軍。
entries.en: En was made grandee secretary and guard general; Lü Ju was made general of the right.
entries.literal: En was made Grandee Secretary and Guard General; Ju was made General of the Right.

entries.zh: 皆縣侯。
entries.en: All were enfeoffed as district marquises.
entries.literal: All were enfeoffed as district marquises.

entries.zh: 幹雜號將軍、亭侯。
entries.en: Gan was made a miscellaneous-number general and village marquis.
entries.literal: Gan was made a miscellaneous-number general and village marquis.

entries.zh: 闓亦封亭侯。
entries.en: Kan was also enfeoffed as village marquis.
entries.literal: Kan was also enfeoffed as village marquis.

entries.zh: 綝一門五侯，皆典禁兵，權傾人主，自吳國朝臣未嘗有也。
entries.en: Five marquises in one Sun Lin household, all commanding palace troops—power beyond any Wu minister before.
entries.literal: Lin's household held five marquisates at once, all commanding forbidden troops; power tilted past the sovereign—never before among Wu court ministers.

entries.zh: 永安三年，都尉嚴密建丹楊湖田，作浦裡塘。
entries.en: Yongan 3: Yan Mi pitched the Puli reclamation on Danyang’s lakes.
entries.literal: Third year of Yongan the Commandant Yan Mi proposed Danyang lake-field works—building Puli Pool.

entries.zh: 詔百官會議，咸以為用功多而田不保成，唯興以為可成。
entries.en: Ministers called the dyke a boondoggle—Puyang Xing alone swore it would pay.
entries.literal: Edict ordered hundred offices conference—all judged labor vast while fields might not hold—only Xing deemed it doable.

entries.zh: 遂會諸兵民就作，功傭之費不可勝數，士卒死亡，或自賊殺，百姓大怨之。
entries.en: Corvée swelled—paymasters drowned—troops died in mutiny and accident—the delta cursed Xing’s name.
entries.literal: Thereupon assembled troops and civilians to labor—merit-pay costs beyond counting—soldiers died—some killed each other—commoners bitterly resented.

entries.zh: 興遷為丞相，與休寵臣左將軍張共布相表裡，邦內失望。
entries.en: Raised to chancellor, he teamed with Zhang Bu—Wu groaned at crony rule.
entries.literal: Xing promoted Chancellor—joined Xiu’s favored minister General of the Left Zhang Bu (the transmitted text inserts a stray graph between the two syllables of the name)—mutual inside-out—the state inwardly despaired.

entries.zh: 七年七月，休薨。
entries.en: Sun Xiu died in the seventh month of the seventh year of his era.
entries.literal: Seventh month seventh year Xiu died.

entries.zh: 左典軍萬彧素與烏程侯孫皓善，乃勸興、布，於是興、布廢休適子而迎立皓。
entries.en: Wan Yu talked Xing and Bu into skipping Xiu’s son for Sun Hao.
entries.literal: Left Army Clerk Wan Yu long favored Marquis of Wucheng Sun Hao—thereupon urged Xing and Bu—thus Xing and Bu deposed Xiu’s heir son of proper line and welcomed Hao.

entries.zh: 皓既踐阼，加興侍中，領青州牧。
entries.en: Sun Hao bought loyalty with palace posts and a Qingzhou title.
entries.literal: Once Hao mounted throne he added Xing Palace Attendant concurrent Governor of Qingzhou.

entries.zh: 俄彧譖興、布追悔前事。
entries.en: Wan Yu then whispered that both ministers regretted enthroning him.
entries.literal: Soon Yu slandered Xing and Bu—regretting prior deeds.

entries.zh: 十一月朔入朝，皓因收興、布，徙廣州，道追殺之，夷三族。
entries.en: On the new moon Hao arrested them—marched them toward Guangzhou—had them killed en route—then wiped three degrees of kin.
entries.literal: First day eleventh month court entry—Hao thereupon seized Xing and Bu—banished Guangzhou—agents overtook them on road killing—extinguished three clans.

entries.zh: 綝死時年二十八。
entries.en: Sun Lin perished at twenty-eight.
entries.literal: Lin died aged twenty-eight.

entries.zh: 休耽與峻、綝同族，特除其屬籍，稱之曰故峻、故綝雲​​。
entries.en: Emperor Xiu struck Sun Jun and Sun Lin from the imperial lineage—only “the late Jun” and “the late Lin” remained on the record.
entries.literal: Xiu was ashamed to share a clan with Jun and Lin, so he specially removed them from the clan registers and referred to them as “the late Jun” and “the late Lin,” it is said.

entries.zh: 休又下詔曰：「諸葛恪、滕胤、呂據蓋以無罪為峻、綝兄弟所見殘害，可為痛心，促皆改葬，各為祭奠。
entries.en: Sun Xiu further issued an edict: “Zhuge Ke, Teng Yin, and Lü Ju were all innocent, yet they were cruelly murdered by the brothers Jun and Lin. This is heartbreaking. Hurry to rebury them all properly, and provide sacrifices for each.
entries.literal: Xiu further issued edict: “Zhuge Ke, Teng Yin, and Lü Ju were innocent yet slaughtered by Jun and Lin brothers—utterly heartbreaking—hasten reburial for each with sacrifices.

entries.zh: 其罹恪等事見遠徙者，一切召還。」
entries.en: As for those implicated in the affairs of Ke and the others and sent into distant exile, summon them all back.”
entries.literal: Those who suffered Ke affair and were banished afar—summon all back.”

entries.zh: 永安元年258年十二月丁卯，建業中謠言明會有變。
entries.en: Yongan 1, month 12, day dingmao (258): Jianye rumor warned of trouble at the bright assembly.
entries.literal: In the twelfth month, day dingmao, of the first year of Yongan, 258 CE, Jianye rumor said the bright assembly would bring upheaval.

entries.zh: 綝聞之，不悅。
entries.en: Sun Lin heard and was displeased.
entries.literal: Lin heard it and was displeased.

entries.zh: 夜大風發木揚沙，綝益恐。
entries.en: That night gale winds uprooted trees and raised sand; Lin grew more afraid.
entries.literal: That night a great wind uprooted trees and raised sand; Lin grew more fearful.

entries.zh: 戊辰臘會，綝稱疾。
entries.en: At the year-end assembly on day wuchen Sun Lin claimed illness.
entries.literal: On day wuchen at the year-end assembly Lin claimed illness.

entries.zh: 休強起之，使者十餘輩。
entries.en: Emperor Xiu forced him to attend; more than ten messengers came.
entries.literal: Xiu forced him to rise; over ten messengers came.

entries.zh: 綝不得已，將人，眾止焉。
entries.en: Sun Lin had no choice and was about to bring men when the crowd stopped him.
entries.literal: Lin had no choice and was about to lead men when the crowd stopped him.

entries.zh: 綝曰：「國家屢有命，不可辭。
entries.en: Sun Lin said, "The state has repeatedly commanded; I cannot refuse.
entries.literal: Lin said, "The state has repeatedly commanded; one cannot refuse.

entries.zh: 可豫整兵，令府內起火，因是可得速還。」
entries.en: Ready troops in advance, set fire inside the mansion, and I can return quickly."
entries.literal: You may ready troops in advance, set fire inside the mansion, and thereby return quickly."

entries.zh: 遂入，尋而火起，綝求出，休曰：「外兵自多，不足煩丞相也。」
entries.en: He entered; soon fire rose; Lin begged to leave; Emperor Xiu said, "Outside troops are plentiful—no need to trouble the chancellor."
entries.literal: He then entered; soon fire rose; Lin begged to leave; Xiu said, "Outside troops are plentiful enough—no need to trouble the Chancellor."

entries.zh: 綝起離席，奉、布目左右縛之。
entries.en: Sun Lin rose; Ding Feng and Zhang Bu signaled attendants to bind him.
entries.literal: Lin rose from his seat; Feng and Bu signaled attendants to bind him.

entries.zh: 綝叩首曰：「願徙交州。」
entries.en: Lin kowtowed: "Banish me to Jiaozhou."
entries.literal: Lin kowtowed and said, "I wish to be banished to Jiaozhou."

entries.zh: 休曰：「卿何以不徙滕胤、呂據？」
entries.en: Emperor Xiu said, "Why did you not banish Teng Yin and Lü Ju?"
entries.literal: Xiu said, "Why did you not banish Teng Yin and Lü Ju?"

entries.zh: 綝復曰：「願沒為官奴。」
entries.en: Lin said, "Make me a government slave."
entries.literal: Lin again said, "I wish to be reduced to government slaves."

entries.zh: 休曰：「何不以胤、據為奴乎！」
entries.en: Emperor Xiu said, "Why not make Yin and Ju the slaves!"
entries.literal: Xiu said, "Why not make Yin and Ju the slaves!"

entries.zh: 遂斬之。
entries.en: Then he was beheaded.
entries.literal: Thereupon he was beheaded.

entries.zh: 以綝首令其眾曰：「諸與綝同謀皆赦。」
entries.en: Holding Lin's head he told the host, "All who plotted with Lin are pardoned."
entries.literal: With Lin's head he addressed the host saying, "All who plotted with Lin are pardoned."

entries.zh: 放仗者五千人。
entries.en: Five thousand who laid down weapons were released.
entries.literal: Five thousand who laid down weapons were released.

entries.zh: 闓乘船欲北降，追殺之。
entries.en: Kan tried to flee north by ship; pursuers killed him.
entries.literal: Kan took ship intending to surrender north; pursuers killed him.

entries.zh: 夷三族。
entries.en: Three clans were exterminated.
entries.literal: Three clans were exterminated.

entries.zh: 發孫峻棺，取其印綬，綝其木而埋之，以殺魯育等故也。
entries.en: Sun Jun's coffin was opened, his seals taken, the wood flayed and buried—for the killing of Lu Yu and others.
entries.literal: Sun Jun's coffin was opened, his seals and ribbons taken, the wood flayed and buried—because of the killing of Lu Yu and others.

entries.zh: 諸葛恪
entries.en: Zhuge Ke
entries.literal: Zhuge Ke.

entries.zh: 王蕃字永元，廬江人也。
entries.en: Wang Fan, courtesy name Yongyuan, came from Lujiang commandery.
entries.literal: Wang Fan, courtesy name Yongyuan, was a man of Lujiang.

entries.zh: 博覽多聞，兼通術藝。
entries.en: He was widely read and well informed, and equally at home with astronomy, mathematics, and the technical arts.
entries.literal: He read widely and heard much, and was also versed in technical arts.

entries.zh: 始為尚書郎，去官。
entries.en: He began as a gentleman clerk in the secretariat, then resigned his post.
entries.literal: At first he was gentleman of the masters of writing, then left office.

entries.zh: 孫休即位，與賀邵、薛瑩、虞汜俱為散騎中常侍，皆加駙馬都尉。
entries.en: When Sun Xiu took the throne, Wang Fan, He Shao, Xue Ying, and Yu Si were all named attendants at ease and regular palace attendants, each with the additional title chief commandant of carriage escort.
entries.literal: When Sun Xiu ascended the throne, together with He Shao, Xue Ying, and Yu Si he became attendant at ease and regular palace attendant, and to each was added chief commandant of carriage escort.

entries.zh: 時論清之。
entries.en: Public opinion ranked them among the court's clearest spirits.
entries.literal: Contemporary opinion deemed them pure.

entries.zh: 遣使至蜀，蜀人稱焉，還為夏口監軍。
entries.en: Sent on embassy to Shu, he won high praise there; on his return he was named supervisor of the army at Xiakou.
entries.literal: He was sent as envoy to Shu; the people of Shu praised him, and on return he became supervisor of the army at Xiakou.

entries.zh: 樓玄字承先，沛郡蘄人也。
entries.en: Lou Xuan, courtesy name Chengxian, came from Qi in Pei commandery.
entries.literal: Lou Xuan, courtesy name Chengxian, was a man of Qi in Pei commandery.

entries.zh: 孫休時為監農御史。
entries.en: Under Sun Xiu he served as censor of agriculture.
entries.literal: In Sun Xiu's time he was censor who supervises agriculture.

entries.zh: 孫皓即位，與王蕃、郭逴、萬彧俱為散騎中常侍，出為會稽太守，入為大司農。
entries.en: When Sun Hao took the throne, Lou Xuan joined Wang Fan, Guo Chuo, and Wan Yu as attendants at ease and regular palace attendants, then served as grand administrator of Kuaiji and grand minister of agriculture.
entries.literal: When Sun Hao ascended the throne, together with Wang Fan, Guo Chuo, and Wan Yu he became all attendant at ease and regular palace attendant; he went out as grand administrator of Kuaiji and entered as grand minister of agriculture.

entries.zh: 舊禁中主者自用親近人作之，彧陳親密近職宜用好人，皓因敕有司，求忠清之士，以應其選，遂用玄為宮下鎮禁中候，主殿中事，玄從九卿持刀侍衛，正身率眾，奉法而行，應對切直，數迕皓意，漸見責怒。
entries.en: By old practice, posts inside the forbidden precinct had always gone to favorites.
